The repo currently cannot use the required full-format gate as a reliable closeout signal: `rch exec -- cargo fmt --check` reports unrelated formatting drift and a parse failure in `crates/franken-node/src/repair/proof_carrying_decode.rs`. - No unrelated source behavior changes are mixed into the formatting repair.

title: Epic: Swarm-scale validation orchestration for 256GB/64-core hosts
description:
## Background
franken_node already has workspace pressure sampling, validation broker, proof cache, proof coalescer, RCH adapter, Agent Mail coordination, and Beads tracker workflows. The missing product-level capability is a first-class swarm orchestration layer that lets many agents share a large host and remote workers without cargo storms, duplicate validation, stale claims, or invisible proof debt.

Idea-wizard phase summary: generated 30 improvement ideas around robustness, reliability, performance, ergonomics, and usefulness; top 5 were lease-aware swarm admission, deterministic swarm simulation, proof single-flight/coalescing policy, stale-handoff recovery, and RCH/target-dir utilization guidance. The next 10 added build-slot leases, NUMA/CPU/memory hints, validation evidence packs, bv-driven work selection, per-agent budgets, non-destructive cleanup, timeout taxonomy, fail-closed local fallback, proof attestation, and operator observability. Existing overlap checks found completed workspace-pressure/resource-governor beads (bd-p9mpd.3, bd-p9mpd.5) but no open swarm-scale backlog.

## Goals
- Make multi-agent validation admission explicit, deterministic, and inspectable.
- Use Agent Mail reservations/build slots, Beads state, RCH queue health, proof cache state, and workspace pressure as inputs to one admission decision.
- Prevent duplicate cargo/RCH work by making proof coalescing and stale-lease recovery visible to agents.
- Preserve the AGENTS.md rule that heavy cargo/test/build work uses `rch exec -- ...`.
- Produce unit, property, and mock-free e2e coverage with detailed JSONL logs.

## Non-Goals
- No destructive cleanup policy. Any cleanup proposal must remain advisory unless a separate explicitly approved cleanup mode exists.
- No replacement for Agent Mail or Beads. This layer consumes their state and improves operator decisions.
- No local cargo fallback when RCH is required by repo policy.

## Success Criteria
- Agents can ask whether to start a validation lane and receive a stable decision: run, coalesce, defer, or hand off.
- Decisions explain exact blockers and safe next actions.
- A mock-free swarm scenario demonstrates multiple agents converging on one proof result instead of duplicating work.
- `br ready --json` exposes at least one granular child task from this epic after dependency refinement.
close_reason: Completed swarm-scale validation orchestration epic. Child beads bd-0x4fy.1 through bd-0x4fy.10 are closed with evidence commits: eb548618b contract, 794e71463 fixtures, e339c2035 planner, 034663124 proof coalescing, 872cc7a9c stale handoff, 420864218 RCH target-dir hints, 49cecd4c3 readiness/doctor surfacing, 0c92fde77 invariant tests, 4f0dbc9d9 mock-free transcript harness, and 20d15b773 evidence-pack checker. br ready --json exposed only the parent epic after .10; br show bd-0x4fy --json confirms all ten parent-child dependents are closed.

title: Design swarm validation admission contract
description:
## What
Define the product contract for a swarm validation admission decision. The contract must name the decision states (`run`, `coalesce`, `defer`, `handoff`, `blocked`), required inputs, output JSON shape, human summary rules, and event codes.

## Why
Many agents currently infer whether to start cargo/RCH work from scattered signals: `br`, `bv`, Agent Mail reservations, RCH status, proof cache state, and workspace pressure. A stable contract reduces duplicate validation and makes the system easier to operate under 256GB/64-core multi-agent load.

## How
Use existing seams rather than inventing a parallel subsystem: `ops::workspace_pressure_policy`, `ops::validation_planner`, `ops::validation_proof_coalescer`, `ops::rch_adapter`, `ops::validation_readiness`, `ops::swarm_handoff`, and `ops::swarm_bead_templates`. Document how each input contributes to the decision and which missing input forces fail-closed behavior.

## Risks
- Over-broad scope could duplicate existing workspace-pressure work. Keep this to the swarm admission contract and reference completed bd-p9mpd.3/bd-p9mpd.5 instead of redoing them.
- Output drift will break automation, so JSON fields must be versioned.

## Success Criteria
- A self-contained spec or code-level contract exists for admission inputs/outputs.
- The contract includes unit-testable fixture cases for all decision states.
- No cargo-heavy validation is needed for this design bead; verify with `git diff --check` and relevant script checks if docs/spec files are touched.
close_reason: Completed: added docs/specs/swarm_validation_admission.md with versioned input/policy/decision schemas, five admission states, reason/event/action matrix, fail-closed rules, source-only fixture matrix, and consumer rules. Validation: git diff --check passed; ASCII check passed; contract grep confirmed five states/schema/event codes; ubs docs/specs/swarm_validation_admission.md exited 0 but reported no recognizable language for Markdown.

title: Add swarm validation evidence-pack checker and closeout contract
description:
## What
Create the evidence-pack contract and checker for swarm validation work: expected JSONL transcript fields, proof-key linkage, RCH command capture, Beads id/thread id linkage, and closeout summary requirements.

## Why
This repo treats validation evidence as part of done. A swarm scheduler without a closeout contract can still leave future agents guessing whether a proof was run, coalesced, deferred, or blocked.

## How
Use existing validation-closeout and operator-transcript patterns where possible. The checker should be deterministic and path-scoped. It should fail closed on missing bead id, missing RCH command, missing decision reason code, missing proof key for coalesced/run cases, or undocumented blocker for defer/blocked cases.

## Risks
- A checker that is too strict can block useful partial evidence. Include explicit partial/blocker states with required fields.
- A checker that is too loose can bless incomplete validation. Require the first real blocker string when proof is not green.

## Success Criteria
- Checker tests cover green proof, coalesced proof, deferred proof, blocked proof, and malformed transcript.
- Closeout guidance requires Agent Mail thread id and Beads id.
- The checker can be run without cargo; any Rust-side companion tests still use `rch exec -- ...`.
close_reason: Completed deterministic swarm validation evidence-pack checker, tests, and closeout contract docs. title: Implement deterministic swarm admission fixtures
description:
## What
Add deterministic fixture structures for swarm admission inputs: active agents, Agent Mail reservations/build slots, Beads issue state, RCH queue and worker health, proof-cache hits, proof-coalescer in-flight leases, target-dir pressure, memory/CPU load, and policy profile.

## Why
The admission policy must be testable without live `pgrep`, live RCH workers, or mutable Agent Mail state. Fixture-first inputs keep unit tests fast and prevent host-specific nondeterminism.

## How
Extend or compose existing ops types from workspace-pressure and validation-planner surfaces. Live adapters should stay narrow; fixture mode should construct the same canonical input shape. Cap all vectors/maps and include unavailable-signal reasons.

## Risks
- Duplicating completed workspace-pressure sampler fields would create drift. Reuse or reference existing structs wherever possible.
- Host-specific timestamps or path ordering can make goldens flaky; normalize ordering and inject time.

## Success Criteria
- Fixture inputs cover empty swarm, single agent, saturated RCH queue, duplicate proof request, stale lease, high memory pressure, and missing Agent Mail state.
- JSON serialization is stable and schema-versioned.
- Focused tests are runnable through `rch exec -- cargo test -p frankenengine-node <target>` when cargo validation is needed.

title: Implement lease-aware swarm validation admission planner
description:
## What
Implement the decision engine that maps deterministic swarm inputs to `run`, `coalesce`, `defer`, `handoff`, or `blocked`.

## Why
Agents need one authoritative answer before starting expensive validation. The planner should stop duplicate RCH jobs, respect reservations, and preserve exact blocker strings for closeout.

## How
Place the policy near `ops::validation_planner` or a narrowly named ops module. Use proof-cache/coalescer state to prefer `coalesce` when an equivalent proof is already running. Use Agent Mail reservations/build slots to avoid conflicting edit/validation lanes. Use workspace pressure and RCH status to choose `defer` rather than local cargo fallback.

## Risks
- Over-eager `run` decisions can recreate cargo storms. Fail closed when critical inputs are stale or unavailable.
- Over-eager `defer` decisions can halt progress. Include clear safe next actions and coalescing opportunities.

## Success Criteria
- Every decision state has a deterministic fixture test.
- Output includes reason code, human summary, safe command shape, input freshness, and coalescing target when relevant.
- No decision recommends bare local cargo for this repo.
close_reason: Implemented lease-aware swarm validation admission planner with deterministic decision fixtures; validated with rch fmt/check/clippy, focused rch test compile, ubs, and git diff --check

title: Expose proof single-flight coalescing for agent swarms
description:
## What
Make proof single-flight/coalescing decisions visible to agents: when an equivalent validation proof is already in flight, the admission layer should return the existing proof key, owner, freshness, expected wait, and safe follow-up action.

## Why
The repo already has proof coalescer and cache concepts, but agents still launch duplicate validations when the evidence is not surfaced at the coordination layer. This wastes remote workers and hides proof debt.

## How
Integrate with `ops::validation_proof_coalescer` and `ops::validation_proof_cache`. Reuse existing lease/fencing protections, including the completed TOCTOU fix history for validation proof work stealing. Add stable reason codes such as `SWARM-COALESCE-IN-FLIGHT`, `SWARM-CACHE-HIT`, and `SWARM-STALE-LEASE`.

## Risks
- Exposing an in-flight proof without fencing can mislead agents if the owner dies. Include stale thresholds and handoff guidance.
- Cache hits must be policy/freshness aware; never coalesce across incompatible feature/profile inputs.

## Success Criteria
- Equivalent proof requests coalesce deterministically.
- Stale or incompatible proof requests fail closed or hand off rather than silently reusing bad evidence.
- Tests cover same-hash, different-profile, expired-proof, owner-dead, and completed-cache-hit cases.
close_reason: Completed proof single-flight coalescing admission: equivalent in-flight proofs now surface owner/wait/action metadata, fresh cache hits coalesce, stale leases hand off, and incompatible/expired/corrupt proof signals fail closed with stable SWARM-* reason codes. Validated with rch fmt/check/clippy/focused test plus git diff --check and UBS.

title: Implement stale-agent handoff and claim recovery policy
description:
## What
Define and implement a non-destructive handoff policy for stale agent claims, stale proof leases, and abandoned validation work.

## Why
Large swarms stall when a bead, proof lane, or file reservation appears owned but the owning agent is inactive. The user explicitly wants stalled work reopened or made actionable without waiting in communication purgatory.

## How
Build on Agent Mail last-active data, Beads status/assignee/updated_at, file reservation expiry, build-slot leases, and validation coalescer leases. The policy should return `handoff` only when objective inactivity thresholds and lease/fencing rules agree. It must emit exact evidence used for handoff and should prefer comments/reopen over destructive state edits.

## Risks
- False-positive handoff can disrupt an active agent. Require multiple stale signals and preserve audit trail.
- Tooling must not delete files, clear reservations forcibly, or reset git state.

## Success Criteria
- Fixture tests cover active owner, recently inactive owner, expired reservation, stale proof lease, and conflicting signals.
- Handoff output names exact safe next commands (`br update`, Agent Mail reply, or wait), not destructive cleanup.
- Agent Mail acknowledgement requirements and Beads comments are preserved in the workflow.
close_reason: Implemented stale-agent handoff and claim recovery policy with validation proof-lease states, safe reopen commands, readiness summaries, replay/runbook fixtures, and focused RCH validation output; rch wrappers required cancellation after green cargo output.

title: Plan RCH target-dir and hardware utilization hints for swarms
description:
## What
Design and implement advisory hints for choosing `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, RCH priority, worker requirements, build-slot names, and validation lane budgets on a 256GB/64-core shared host.

## Why
The existing workflow depends on `rch exec -- ...`, but agents still collide on target directories or launch broad jobs when a narrow target would do. Better hints improve throughput without violating repo policy.

## How
Use the swarm admission inputs plus existing RCH adapter/status data. Prefer narrow validation scopes, unique target dirs for diagnostic probes, and coalescing with existing proof work. Hints must be advisory and must never recommend bare cargo for heavy work in this repo.

## Risks
- Hard-coding machine assumptions could make the feature brittle. Express hardware as inputs and defaults, not constants.
- Too many target dirs can create disk pressure; pair hints with workspace-pressure signals.

## Success Criteria
- Output includes stable hint fields for target-dir strategy, worker requirements, priority, and coalescing key.
- Tests cover high memory headroom, disk pressure, RCH saturated, and narrow diagnostic probe cases.
- Documentation explains how hints preserve AGENTS.md RCH requirements.
close_reason: Implemented stable RCH target-dir and hardware utilization hints with focused public integration coverage; validated with RCH fmt/check/clippy/test and RCH UBS. Broad inline cfg test remains blocked by unrelated existing feature/import failures.

title: Surface swarm admission decisions in doctor and validation readiness
description:
## What
Expose swarm admission decisions through stable JSON and concise human output in doctor/workspace-pressure or validation-readiness surfaces.

## Why
Agents and operators need to see why validation should run, coalesce, defer, hand off, or remain blocked. Without a visible surface, the admission planner cannot guide real workflows.

## How
Extend existing `ops::doctor`, `ops::workspace_pressure_policy`, or `ops::validation_readiness` surfaces rather than adding an unrelated command. Include schema version, decision, reason code, input freshness, proof key, owner/handoff evidence when present, and safe next action.

## Risks
- Human output can become noisy. Keep human text compact and put full diagnostics in JSON.
- JSON contract must be stable and golden-tested.

## Success Criteria
- JSON fixtures exist for run, coalesce, defer, handoff, blocked, and stale-input cases.
- Human output is concise and never recommends destructive cleanup or local cargo fallback.
- Event codes are documented and test-covered.

title: Unit and property tests for swarm admission invariants
description:
## What
Add focused unit/property tests for swarm admission invariants.

## Why
The admission planner is a safety-critical coordinator: a small regression can create duplicate RCH work, bless stale proof evidence, or tell an agent to run local cargo against repo policy. Fast deterministic tests are the cheapest guardrail.

## Coverage Requirements
- Empty input fails closed with a missing-input reason.
- Active equivalent proof returns `coalesce`, not `run`.
- Stale proof lease returns `handoff` or `blocked` with exact evidence.
- Saturated RCH or high workspace pressure returns `defer`, never bare local cargo.
- Agent Mail reservation conflict returns `blocked` with holder details.
- Different feature/profile/command hashes never coalesce.
- Bounded list/map caps preserve newest or most relevant diagnostics deterministically.

## Risks
- Fixture-only coverage can drift from live adapters; include at least one adapter-shape regression when implementation exposes it.
- Property tests must keep generated data bounded so they do not become a new resource-pressure source.

## Logging
Tests should log the fixture name, decision, reason code, coalescing key, and safe next action when run with `--nocapture`.

## Success Criteria
- Tests run through a focused `rch exec -- cargo test -p frankenengine-node <swarm admission target>` command.
- Failures preserve the exact decision and reason-code mismatch.
- No broad all-target cargo command is required unless implementation touches shared exports.

title: Mock-free e2e swarm validation transcript harness
description:
## What
Build a mock-free e2e scenario that exercises multiple agent intents converging on one validation proof, with detailed transcript and JSONL evidence.

## Why
The most important user-facing property is not just that a planner function returns the right enum. It is that multiple agents can coordinate under real workflow pressure and end up with one audit trail, one proof lane, and no duplicate heavy cargo/RCH jobs.

## Scenarios
- Agent A starts a focused RCH validation lane.
- Agent B requests the same proof and receives `coalesce` with the existing proof key.
- Agent C hits an edit reservation conflict and receives `blocked` with holder details.
- Agent D observes a stale proof lease and receives `handoff` with safe recovery steps.
- RCH saturation or workspace pressure returns `defer` with no local cargo fallback.

## Risks
- A fully live multi-agent test can become flaky. Prefer deterministic local fixture state for coordination inputs, but keep critical behavior faithful to real Agent Mail/Beads/RCH contracts.
- Shell-script-only mocks can lie about the real product surface. Avoid fake-success validation for the critical proof path.

## Logging
Capture command, bead id, agent identity, decision, reason code, proof key, reservation/build-slot evidence, RCH status class, and final closeout recommendation.

## Success Criteria
- The harness uses real repo coordination abstractions or deterministic local fixture state, not shell-script-only mocks for critical behavior.
- It emits a stable JSONL transcript suitable for a golden or checker script.
- Validation command is focused and explicitly offloaded through `rch exec -- ...` when Rust tests are run.

title: [SEC] migration: numeric comparison boundaries fail-open on NaN/infinity values
description:
File: dgis_migration_gate.rs:135,192-197

**Threat**: Migration gate threshold comparisons using >= and <= can fail-open when cascade_risk_delta contains NaN or infinity values, bypassing safety checks and allowing dangerous migrations.

**Lines**:
- Line 135: delta.cascade_risk_delta >= thresholds.max_cascade_risk_delta fails-open on NaN 
- Lines 192-197: lower_risk_than_blocked() comparisons can bypass on NaN/infinity
- Line 133-134: is_finite() checks exist but comparisons still proceed

**Impact**:
- Migration safety gates bypassed via NaN injection
- Dangerous migrations approved when they should be blocked  
- Fail-open behavior violates security-critical boundary checks

**Fix**: Use fail-closed numeric comparisons: reject any migration with non-finite risk values before threshold evaluation. Add explicit NaN/infinity validation with migration rejection on boundary condition violations.

title: [10.9] Build trust economics dashboard with attacker-ROI deltas.
description:
## [10.9] Build trust economics dashboard with attacker-ROI deltas

### Why This Exists

Section 9A.9 (Economic Trust Layer) and Section 9B.9 (decision-theoretic expected-loss and robust posterior updates) require that franken_node's security value proposition be quantified in economic terms, not just binary pass/fail security assessments. Decision-makers (CISOs, engineering leads) need to see how much harder and more expensive attacks become with franken_node compared to baseline Node.js or Bun. Threshold-based security ("we block X% of attacks") is insufficient — what matters is the economic impact: attacker cost amplification, defender cost reduction, and the ROI of trust policy investments. This dashboard makes the economic case with quantified models.

### What It Must Do

Build a trust economics dashboard that presents attacker-ROI analysis and trust policy optimization recommendations:

- **Attack-cost amplification metrics**: For each attack category (credential exfiltration, privilege escalation, supply-chain compromise, policy evasion, data exfiltration), compute the estimated attacker cost under three scenarios: (a) baseline Node.js (no hardening), (b) Bun (default security), (c) franken_node (full trust verification). Cost is measured in: time (hours of attacker effort), compute (resources required), tooling (sophistication of required tools), and detection risk (probability of being caught). The dashboard shows the amplification factor (franken_node cost / baseline cost) for each category.
- **Privilege-risk pricing curves**: For each trust privilege level (unrestricted, standard, restricted, quarantined), compute the risk-adjusted cost of granting that privilege. Higher privilege = higher potential damage = higher implicit price. Curves show how trust policy configuration affects the privilege-risk balance.
- **Trust policy tuning recommendations**: Based on the economic model, recommend trust policy configurations that optimize for specific objectives: minimize expected loss, maximize attacker cost, minimize defender operational overhead, or balance all three. Recommendations include: specific policy parameter values, expected economic impact, and confidence intervals.
- **Economic models**: All metrics are computed from explicit economic models, not heuristic thresholds. Models are documented, versioned, and parameterizable. Model inputs include: attack frequency estimates (from adversarial campaign data, bd-9is), defense effectiveness measurements (from benchmark data, bd-f5d), and operational cost measurements (from telemetry).
- **Decision-theoretic framing**: Per Section 9B.9, the dashboard uses expected-loss calculations with robust posterior updates. As new adversarial campaign results and telemetry data arrive, the economic model updates its estimates. The dashboard shows confidence intervals and model uncertainty, not just point estimates.
- **Comparative visualization**: Side-by-side comparison of economic posture across Node.js, Bun, and franken_node with configurable trust policies. Visualizations include: attack-cost radar charts, privilege-risk curves, expected-loss timelines, and policy sensitivity analysis.

### Acceptance Criteria

1. Attack-cost amplification metrics are computed for at least five attack categories with three-way comparison (Node.js baseline, Bun, franken_node).
2. Amplification factors are derived from explicit economic models with documented assumptions and parameterizable inputs.
3. Privilege-risk pricing curves are generated for at least four trust privilege levels with configurable policy parameters.
4. Trust policy tuning recommendations are generated with specific parameter values, expected economic impact, and confidence intervals.
5. Economic models use decision-theoretic expected-loss calculations with posterior updates from incoming data.
6. Dashboard data is available via structured JSON API; a reference visualization is provided.
7. Model versioning ensures that metric changes are attributable to model updates vs. data updates; model changelog is maintained.
8. A verification script validates model consistency, data freshness, and recommendation quality against test scenarios.

### Key Dependencies

- Adversarial campaign runner (bd-9is) for attack frequency and defense effectiveness data
- Benchmark infrastructure (bd-f5d) for performance and resilience measurements
- Telemetry namespace (10.13) for operational cost measurements
- Trust policy infrastructure (10.4, 10.5) for privilege level definitions

### Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests for economic model calculations, posterior updates, and recommendation generation.
- Integration test with synthetic attack/defense data verifying end-to-end metric computation.
- Verification script (`scripts/check_trust_economics.py`) with `--json` and `self_test()`.
- Model updates logged at INFO; recommendation changes logged at WARN; data freshness issues logged at ERROR.

### Expected Artifacts

- `docs/specs/section_10_9/bd-10c_contract.md` — trust economics specification and model documentation
- `scripts/check_trust_economics.py` — verification script
- `tests/test_check_trust_economics.py` — unit tests
- `fixtures/economic-models/` — model definitions and test scenarios
- `artifacts/section_10_9/bd-10c/verification_evidence.json`
- `artifacts/section_10_9/bd-10c/verification_summary.md`
acceptance_criteria:
1. Dashboard displays attacker-ROI deltas: estimated cost-to-compromise franken_node vs. Node.js across at least 5 attack categories (supply-chain, privilege escalation, resource exhaustion, data exfiltration, denial of service).
2. Per Section 3 category targets: dashboard highlights where franken_node achieves >= 10x compromise reduction (cost increase for attacker).
3. Metrics are computed from empirical data: adversarial campaign results (bd-9is), fuzz findings, CVE analysis, and audit results.
4. Dashboard includes time-series views showing how attacker-ROI evolves across releases.
5. Data sources are documented and each metric includes a methodology note explaining how the ROI delta was calculated.
6. Dashboard is generated as a static HTML report (no external runtime dependencies) from a structured JSON data source under artifacts/.
7. Per Section 9F moonshot bets: dashboard includes a 'trust economics summary' section quantifying the aggregate security value proposition with reproducible calculations.

title: [REVIEW] Remote computation registry count cap ignores schema byte size
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/remote/computation_registry.rs:181,187,242,264,286,305
PATTERN: bounded-capacity hardening bypass / Vec or map growth bounded only by count
WHY IT'S A BUG: RegistryCatalog accepts Vec<ComputationEntry> values whose description, input_schema, and output_schema strings are caller-supplied. from_catalog iterates the already-deserialized vector and register_computation only rejects empty schemas and caps the number of entries at MAX_COMPUTATION_ENTRIES. A catalog with a small number of huge schema strings, or up to 4096 large entries, can force unbounded memory retention in the registry even though the code advertises a capacity boundary.
SUGGESTED FIX: add validated per-entry and total byte budgets for description/input_schema/output_schema before normalization/insertion, reject over-limit catalogs fail-closed, and add regressions for one huge schema plus many near-limit schemas. If catalogs are loaded from disk/JSON, apply the budget at the parser boundary where possible.
EVIDENCE: nl -ba shows from_catalog consumes catalog.entries at lines 181-189, register_computation only checks empty schema fields at 264-275 and entry count at 286-302 before self.entries.insert(...) at 305-306. git blame -L236,292 points these validation paths to af1a268fa/128d21a5d/976b4f583 with no byte-size guard.
close_reason: Already fixed in 4380f152: remote computation registry enforces per-field and aggregate text byte budgets with regressions.

title: [FINAL-SEC-REVIEW] ops rotate-key (69af4957) is a no-op that lies to operators — no signer update, no ledger append, no key fence
description:
**Commit:** 69af4957 "feat(ops): add key rotation subcommand for crypto agility (bd-2xya9 Phase 1)"

**Severity:** P1. The 'rotate-key' command is a no-op disguised as a successful rotation. It announces success to the operator while leaving every signer config and every previously-signed receipt verifiable under the OLD compromised key.

**Evidence — main.rs:6595-6665, function `handle_ops_rotate_key`:**

1. **Evidence ledger is NEVER mutated.** Line 6619-6641 constructs an `EvidenceEntry` describing the rotation event, but line 6643 carries the comment:
   `// TODO Phase 2: Actually update the configured signer and add the evidence entry to ledger`
   The local `evidence_entry` variable is dropped when the function returns. No `ledger.append(...)` call exists in this function. The hash-chain'd evidence ledger has zero record of the 'rotation' having occurred.

2. **No signer config is updated.** The function reads a key from disk, computes its fingerprint, and returns. No global signer state, no `SigningKey` registry, no module that produces signatures (decision_receipt, evidence_ledger sign_evidence_entry, supply_chain artifact_signing, etc.) is touched. The next signing operation continues to use whatever the previous key was.

3. **Old-key signatures are not fenced.** There is no revocation-list update, no key-id rotation epoch bump, no consumer of the 'rotation event' that would reject signatures from the old fingerprint after rotation. An attacker holding the compromised old key continues forging valid signatures indefinitely.

4. **Old-key fingerprint is a literal placeholder string.** Line 6613:
   `let old_key_fingerprint = "phase1-placeholder".to_string();`
   The reported 'old_key_fingerprint' is not even the actual key being rotated FROM — it's a hardcoded sentinel. So the rotation event payload (even if it were appended) would be useless for incident response or audit reconstruction.

5. **The user-facing output lies.** Line 6658:
   `println!("Key rotation completed successfully");`
   Nothing was rotated. The success line is unconditional on reading the new key file successfully — it's reachable even though the actual rotation never happened.

6. **Even if appended, the evidence entry is unsigned.** Line 6639:
   `signature: String::new(), // Phase 1 doesn't sign evidence entries`
   The evidence ledger's `verify_evidence_entry` path expects ed25519 signatures. An unsigned rotation entry would either be rejected on read or break the hash chain — meaning the audit trail is broken even on the hypothetical success path.

**Threat model impact:**

- An operator with a compromised signing key runs `franken-node ops rotate-key --new-key /path/to/new-key` to recover from the compromise.
- The CLI prints 'Key rotation completed successfully' and the operator believes the compromise is contained.
- Behind the scenes: nothing has rotated. The compromised key continues to sign decision receipts, evidence entries, fleet quarantine receipts, etc. The attacker's forgery capability is undiminished.
- This is strictly worse than not having rotation at all — operators get false confidence that the threat is contained while the breach continues.

**Required remediation (not part of this bead — file follow-ups):**

1. The Phase 1 command should refuse to print 'rotation completed' when no actual rotation occurred. Either:
   (a) Mark the subcommand as `--phase=preview` / `--dry-run` until Phase 2 lands, OR
   (b) Print a loud warning: 'WARNING: Phase 1 rotate-key validates the key file but does NOT update any signer config. The old key remains active. See bd-2xya9 Phase 2.' OR
   (c) Hide the subcommand behind a feature flag (e.g., `--features=key-rotation-preview`) so it's not callable from a stable build.

2. Phase 2 must:
   (a) Read the actual current signing key (not return a placeholder fingerprint).
   (b) Append the rotation event to the evidence ledger atomically (`ledger.append(...)`).
   (c) Sign the rotation entry with the OLD key (last act of the old key's authority).
   (d) Update the configured signer to the NEW key.
   (e) Add the OLD key fingerprint to a fence list so post-rotation verifications reject signatures bound to the old key, OR introduce a key-rotation epoch bump that decision_receipt verifiers honor.

**Verification command:**
```bash
git show 69af4957 -- crates/franken-node/src/main.rs | grep -B2 -A40 'fn handle_ops_rotate_key'
grep -n 'rotation_event_id\|phase1-placeholder\|new_key_fingerprint' crates/franken-node/src/main.rs
```

title: [10.14] Implement append-only marker stream for high-impact control events with dense sequence invariant checks.
description:
## Why This Exists

The append-only marker stream is the tamper-evident audit log for high-impact control events in the 9J runtime. Every epoch transition, policy change, security decision, and remote effect commitment is recorded as a marker in a dense, hash-chained sequence. This provides the evidence backbone for runtime invariant #8 (evidence-by-default: every control action has a recorded marker) and the integrity foundation for fork detection (bd-xwk5), MMR proofs (bd-1dar), and efficient lookup (bd-129f). Without a dense, hash-chained marker stream, there is no way to prove that the control history is complete and untampered -- gaps or hash-chain breaks would indicate either data loss or malicious modification. The root pointer publication (bd-nwhn) depends on this stream as the data structure it points to.

## What This Must Do

1. Implement `MarkerStream` in `src/control_plane/marker_stream.rs` as an append-only data structure where each marker contains: `(sequence_number: u64, timestamp: Timestamp, event_type: MarkerEventType, payload: Vec<u8>, prev_hash: Hash, self_hash: Hash)`.
2. Enforce dense sequence invariant: `marker[n].sequence_number == marker[n-1].sequence_number + 1` for all n > 0. Any attempt to append with a gap or duplicate sequence number is rejected with `SequenceInvariantError`.
3. Enforce hash-chain invariant: `marker[n].prev_hash == marker[n-1].self_hash` for all n > 0. Broken chains are rejected with `HashChainError`.
4. Implement `self_hash` computation as `H(sequence_number || timestamp || event_type || payload || prev_hash)` using a specified hash function (SHA-256).
5. Implement torn-tail recovery: on startup, detect and truncate any partially-written marker at the end of the stream. Recovery is deterministic: the same incomplete write always produces the same recovery outcome. Log `MARKER_TORN_TAIL_RECOVERED` with the truncated sequence number.
6. On invariant break detection (via verification scan), emit `MARKER_INVARIANT_BREAK` hard alert with the exact sequence position, expected values, and actual values.
7. Implement `verify_stream_integrity(start: u64, end: u64) -> Result<(), IntegrityError>` that validates dense sequence and hash-chain invariants over a range.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Marker stream is append-only with dense sequence and hash-chain invariants; torn-tail recovery is deterministic; invariant breaks trigger hard alert.
- Appending 10,000 markers produces a dense sequence from 0 to 9,999 with valid hash chains.
- Attempting to append with sequence gap returns `SequenceInvariantError`.
- Attempting to append with wrong `prev_hash` returns `HashChainError`.
- Torn-tail recovery after simulated crash during write truncates exactly the incomplete marker and no more.
- `verify_stream_integrity` over the full stream succeeds after clean appends and fails after injected corruption.
- Hard alert fires on detected invariant break with full diagnostic context.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: append single marker; append 10,000 markers with dense sequence check; gap rejection; hash-chain break rejection; torn-tail recovery with various truncation points; integrity verification pass and fail cases.
- Integration tests: concurrent appends (serialized by design, test that concurrency doesn't corrupt); crash-recovery cycle with torn-tail; stream integrity after 100,000 appends.
- Conformance tests: `tests/conformance/marker_stream_invariants.rs` -- normative tests for all invariants.
- Structured logs: `MARKER_APPENDED` (seq, event_type, self_hash_prefix, trace_id), `MARKER_TORN_TAIL_RECOVERED` (truncated_seq, recovered_tail_seq, trace_id), `MARKER_INVARIANT_BREAK` (seq, expected_hash, actual_hash, invariant_type, trace_id), `MARKER_INTEGRITY_VERIFIED` (start_seq, end_seq, marker_count, trace_id).

## Expected Artifacts

- `src/control_plane/marker_stream.rs` -- marker stream implementation
- `tests/conformance/marker_stream_invariants.rs` -- normative conformance tests
- `artifacts/10.14/marker_stream_integrity_report.json` -- integrity report from conformance run
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-126h/verification_evidence.json` -- machine-readable CI/release gate evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-126h/verification_summary.md` -- human-readable verification summary

## Dependencies

- Upstream: none (root of marker subsystem dependency chain).
- Downstream: bd-129f (O(1)/O(log N) marker lookup), bd-xwk5 (fork/divergence detection), bd-1dar (MMR checkpoints and proofs), bd-nwhn (root pointer publication), bd-2ms (10.10 rollback/fork detection), bd-3epz (section gate), bd-5rh (section gate).

title: Implement real rollback proof verification instead of structural-only check (connector/operator_intelligence.rs:227)
close_reason: Added content_hash() method and rollback_spec format verification to RollbackProof::verify(). Now checks rollback_spec matches format rollback:{action_spec}.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/connector/operator_intelligence.rs around line 226-241
METHOD: RollbackProof::verify() -> Result<bool, OIError>

CURRENT CODE:
  pub fn verify(&self) -> Result<bool, OIError> {
      // In a real system, this would execute the rollback and compare hashes.
      // Here we verify structural soundness: both hashes present and specs non-empty.
      if self.action_spec.is_empty() { ... error ... }
      if self.rollback_spec.is_empty() { ... error ... }
      if ct_eq_bytes(&self.pre_state_hash, &self.post_state_hash) { ... error ... }
      Ok(true)
  }

PROBLEM: verify() always returns Ok(true) as long as fields are non-empty and hashes differ. It never actually verifies that applying rollback_spec to post_state_hash produces pre_state_hash, which is the claimed invariant INV-OIR-ROLLBACK-SOUND. This means any structurally-valid-looking proof passes, regardless of whether the rollback would actually work.

REQUIRED FIX: Implement actual verification:
  1. Apply rollback_spec to the post_state to produce a candidate pre-state
  2. Hash the candidate pre-state
  3. Compare candidate hash to self.pre_state_hash using ct_eq_bytes
  4. Only return Ok(true) if they match

CONSIDERATIONS:
- Need to understand the rollback execution model: what does action_spec/rollback_spec contain? Is it a list of operations? A diff? A state snapshot?
- The "execute the rollback" step may require access to the actual state store or a sandbox
- If full execution is too expensive for verification, consider at minimum verifying:
  a. Cryptographic binding between spec and hashes (sign the spec with the state hash)
  b. Structural validation that the rollback spec is the inverse of the action spec
- Check what calls verify() — if it is called in hot paths, execution-based verification may need to be async or deferred
- The existing ct_eq_bytes check (pre != post) is good — keep it as a fast-path rejection
- Consider adding a verification_depth parameter: structural (current), cryptographic, or full-execution

INVARIANTS AFFECTED: INV-OIR-ROLLBACK-SOUND

title: [10.14] Implement O(1) marker lookup by sequence and O(log N) timestamp-to-sequence search.
description:
## Why This Exists

Efficient marker lookup is essential for real-time control-plane operations that must query the marker stream under latency constraints. O(1) lookup by sequence number enables instant access to any marker by its position, while O(log N) timestamp-to-sequence search enables temporal queries like "find the marker active at time T." Without these complexity guarantees, marker-dependent operations (divergence detection, proof generation, incident investigation) degrade to O(N) scans that become unusable as the marker stream grows. This bead provides the access layer that makes the marker stream (bd-126h) operationally viable at scale, directly supporting runtime invariant #9 (deterministic verification gates must complete within bounded time).

## What This Must Do

1. Implement `marker_by_sequence(stream: &MarkerStream, seq: u64) -> Option<&Marker>` with O(1) complexity via direct slot computation (the marker stream is dense, so `seq` maps directly to an array offset or file offset).
2. Implement `sequence_by_timestamp(stream: &MarkerStream, ts: Timestamp) -> Option<u64>` with O(log N) complexity via binary search over the timestamp-ordered marker sequence. Since markers are appended in timestamp order (modulo clock skew tolerance), binary search is valid.
3. Define and enforce performance targets: sequence lookup must complete in < 1 microsecond for any stream size; timestamp lookup must complete in < 100 microseconds for streams up to 10 million markers.
4. Handle edge cases: empty stream returns `None`; timestamp before first marker returns `None` or the first sequence; timestamp after last marker returns the last sequence.
5. Produce a spec document defining the lookup algorithms, complexity proofs, and performance targets.
6. Produce performance benchmarks on large history sets (1M, 10M markers) demonstrating the O(1) and O(log N) bounds.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Sequence lookup performs O(1) slot math; timestamp lookup uses bounded O(log N) search; performance targets are met on large history sets.
- `marker_by_sequence` returns the correct marker for any valid sequence number in the stream.
- `marker_by_sequence` for an out-of-range sequence returns `None` without panicking.
- `sequence_by_timestamp` returns the correct sequence for timestamps that exactly match a marker.
- `sequence_by_timestamp` for timestamps between markers returns the most recent marker at or before that timestamp.
- Performance benchmark on 10M markers: sequence lookup < 1 microsecond (p99), timestamp lookup < 100 microseconds (p99).
- Benchmark results are recorded in `artifacts/10.14/marker_lookup_benchmarks.csv`.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: sequence lookup for first, last, and middle markers; out-of-range sequence returns None; timestamp lookup for exact match, between-markers, before-first, after-last; empty stream edge cases.
- Integration tests: lookup correctness on streams of 1K, 100K, 1M markers; concurrent reads during stream growth.
- Conformance tests: `tests/perf/marker_lookup_complexity.rs` -- performance benchmark tests with complexity assertions.
- Structured logs: `MARKER_LOOKUP_SEQ` (seq, found, elapsed_ns, trace_id), `MARKER_LOOKUP_TS` (timestamp, result_seq, elapsed_ns, trace_id). Debug-level only to avoid log volume impact.

## Expected Artifacts

- `tests/perf/marker_lookup_complexity.rs` -- performance benchmark and complexity tests
- `docs/specs/marker_lookup_algorithms.md` -- algorithm specification and complexity proofs
- `artifacts/10.14/marker_lookup_benchmarks.csv` -- benchmark results from large-scale runs
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-129f/verification_evidence.json` -- machine-readable CI/release gate evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-129f/verification_summary.md` -- human-readable verification summary

## Dependencies

- Upstream: bd-126h (append-only marker stream -- provides the `MarkerStream` data structure this bead indexes).
- Downstream: bd-3epz (section gate), bd-5rh (section gate).

title: [10.14] Implement idempotency key derivation from request bytes with epoch binding.
description:
## Why This Exists
Remote computations in the three-kernel architecture must be idempotent — network retries, crash recovery replays, and operator-initiated re-executions must not cause duplicate side effects. The standard approach is to derive a deterministic idempotency key from the request content, but naive hashing is insufficient: keys must be domain-separated (different computation types with identical payloads must produce different keys) and epoch-bound (a request valid in epoch N must not be replayed in epoch N+1 after a key rotation or trust boundary change). The 9J map requires a formally specified key derivation function that is deterministic, collision-resistant, and bound to both the computation domain and the control epoch.

## What This Must Do
1. Implement `IdempotencyKeyDeriver` in `crates/franken-node/src/remote/idempotency.rs` with method `derive_key(computation_name: &str, epoch: u64, request_bytes: &[u8]) -> IdempotencyKey`.
2. Key derivation must use a cryptographic hash (SHA-256 or BLAKE3) with domain separation: the hash input must be structured as `domain_prefix || computation_name || epoch_bytes || request_bytes` where `domain_prefix` is a fixed, version-specific constant (e.g., `"franken_node.idempotency.v1"`).
3. Epoch binding: the derived key changes when the epoch changes, even if the request bytes are identical. This prevents cross-epoch replay.
4. Publish derivation test vectors at `artifacts/10.14/idempotency_vectors.json` containing: input tuples (computation_name, epoch, request_bytes_hex) and expected output key (hex). At least 20 vectors covering normal cases, edge cases (empty payload, max-length payload, epoch 0, epoch u64::MAX), and cross-domain separation verification.
5. Implement collision analysis: include a test that generates keys for 10,000+ distinct request payloads and verifies zero collisions (empirical negligibility check).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Key derivation is deterministic: identical inputs always produce identical keys across runs, platforms, and compilations.
- Domain separation: different computation names with identical epoch and payload produce different keys.
- Epoch binding: identical computation name and payload with different epochs produce different keys.
- Collisions on distinct requests are empirically negligible (verified by collision test with 10,000+ samples).
- Derivation vectors are published and cover normal + edge cases (at least 20 vectors).

## Testing & Logging Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Determinism (same input -> same key across multiple calls); domain separation (different computation_name -> different key); epoch binding (different epoch -> different key); edge cases (empty payload, zero-length name, epoch 0, epoch u64::MAX).
- **Conformance tests**: `tests/conformance/idempotency_key_derivation.rs` — vector-driven tests that load `artifacts/10.14/idempotency_vectors.json` and verify each expected output; cross-platform determinism test (if CI supports multiple targets).
- **Integration tests**: Key derivation integrated with computation registry (bd-ac83) — verify that registered computation name produces valid key; unregistered name is caught before derivation.
- **Collision tests**: Generate 10,000+ keys from distinct payloads, verify zero collisions; generate keys across epoch boundaries, verify separation.
- **Event codes**: `IK_KEY_DERIVED` (key successfully derived), `IK_DERIVATION_ERROR` (derivation failed — invalid inputs), `IK_VECTOR_VERIFIED` (test vector matched), `IK_COLLISION_CHECK_PASSED` (collision analysis clean).
- **Replay fixture**: Set of (computation_name, epoch, request_bytes) tuples with pre-computed expected keys.

## Expected Artifacts
- `crates/franken-node/src/remote/idempotency.rs` — key derivation implementation
- `tests/conformance/idempotency_key_derivation.rs` — conformance test suite

[10.4] Integrate revocation propagation with canonical freshness checks (from `10.13`) in extension workflows.
description:
## Why This Exists

The extension ecosystem must reject stale, revoked, or compromised artifacts *before* they execute or propagate. Section 10.13 implements the canonical revocation registry and freshness checking infrastructure at the connector/protocol layer. This bead bridges that infrastructure into the extension workflow: when an extension is installed, updated, loaded, or invoked, the system must consult the revocation registry with freshness guarantees appropriate to the operation's risk tier.

Without this integration, an extension could be revoked in the registry but still execute on nodes that have not yet received the revocation signal — the classic revocation propagation delay that enables "use-after-revoke" attacks. This bead closes that gap for the extension ecosystem specifically.

## What This Must Do

1. Define the revocation check integration points in extension workflows: install, update, load, invoke, and periodic background refresh.
2. Integrate with the 10.13 revocation registry (bd-1m8r, bd-y7lu) to query revocation status with monotonic revocation-head checkpoints.
3. Implement freshness tier mapping: map extension operation risk levels (e.g., install = medium, invoke with network access = high, invoke with fs write = high) to required freshness windows (e.g., high-risk requires revocation-head within 60s, medium within 5m).
4. Implement the revocation propagation consumer that subscribes to revocation events and updates local revocation state.
5. Define fail-closed behavior: if revocation freshness cannot be established within the required window, the operation must be denied with a clear diagnostic.
6. Define the revocation cascade semantics: when an extension is revoked, dependent extensions and active sessions must be notified and follow quarantine/recall procedures.
7. Emit structured audit events for every revocation check decision (pass, fail-stale, fail-revoked, fail-unavailable).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every extension operation has a documented revocation check integration point.
- Freshness tiers are defined and mapped to operation risk levels with configurable windows.
- Revocation checks are monotonic: once a revocation is seen, it cannot be un-seen by local state regression.
- Fail-closed behavior is the default for all high-risk operations; fail-open requires explicit policy override with audit trail.
- Revocation propagation latency is bounded and measurable.
- Integration with 10.13 revocation registry uses the canonical API (no parallel/duplicate revocation stores).

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: freshness window enforcement, stale-state rejection, monotonic revocation state.
- Integration tests: end-to-end revocation flow (registry revocation -> propagation -> extension workflow rejection).
- Adversarial tests: time-travel attacks (resetting local revocation state), split-brain scenarios, network partition during revocation propagation.
- Structured logs: REVOCATION_CHECK_PASS, REVOCATION_CHECK_FAIL_STALE, REVOCATION_CHECK_FAIL_REVOKED, REVOCATION_CHECK_FAIL_UNAVAILABLE, REVOCATION_PROPAGATION_RECEIVED, REVOCATION_CASCADE_INITIATED. All with trace IDs.
- Deterministic replay fixtures for each revocation check outcome class.

## Expected Artifacts

- `docs/specs/section_10_4/bd-12q_contract.md` — revocation integration spec
- `src/supply_chain/revocation_integration.rs` — Rust types for extension revocation checks
- `scripts/check_revocation_integration.py` — verification script with `--json` and `self_test()`
- `tests/test_check_revocation_integration.py` — unit tests for verification script
- `artifacts/section_10_4/bd-12q/verification_evidence.json` — CI/release gate evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_4/bd-12q/verification_summary.md` — outcome summary

## Dependencies

- **bd-1m8r** (blocks this) — 10.13 revocation freshness enforcement per safety tier
- **bd-y7lu** (blocks this) — 10.13 revocation registry with monotonic checkpoints
- Blocks: bd-261k (section gate), bd-1vm (quarantine/recall needs revocation signals), bd-1xg (plan tracker)
acceptance_criteria:
1. Extension install/update workflows query the revocation registry (from 10.13 bd-y7lu) before admitting any extension, using the monotonic revocation-head checkpoint to verify freshness.
2. Revocation freshness check applies the safety-tier policy (from 10.13 bd-1m8r): high-safety extensions require revocation data fresher than configurable threshold (default: 1 hour); low-safety extensions tolerate longer staleness.
3. Stale revocation data triggers: (a) rejection for high-safety extensions with structured error REVOCATION_DATA_STALE, (b) warning annotation for low-safety extensions that proceeds but flags the stale check in the trust card and audit trail.
4. Revocation propagation subscribes to the revocation registry change feed and processes updates within the configured SLA (default: 60 seconds from registry update to local enforcement).
5. Extension lifecycle events (install, update, uninstall) emit structured log events: EXTENSION_REVOCATION_CHECK_PASSED, EXTENSION_REVOCATION_CHECK_FAILED, EXTENSION_REVOCATION_STALE_WARNING with extension ID, revocation-head position, staleness duration, and trace IDs.
6. Integration test: simulate revocation of an installed extension, verify propagation to the extension workflow, and confirm the extension is blocked/quarantined within SLA.
7. Freshness check results are recorded in the evidence ledger for audit trail completeness.

title: [HIGH] bd-3b07b WIP RemoteCap fsync batching weakens per-call replay durability
description: Per fresh-eyes review of bd-3b07b WIP commit b67540fb (and the bd-35zls retry-set fix on top): DurableReplayStore::consume() now writes marker file then queues for batched fsync. It returns Ok(true) before flush_pending_markers runs. Callers (e.g. remote_cap.rs:2330 auth flow) treat Ok(true) as 'replay protection is in effect for this key'. But: between two batch flushes (default sync_batch_size=32), a process crash (panic/kill -9/OOM/host crash) loses ALL un-fsynced markers AND their directory entries. On restart, those replay_keys appear unconsumed → caps can be replayed, bypassing replay protection for up to 31 keys per crash. Original (pre-batching) code did per-call sync_all + sync_directory, providing strict durability. Fix options: (a) revert batching for consume() and keep batch infrastructure for non-critical paths; (b) make consume() flush before returning Ok(true) (defeats batching purpose); (c) add public flush_replay_store() on CapabilityGate + document caller MUST call before granting auth; (d) write-ahead log with periodic checkpoint that's strictly durable. Recommend (c) with explicit flush at the auth-grant site (remote_cap.rs:~2330) to keep batching benefits without security gap. Touched: src/security/remote_cap.rs:553-583. WIP marker on the original commit confirms author knew it was incomplete.
close_reason: Fixed in two parts: (a) commit aed79592 by parallel reviewer made consume() flush pending markers on every Ok(true) return so per-call durability is restored; (b) commit 38c8eb56 (this session) removed the sync_batch_size scaffolding that became dead config after the always-flush change. Pending_syncs queue stays — concurrent callers still amortize sync_directory through the shared lock — but threshold-gated flushing is gone. New test durable_replay_store_consume_flushes_marker_before_returning is the regression guard.

title: [10.5] Implement policy-visible compatibility gate APIs.
description:
Master Plan Source: PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_NODE.md — Section 10.5, cross-ref Section 3.2 #5, 9A.5, 9B.5, 9C.5, 9D.5

## Why This Exists
This is one of the 10 Impossible-by-Default capabilities (Section 3.2 #5). Policy-visible compatibility gates are the mechanism by which operators control which compatibility behaviors are active, at what risk level, with full traceability. Without this, compatibility shims operate as hidden magic — the exact opposite of trust-native operations.

## What Policy-Visible Compatibility Gate APIs Must Do
1. **Typed shim registry exposure:** Every compatibility shim registered in the compatibility behavior registry (10.2) must be queryable via API with full metadata: shim ID, behavior description, risk category, activation policy, and divergence rationale.

2. **Mode selection API:** Operators can select compatibility modes (strict, balanced, legacy-risky) per project, per tenant, or per extension scope. Mode selection is policy-gated and produces signed configuration receipts.

3. **Gate evaluation API:** Before executing a compatibility-shimmed behavior, the gate API checks current policy state, evaluates risk constraints, and returns allow/deny/audit decisions with structured rationale.

4. **Policy-as-data contracts:** Shim activation constraints are expressed as machine-verifiable policy predicates (per 9B.5: policy-as-data signatures with attenuation semantics). This means shim activation is cryptographically constrained, not just configuration-driven.

5. **Non-interference and monotonicity checks:** Per 9C.5, the API must enforce that enabling additional shims does not weaken existing security guarantees (monotonicity) and that shim activation in one scope does not leak side effects into another (non-interference).

6. **Performance-optimized evaluation path:** Per 9D.5, the policy evaluation path must be optimized while preserving deterministic rule order. Precompiled decision DAGs or cached policy compilations where safe.

## Context from Section 9 Enhancement Maps
- 9A.5: "Any behavior shim must be typed, auditable, and policy-gated, so operators can choose compatibility level by risk appetite with full traceability."
- 9B.5: "Use policy-as-data signatures and attenuation semantics so shim activation is cryptographically constrained and auditable."
- 9C.5: "Encode non-interference and monotonicity checks as machine-verifiable policy compiler outputs."
- 9D.5: "Optimize policy evaluation path while preserving deterministic rule order."

## Acceptance Criteria
1. API surface exposes all registered compatibility shims with full typed metadata.
2. Mode selection (strict/balanced/legacy-risky) is per-scope and produces signed receipts.
3. Gate evaluation returns structured allow/deny/audit decisions with machine-readable rationale.
4. Policy-as-data contracts are cryptographically verifiable.
5. Non-interference property: shim activation in scope A has no observable effect in scope B.
6. Monotonicity property: adding shims never weakens existing security guarantees (formally testable).
7. Gate evaluation latency meets interactive budget (< 1ms p99 for cached policy).
8. All gate decisions emit structured audit events with trace correlation IDs.

## Expected Artifacts
- docs/specs/section_10_5/bd-137_contract.md: API design, policy-as-data contract format, non-interference/monotonicity proof strategy
- artifacts/section_10_5/bd-137/verification_evidence.json: Machine-readable test results
- artifacts/section_10_5/bd-137/verification_summary.md: Human-readable outcome summary

## Testing & Logging Requirements
- Unit tests: shim registry query completeness, mode selection receipt signing, gate evaluation determinism, non-interference property, monotonicity property
- Integration tests: full mode-selection -> gate-evaluation -> audit-emission pipeline
- E2E tests: operator workflow from selecting mode through executing shimmed behavior to reviewing audit trail
- Performance tests: gate evaluation latency under policy load
- Adversarial tests: policy bypass attempts, malformed gate requests, conflicting mode selections
- Structured logs: stable event codes for gate decisions, policy receipt generation, and audit emission
acceptance_criteria:
1. Expose a PolicyGateStatus struct containing: gate_name (string), pass (bool), evaluated_at (RFC-3339 timestamp), evidence_hash (SHA-256 hex), policy_version (semver string), and detail (human-readable summary).
2. Implement at least three concrete gate checks: CompatibilityMatrixGate (validates current capability matrix against minimum compatibility floor), RevocationPrecheckGate (confirms no active revocation entries block the requested action), and VersionFenceGate (ensures target version satisfies the fencing predicate from state_model.rs).
3. Each gate check must complete within 50 ms on a single core; add a benchmark test that asserts this.
4. Provide a query_gates(action: &str) -> Vec<PolicyGateStatus> API that evaluates all registered gates for a given action name and returns their statuses.

title: [REASONING] divergence_gate silently drops second-fork evidence while in Diverged
description:
LENS: First-principles correctness
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/control_plane/divergence_gate.rs:591-632 (transition_to_diverged) and 542-589 (check_propagation)
CONCERN: transition_to_diverged early-returns if state != GateState::Normal (lines 602-604). check_propagation calls it for every Forked/RollbackDetected/GapDetected outcome. Once the gate is in Diverged, a *second*, distinct divergence (different remote_hash, different fork_epoch, possibly a worse rollback) is silently dropped: no audit entry, no event push, active_divergence keeps the first observation, no operator alert. The comment on line 600 frames this as 'guard to avoid overwriting quarantine/alert/recovery state' but the consequence is the gate amnesias new fork evidence after the first one.
WHY IT MATTERS: An attacker (or natural reorg) can race two divergent updates so the *worse* one arrives second and is invisible. Operators recover against the wrong fork checkpoint. The audit log lies by omission. INV-DG-VALID-TRANSITIONS is satisfied by the early return but the safety property 'every observed divergence is recorded' is violated.
SUGGESTED REMEDIATION: When already Diverged and a *new distinct* (local_hash, remote_hash, fork_epoch) tuple is observed, append a DG_001_DIVERGENCE_DETECTED audit entry with detail='subsequent_divergence_during_diverged' and either (a) extend ActiveDivergence with a bounded Vec of additional observations, or (b) add a 'subsequent_divergences' counter and a DG_NNN event. Add a property test: invoke check_propagation N times with N distinct remote_hashes, assert audit_log() shows N divergence entries (modulo capacity).
close_reason: Audited distinct subsequent divergence observations while already Diverged without overwriting active divergence; added registered e2e coverage and cleaned e2e panic fallbacks.

title: [10.10] Adopt canonical stable error namespace and compatibility policy (from `10.13`) across product surfaces.
description:
[10.10] Adopt canonical stable error namespace and compatibility policy (from 10.13) across product surfaces.

## Why This Exists

Section 9E.9 mandates a unified, stable error namespace across all product surfaces. The 10.13 work established a stable error code registry (`error_code_registry.json`) and error code contract (`error_code_contract.md`) that define structured error codes with retryable flags, retry_after hints, and recovery hints. However, these are currently only enforced within the connector module. This bead extends enforcement to ALL product surfaces: CLI output, REST API responses, trust protocol messages, migration reports, operator dashboards, and SDK error returns. Every error a user or machine consumer sees must carry a stable, documented code from the canonical namespace.

## What It Must Do

1. **Error namespace adoption audit.** Scan all product surfaces (CLI, API, protocol messages, logs, SDK) and identify every error path. Produce an audit report listing each error path, its current error representation, and whether it maps to a stable code. Unmapped errors are violations.

2. **Surface-specific error formatters.** Implement error formatting adapters for each product surface:
   - CLI: human-readable message with error code in brackets, e.g., `[FN-CONN-0012] Connection refused: retry in 5s`.
   - JSON API: `{"error_code": "FN-CONN-0012", "message": "...", "retryable": true, "retry_after_ms": 5000, "recovery_hint": "..."}`.
   - Protocol messages: compact binary error frame with code, retryable bit, and optional payload.
   - Logs: structured log fields `error.code`, `error.retryable`, `error.recovery_hint`.

3. **Compatibility policy enforcement.** Once an error code is published in a stable release, it cannot be removed or have its semantics changed (retryable flag, code number). New codes can be added. Deprecated codes must remain valid for at least 2 major versions. The compatibility policy is enforced by a CI check that compares the current registry against the last released registry.

4. **Error code coverage gate.** A verification script ensures that every `Err(...)` return in the Rust codebase and every `raise` / error return in the Python codebase maps to a registered error code. Unregistered errors fail the gate.

5. **Recovery hint quality.** Every error code must have a non-empty `recovery_hint` field that provides actionable guidance. Hints are validated for minimum length (> 20 chars) and must not be generic ("an error occurred").

6. **Cross-surface consistency.** The same error code must produce semantically equivalent messages across all surfaces. A test suite generates errors and checks that CLI, API, and log representations all carry the same code and retryable flag.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Error namespace audit report exists at `artifacts/section_10_10/bd-13q/error_audit.json` with zero unmapped errors.
2. Surface-specific formatters implemented in `crates/franken-node/src/connector/error_surface.rs`.
3. Compatibility policy enforced by `scripts/check_error_compat.py` comparing current vs. baseline registry.
4. Error code coverage gate (`scripts/check_error_coverage.py`) passes with zero unregistered errors.
5. All error codes have recovery hints > 20 characters.
6. Cross-surface consistency test confirms code/retryable agreement across CLI, API, and log outputs.
7. Verification script `scripts/check_error_namespace.py` with `--json` flag confirms all criteria.
8. Evidence artifacts written to `artifacts/section_10_10/bd-13q/`.

## Key Dependencies

- 10.13 error code registry (`error_code_registry.json`) — source of truth.
- 10.13 error code contract (`error_code_contract.md`) — policy definition.
- bd-1l5 (trust object IDs) — error codes for malformed IDs flow from this namespace.
- CLI module (`src/cli.rs`) — surface adapter integration point.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests in `tests/test_check_error_namespace.py` covering: format validation, compatibility diff detection, coverage gap detection, recovery hint quality.
- Integration test that exercises error paths end-to-end across CLI and API surfaces.
- Self-test mode validates detection of deliberately unregistered error codes.
- Structured logging: `error_namespace.unmapped_error`, `error_namespace.compat_violation`, `error_namespace.coverage_gap` events.

## Expected Artifacts

- `docs/specs/section_10_10/bd-13q_contract.md` — specification document.
- `crates/franken-node/src/connector/error_surface.rs` — surface formatters.
- `scripts/check_error_namespace.py` — verification script.
- `scripts/check_error_compat.py` — compatibility checker.
- `scripts/check_error_coverage.py` — coverage gate.
- `tests/test_check_error_namespace.py` — unit tests.
- `artifacts/section_10_10/bd-13q/verification_evidence.json` — evidence.
- `artifacts/section_10_10/bd-13q/verification_summary.md` — summary.
- `artifacts/section_10_10/bd-13q/error_audit.json` — audit report.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Adopt the canonical error code registry from 10.13 (error_code_registry.rs) as the single source of truth for all product-surface error codes. Every error returned to users or operators MUST reference a registered error code from this registry.
2. Define product-surface error namespace prefixes: FN-CTRL-* (control plane), FN-MIG-* (migration), FN-AUTH-* (authentication/authorization), FN-POL-* (policy), FN-ZON-* (zone/tenant), FN-TOK-* (token). Each prefix MUST be registered in the canonical registry.
3. Implement an ErrorCompatibilityPolicy with rules: (a) error codes are append-only (existing codes MUST NOT be removed or renumbered), (b) error message text may be refined but the code and category (TRANSIENT, PERMANENT, CONFIGURATION) MUST NOT change, (c) new error codes MUST include a human-readable description and a machine-readable severity tag.
4. Implement a compatibility check: given two versions of the error registry (old and new), verify no codes were removed, no categories changed, and all new codes have required metadata. Return a CompatibilityReport with added/unchanged/violated lists.
5. Provide a product_error! macro or builder that constructs errors with: (a) registered code, (b) message, (c) trace correlation ID, (d) optional structured context map. Reject construction with unregistered codes at compile time or test time.
6. Integrate with the telemetry_namespace module from 10.13: error metrics MUST use the registered code as a dimension, not free-form strings.
7. Unit tests: (a) all existing product errors map to registered codes, (b) compatibility check passes for additive changes, (c) compatibility check fails for removal, (d) compatibility check fails for category change, (e) product_error! with valid code succeeds, (f) product_error! with unknown code fails.
8. CI gate: run the compatibility check between the previous release registry and the current one; fail the build on violations.
9. Verification: scripts/check_error_namespace.py --json, artifacts at artifacts/section_10_10/bd-13q/.

Why This Improves User Outcomes:
- "[12] Risk control: signal poisoning and Sybil" is required to reduce operator error, increase deterministic safety guarantees, and improve time-to-diagnosis for failures in real-world workflows.
- Explicit success/failure evidence for "[12] Risk control: signal poisoning and Sybil" prevents false confidence and improves trust in migration/compatibility/security outcomes.

acceptance_criteria:
RISK: Signal poisoning and Sybil attacks — malicious nodes inject false reputation/trust signals or create multiple fake identities to manipulate the trust graph.
IMPACT: Corrupted trust decisions, malicious extensions gaining undeserved trust, legitimate extensions being suppressed.
COUNTERMEASURES:
  (a) Robust aggregation: trust signal aggregation uses trimmed-mean or median (not simple average) to resist outlier injection.
  (b) Stake weighting: trust signals are weighted by the contributor's own stake/reputation, making Sybil attacks expensive.
  (c) Adversarial gates: CI includes adversarial test suites that simulate poisoning and Sybil scenarios; trust system must maintain correct rankings.
VERIFICATION:
  1. Robust aggregation: injecting 20% poisoned signals shifts the aggregate by <= 5% from the true value.
  2. Stake weighting: a newly-created node's signal has <= 1% weight vs an established node's signal.
  3. Sybil resistance: creating 100 fake identities has less influence than 5 established honest nodes.
  4. Adversarial test suite with >= 10 attack scenarios passes in CI.
TEST SCENARIOS:
  - Scenario A: Inject 20% maximally-adversarial signals; verify trust ranking of honest nodes changes by <= 1 position.
  - Scenario B: Create 100 Sybil identities all endorsing a malicious extension; verify it does not enter the top-50% trust tier.
  - Scenario C: Simulate a coordinated signal poisoning campaign over 10 rounds; verify trust system converges back to correct rankings within 3 rounds after attack stops.
  - Scenario D: Verify that stake-weighting function is monotonically increasing with verified history length.

title: [PROFILE] control_plane/mmr_proofs.rs: hex-string Hash type forces alloc + hex roundtrip per merkle level
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/control_plane/mmr_proofs.rs

PATTERN:
`pub type Hash = String;` (L32) — every MMR node hash is a 64-byte hex String. Internal merkle ops therefore allocate and hex-encode/decode at every level:

1. L490-510 `merkle_audit_path`:
   - `level.to_vec()` clones all hex Strings at start
   - `level.last()?.clone()` — String clone for odd-padding at every odd level
   - `path.push(level[sibling_idx].clone())` — String clone per level
   - `next.push(hash_pair(...))` — `hash_pair` re-encodes to hex String at every node

2. L513-532 `merkle_root_from_leaf_hashes` is the same algorithm without the path; called separately (e.g. when only the root is needed) — duplicate work if both are computed for the same tree.

3. L534-542 `hash_pair`:
   - `hex::encode(hasher.finalize())` — allocates a 64-byte hex String per node
   - Caller then passes `left.as_bytes()` / `right.as_bytes()` back into the next level's hasher — i.e. hex-encode at one level just to feed the bytes back in at the next level

For n=1024 leaves: ~10 levels, ~2k node hashes, ~2k hex encodes + ~2k String clones (audit_path) + another ~2k of each if root is also computed.

IMPACT: Allocation-heavy proof construction; every checkpoint/proof verification walks this code. Replacing String hex with `[u8; 32]` would 5–10x throughput and eliminate all the per-node allocation.

SUGGESTED FIX:
- Define `type Hash = [u8; 32]` (or a newtype around it) for internal merkle ops
- Keep hex String only at API boundaries (serialization, logging)
- Convert `marker_leaf_hash`, `hash_pair`, `merkle_audit_path`, `merkle_root_from_leaf_hashes` to operate on `[u8; 32]`
- For `merkle_root_from_leaf_hashes` + `merkle_audit_path` co-call sites: provide a single function that returns both

EVIDENCE:
- L32 `pub type Hash = String;`
- L455-462 marker_leaf_hash hex-encodes
- L485-511 merkle_audit_path: level.to_vec() + per-level String clone + hash_pair (hex)
- L513-532 merkle_root_from_leaf_hashes: same algorithm sans path
- L534-542 hash_pair: hex::encode per node + re-decode of left.as_bytes()/right.as_bytes() at next level
close_reason: Completed: MMR proof construction now uses raw 32-byte hashes internally and keeps hex at proof/API boundaries.

title: [10.15] Integrate deterministic lab runtime scenarios for all high-impact control protocols.
description:
## Why This Exists
Hard Runtime Invariant #9 (deterministic verification gates) requires that all high-impact control protocols can be exercised in a deterministic lab runtime where execution is controlled by a seed, making failures reproducible. Section 10.14 built two canonical testing primitives: bd-876n (cancellation injection at all await points) and bd-2qqu (virtual transport fault harness for drop/reorder/corrupt). This bead integrates those into a unified deterministic lab runtime that runs canonical control scenarios (lifecycle orchestration, rollout transitions, epoch barriers, saga compensations, evidence capture) with seed-controlled scheduling. Protocol invariants are asserted within each scenario, and failure artifacts are deterministic (same seed -> same failure).

## What This Must Do
1. Author `docs/testing/control_lab_scenarios.md` defining:
   - The deterministic lab runtime model: seed-controlled scheduler, mock clock, injected faults.
   - The scenario inventory: one scenario per high-impact control protocol (lifecycle start/stop, rollout go/abort, epoch transition commit/abort, saga forward/compensate, evidence capture/replay).
   - Per-scenario invariant assertions: what properties must hold (quiescence, no leaks, no half-commits, evidence completeness).
   - Failure artifact format: seed, scenario name, invariant violated, trace snapshot.
2. Implement `tests/lab/control_protocol_scenarios.rs` containing:
   - A deterministic lab runtime harness that accepts a seed and replays the scenario.
   - At least one scenario per protocol: lifecycle, rollout, epoch barrier, saga, evidence.
   - Invariant assertion macros that capture structured failure artifacts on violation.
   - Seed matrix: a set of known-interesting seeds that exercise boundary conditions.
3. Generate `artifacts/10.15/control_lab_seed_matrix.json` with: seed values, scenario names, expected outcomes, actual outcomes, pass/fail.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Canonical control scenarios replay identically by seed; protocol invariants are asserted with deterministic failure artifacts.
- The same seed always produces the same execution trace and the same pass/fail result.
- Every high-impact protocol has at least one lab scenario.
- Failure artifacts include the seed, the invariant violated, and a trace snapshot sufficient to diagnose the failure without re-running.
- The seed matrix JSON is consumed by the section gate (bd-20eg).

## Testing & Logging Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Validate the lab runtime harness with a trivial scenario (assert seed reproducibility).
- **Integration tests**: Run each protocol scenario with multiple seeds; assert deterministic replay.
- **Conformance tests**: Run a scenario that is known to pass; flip one bit in the seed; assert the trace changes but the harness still produces a valid failure artifact if an invariant is violated.
- **Adversarial tests**: Inject a non-deterministic element (wall-clock read) into a scenario; assert the lab runtime detects and rejects it. Run a scenario with a seed that triggers a known boundary condition; assert the invariant assertion captures the failure.
- **Structured logs**: Event codes `LAB-001` (scenario started with seed), `LAB-002` (scenario completed — pass), `LAB-003` (scenario completed — invariant violation), `LAB-004` (failure artifact emitted), `LAB-005` (non-determinism detected in scenario). Include scenario_name, seed, and trace correlation ID.

## Expected Artifacts
- `docs/testing/control_lab_scenarios.md`
- `tests/lab/control_protocol_scenarios.rs`
- `artifacts/10.15/control_lab_seed_matrix.json`
- `artifacts/section_10_15/bd-145n/verification_evidence.json`
- `artifacts/section_10_15/bd-145n/verification_summary.md`

## Dependencies
- **Upstream**: bd-876n (10.14 — cancellation injection at all await points), bd-2qqu (10.14 — virtual transport fault harness)
- **Downstream**: bd-20eg (section gate), bd-2ko (10.11 adopts lab scenarios for product logic)
