title: Decide local semantic twin policy versus canonical franken_engine/asupersync adapters
description:
Why this exists:
`franken_node` contains local semantic twins of several Asupersync-flavored concepts while `frankenengine-engine` already centralizes canonical upstream primitive imports. If the repo does not define that boundary explicitly, future contributors will oscillate between duplicate-type sprawl and premature migration churn.

What this cluster must do:
- inventory the local semantic twins and classify each one against the canonical upstream ownership boundary,
- explain why each surface should stay local, wrap canonical primitives, migrate only when a live runtime boundary exists, or be forbidden as a duplicate fork,
- add anti-drift proof obligations so the policy remains actionable instead of decaying into prose.

Why this matters:
This is where the project decides what belongs locally for modeling/spec reasons versus what should ultimately collapse onto upstream-owned primitives. The output must be self-contained enough that future maintainers can make consistent decisions without reopening this chat.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The repo has an explicit inventory of local Asupersync-like semantic twins in `franken_node`.
2. Each inventoried surface has a clear policy outcome: keep local, wrap canonical, migrate later under trigger conditions, or forbid as a duplicate primitive fork.
3. The cluster includes anti-drift safeguards, repository-level validation scripts, detailed versioned logging/artifacts, and explicit mapping from policy entries to enforcement/proof surfaces so the policy is enforceable rather than purely narrative.
4. The policy preserves the existing upstream ownership boundary in `frankenengine-engine` and gives future contributors a reliable decision procedure for new concepts, including how to find the rule/check/script that enforces or exemplifies the chosen classification.
5. Any heavy validation needed by this cluster is routed through `rch`.
notes: This is a semantic-boundary cluster, not a mandate to rewrite everything. A successful outcome may explicitly keep several node-side surfaces local. The important thing is to make those decisions principled, testable where feasible, and reusable by future contributors.

title: Inventory and classify node-side semantic twins against canonical upstream boundaries
description:
Why this exists:
Before the repo can defend a boundary policy, it needs an explicit inventory and classification matrix for the local semantic twins already present.

What this task must do:
Inventory the relevant node-side semantic twins and classify each one against canonical upstream ownership.

The inventory must cover at least:
- `connector/region_ownership.rs`,
- `connector/supervision.rs`,
- `runtime/region_tree.rs`,
- performance budget guards,
- any additional node-side semantic twin discovered while implementing the matrix.

For each surface, capture:
- what problem it solves locally,
- which upstream canonical primitive or adapter it relates to (if any),
- whether it should stay local, wrap canonical ownership, migrate only under a future trigger, or be treated as forbidden duplicate/fork surface,
- what user/operator consequence exists if the surface drifts semantically.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The inventory/classification matrix covers the known node-side semantic twins and any additional relevant surfaces found during implementation.
2. Each entry contains a concrete policy outcome plus the reasoning behind it.
3. Each entry records the user/operator or contributor-facing consequence of semantic drift so the classification is grounded in behavior rather than aesthetics.
4. The matrix includes representative decision examples future contributors can analogize from, including at least one “keep local” case and one “must not fork / should align upstream” case.
5. The matrix is self-contained enough that future contributors can classify a new similar surface by analogy instead of improvising.
6. Each matrix entry points to the intended enforcement/proof surface (checker, test, script, or an explicit justification for why the entry is document-only for now) so the policy is operational rather than merely classificatory.
notes: Bias toward explicit reasoning over short labels. The goal is for future maintainers to understand why a surface stays local or moves upstream, not just to see a terse classification word.

title: Add anti-drift safeguards, examples, and consistency checks for semantic-boundary policy
description:
Why this exists:
A classification matrix without anti-drift proof obligations will decay as soon as new local helpers, wrappers, or canonical imports get added under delivery pressure.

What this task must do:
Add the anti-drift layer for the semantic-boundary policy.

Depending on the surfaces involved, that anti-drift layer may include:
- deterministic unit tests or snapshot tests that protect key local-vs-canonical classification tables,
- examples / contributor-facing decision cases that show when a new concept stays local versus when it must reference canonical upstream ownership,
- cheap checkers that fail when a forbidden duplicate/fork pattern or undocumented boundary crossing reappears,
- stable failure logging or reason codes so policy violations are easy to triage.

Why this matters:
This is what makes the semantic-boundary policy reusable and enforceable rather than a one-time document.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The semantic-boundary policy has deterministic anti-drift safeguards appropriate to the actual surfaces involved (tests, snapshots, examples, checkers, or a justified combination).
2. The safeguards make it obvious when a contributor is creating an undocumented duplicate fork or boundary crossing.
3. Failure output is detailed enough for contributors to understand what changed and which policy rule they violated.
4. The safeguards export stable rule ids/messages and, where applicable, machine-readable fields that the repo-level proof harness can reuse instead of inventing a second policy vocabulary.
5. This bead delivers the implementation-layer safeguards; the repo-level scripted/E2E proof lane is tracked separately.
6. If cargo-heavy validation is needed, it is executed through `rch`.
notes:
Do not overfit this to one current file layout. The anti-drift layer should help future contributors make correct ownership decisions even if files move or additional local semantic surfaces appear.

Keep the implementation-layer checks composable so the later repo-level proof harness can reuse the same rule ids, messages, and artifacts instead of inventing parallel policy logic.

title: Deferred trigger: adopt native Asupersync request-region boundaries when a real async server lands
description:
Why this exists:
The audit deliberately rejected an immediate native-Asupersync migration of the control-plane service skeleton because `crates/franken-node/src/api/service.rs` is still a skeleton/catalog layer rather than a live async HTTP or gRPC server boundary.

What this deferred task must preserve for future self:
If `franken_node` later grows a real async network boundary, that is the moment to revisit native Asupersync request-region/capability-narrowing patterns.

Future trigger conditions:
- real socket accept loop or gRPC call boundary is introduced in this crate,
- request cancellation and per-request lifecycle become real runtime concerns,
- middleware begins owning spawn/time/IO authority rather than just metadata,
- the crate needs deterministic request shutdown/drain semantics.

When the trigger fires, the future implementation should evaluate:
- request-region ownership,
- narrowed request `Cx` capability exposure,
- explicit lifecycle/Outcome mapping at transport boundaries,
- whether the crate should own an `AppSpec`-like supervised service topology.

Why this bead exists now:
It prevents future contributors from forgetting that the right answer for HTTP/gRPC boundaries may eventually be native Asupersync — while also making clear that today is not that day.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The deferred bead captures the exact trigger conditions that would justify revisiting native Asupersync request/call boundary patterns in `franken_node`.
2. The bead makes it explicit that the current service skeleton is not yet sufficient justification for a migration.
3. Future contributors can pick this bead up without needing to rediscover why the work was deferred, what proof obligations wake it up, and what evidence shape the eventual cluster must produce.
notes:
This bead should remain deferred until the crate owns a real async server boundary. Treat premature activation as a design smell.

When this bead is eventually activated, the very first execution move should be a fresh design + verification cluster that includes:
- request-boundary ownership/lifecycle design,
- deterministic unit tests for boundary semantics,
- transport-level end-to-end scripts,
- structured lifecycle logging/artifacts with stable schema/version markers,
- baseline comparison against predecessor transport behavior where relevant,
- operator/contributor guidance for any exposed tuning or backpressure budgets,

title: bd-1now support: make telemetry bridge drain stop-aware for idle open clients
description: Why this exists: crates/franken-node/src/ops/telemetry_bridge.rs::handle_connection() reads accepted UnixStream clients with blocking BufRead::lines(). stop() only flips a flag, so an idle-but-open client can keep a connection worker blocked forever waiting for another line. During drain, TelemetryRuntimeHandle::join() waits on those workers and can report a false drain-timeout/failure even though the bridge has no pending work to flush. What this task must do: make the telemetry bridge connection loop stop-aware during drain without dropping normal line-oriented ingestion, keep scope limited to ops/telemetry_bridge.rs, and add a regression proving stop_and_join() completes cleanly when a client stays connected but idle. Acceptance criteria: 1. A connection worker exits promptly after stop() even if the client keeps the socket open and sends no further newline-delimited events. 2. Normal line-delimited event ingestion still succeeds. 3. A focused regression test covers the idle-open-client drain case. 4. Validation uses only light local checks plus rch for any cargo-heavy run if needed.
close_reason: Fixed stop-aware idle-client drain path in telemetry bridge; added regression; validated via rch

[10.18] Implement proof-verification gate API for control-plane trust decisions.
description:
## Why This Exists

Section 10.18 implements the Verifiable Execution Fabric (VEF) — Enhancement Map 9L — delivering proof-carrying runtime compliance. This is a Track C (Trust-Native Ecosystem Layer) critical gate that makes franken_node's trust decisions depend on cryptographic verification rather than trust-by-assertion.

This bead implements the proof-verification gate API — the component that control-plane trust decisions invoke to validate proofs before authorizing high-risk actions or trust transitions. The proof-generation service (bd-1u8m) produces proofs; this gate validates them. It is the trust boundary between "a proof exists" and "the proof is valid and binds to the correct policy and receipt window."

This gate is security-critical: it must be fail-closed (invalid or missing proofs default to denial), must validate the full binding chain (proof -> receipt-window commitment -> policy hash), and must produce stable verdict classes that downstream components (bd-8qlj for control transitions, bd-3pds for verifier SDK) can reason about deterministically.

## What This Must Do

1. Implement a verification gate API that accepts a proof envelope (from bd-1u8m) and validates it against the receipt-window commitment and policy hash binding.
2. Validate the full binding chain: proof envelope -> proof validity -> receipt-window commitment match -> policy hash match.
3. Return stable, classified verdict types: `VALID`, `INVALID_PROOF`, `MISSING_PROOF`, `STALE_POLICY`, `COMMITMENT_MISMATCH`, `VERIFICATION_ERROR`.
4. Enforce fail-closed semantics: any verification failure or missing input defaults to denial with a specific verdict class.
5. Support multiple proof backends transparently — the gate verifies proofs regardless of which backend generated them, using backend-specific verification parameters from the proof envelope.
6. Produce auditable verification records: every gate invocation (pass or fail) emits a signed, replayable verification record.
7. Expose a synchronous API suitable for hot-path integration in control-plane trust decisions.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Verification gate validates proof, receipt-window commitment, and policy hash binding; invalid/missing proofs return stable fail-closed verdict classes.
- All verdict classes are stable, enumerated, and documented with remediation guidance.
- Fail-closed behavior: missing proof -> `MISSING_PROOF` denial; malformed proof -> `INVALID_PROOF` denial; expired policy binding -> `STALE_POLICY` denial.
- Multi-backend support: proofs from different backends validate correctly through the same gate API.
- Verification records are signed and contain enough context for independent replay.
- Gate latency is bounded and suitable for synchronous control-plane integration.
- No silent pass-through: the gate never returns an affirmative verdict without completing full validation.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests for each verdict class: valid proof, invalid proof, missing proof, stale policy, commitment mismatch, verification error.
- Fail-closed tests: null inputs, partial inputs, corrupted proof bytes — all must return denial verdicts.
- Multi-backend tests: validate proofs from the reference backend and any additional backends through the same gate.
- Binding chain tests: modify the receipt-window commitment after proof generation — must detect mismatch; modify policy hash — must detect stale policy.
- Replay tests: verification records contain sufficient context to re-execute the verification and reach the same verdict.
- Latency benchmark: measure gate verification time under load, confirm it stays within control-plane hot-path budget.
- Structured logging: `VEF-VERIFY-001` (verification requested), `VEF-VERIFY-002` (verdict issued), `VEF-VERIFY-ERR-*` (per verdict class).
- Trace correlation IDs linking verification requests to proof job IDs, receipt window ranges, and originating action contexts.

## Expected Artifacts

- `src/trust/vef_verification_gate.rs` — proof-verification gate API implementation.
- `tests/security/vef_verification_gate.rs` — security-focused tests for all verdict classes and fail-closed behavior.
- `artifacts/10.18/vef_verification_gate_report.json` — verification gate test report with verdict class coverage.
- `artifacts/section_10_18/bd-1o4v/verification_evidence.json` — machine-readable CI/release gate evidence.
- `artifacts/section_10_18/bd-1o4v/verification_summary.md` — human-readable summary linking intent to measured outcomes.

## Dependencies

- bd-1u8m (blocks) — Proof-generation service interface: produces the proof envelopes that this gate validates.

Dependents: bd-8qlj (VEF integration into control transitions), bd-3pds (verifier SDK integration), bd-2hjg (section gate), bd-32p (plan-level tracker).
acceptance_criteria: - Verification gate validates proof, receipt-window commitment, and policy hash binding; invalid/missing proofs return stable fail-closed verdict classes.

CURRENT STATE: The value 4096 appears as a const in ~150+ different files. Related values (2048, 8192, 65536) appear in ~30 more. Each module independently defines its own MAX_* constants, leading to:
  - No single place to adjust defaults for scaling
  - Inconsistent limits across related modules

SPECIFIC CONSTANTS TO CENTRALIZE (representative list, not exhaustive):
  - MAX_AUDIT_LOG_ENTRIES: 4096 (in lane_scheduler, time_travel, repro_bundle, compat_gate, control_evidence, etc.)

  - MAX_TRACE_STEPS: 8192 (time_travel_engine)

DESIGN APPROACH:

description: Fresh-eyes audit of sdk/verifier/src/lib.rs and sdk/verifier/src/bundle.rs found that VerifierSdk::verify_migration_artifact() and verify_trust_state() call bundle::verify(), but bundle::verify() only checks canonical bytes, integrity_hash, and the public structural signature_hex = sha256(domain || integrity_hash). [10.4 bug] Bind trust cards and certification to verified evidence, not asserted trust inputs
description:
Why this exists:
The deeper 10.4 failure is downstream, not just at registry admission. `crates/franken-node/src/supply_chain/trust_card.rs` defines `TrustCardInput` as a bag of caller-supplied trust facts and then signs whatever it is given, while `crates/franken-node/src/supply_chain/certification.rs` evaluates `CertificationInput` from caller-supplied provenance/reputation/evidence fields instead of deriving them from verified upstream state. That means the project can mint polished, signed-looking trust cards and policy certification decisions from unverified assertions.

What this bead must do:
Bind trust-card materialization and certification to verified evidence handles, not free-form caller assertions. The design target is a typed trust pipeline: registry-admitted artifacts produce immutable verified evidence records; trust cards and certification consume those records by reference; every rendered trust claim is traceable back to canonical manifest/provenance/reputation/revocation evidence. Compile the abstruse parts into concrete artifacts: evidence IDs, append-only derivation receipts, minimal counterexample witnesses for disputed trust decisions, and deterministic replay bundles that let another verifier reconstruct why a card or certification level existed. Use the mathematically ambitious ideas only where they buy real leverage: Galois-style monotone trust derivations, lattice-safe demotion rules, and fraud-proof style witnesses for downstream trust disagreements.

Acceptance criteria:
1. Trust cards can no longer be created or mutated from raw caller-supplied provenance/reputation/certification claims; they must be derived from verified upstream evidence records or fail closed.
2. Certification evaluation consumes verified provenance/reputation/evidence references, not ad hoc booleans and free-form asserted levels.
3. Every trust card and certification result carries derivation metadata that links back to specific verified manifest/provenance/revocation/reputation inputs and survives deterministic replay.
4. Demotion and quarantine flows are monotone: once upstream evidence degrades or is revoked, downstream trust cards/certification cannot silently remain at the old level.
5. `bd-2yh`, `bd-273`, and `bd-y4g` share one canonical trust-derivation kernel instead of each accepting local asserted trust inputs.
6. Adversarial fixtures cover caller-injected fake provenance summaries, forged reputation jumps, stale certification evidence, conflicting upstream inputs, and trust-card mutation attempts that bypass verified evidence binding.
7. Add a checker that fails if replacement-critical trust surfaces reintroduce input structs or code paths that let callers inject final trust claims without verified evidence handles.
8. Deliver unit tests, integration/E2E trust-materialization fixtures, structured logs, and machine-readable derivation artifacts proving that downstream trust objects are grounded in verified state.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Trust-card and certification APIs consume verified evidence handles only; callers cannot supply final trust facts, provenance summaries, or certification levels directly on any replacement-critical path.
2. Downstream trust behavior is user-explainable: every trust card or certification result carries a derivation tree, downgrade and quarantine reasons, and stable reason codes suitable for UI, CLI, and incident bundles.
3. Unit tests cover handle typing, monotone demotion rules, revocation propagation, conflicting upstream evidence resolution, stale evidence rejection, and regression checks against asserted-input shortcuts.
4. Integration tests exercise registry admit -> trust-card materialization -> certification -> revocation -> downgrade -> quarantine -> recovery, proving downstream state changes track upstream evidence exactly.
5. At least one deterministic operator E2E shell script under tests/e2e/ reproduces trust-card issuance, certification changes, revocation-driven demotion, and quarantine behavior with detailed logs and replayable fixtures.
6. Structured logs expose stable TRUST_DERIVATION_* and CERTIFICATION_DECISION_* event families with required fields: trace_id, evidence_ids, subject_id, previous_level, new_level, reason_code, and replay_bundle_id.
7. Evidence artifacts under artifacts/replacement_gap/bd-1oju/ include machine-readable derivation receipts, human-readable trust summaries, adversarial fixture indexes, and rch offload build IDs for the verification run.
8. Completion requires a static regression checker that fails if replacement-critical trust surfaces reintroduce free-form asserted-input structs or bypass verified evidence handles.

title: [10.14] Attach trace-witness references to every high-impact ledger entry.
description:
## Why This Exists
High-impact control decisions (e.g., quarantine promotions, durability mode changes, hardening escalations) need more than just an evidence entry — they need traceable links to the specific observations and system state snapshots that caused the decision. Trace-witness references provide this linkage by embedding stable witness IDs into evidence entries, allowing operators and automated replay tools to resolve the exact context that led to a decision. Without witness references, evidence entries are self-contained records but lack the "because of what?" connection needed for deep root-cause analysis. This is a key requirement of the 9J enhancement map's witness-linked audit trail and supports Section 8.5 Invariant #3 (deterministic replay) by ensuring replay bundles can reconstruct the full decision context.

## What This Must Do
1. Define a `WitnessRef` type in `crates/franken-node/src/observability/witness_ref.rs` containing:
   - `witness_id: WitnessId` — stable, unique identifier for the witness observation.
   - `witness_kind: WitnessKind` enum (Telemetry, StateSnapshot, ProofArtifact, ExternalSignal).
   - `replay_bundle_locator: Option<String>` — URI or path where the full witness can be resolved.
   - `integrity_hash: [u8; 32]` — SHA-256 hash of the witness content for tamper detection.
2. Define "high-impact" classification criteria in code: a predicate `fn is_high_impact(entry: &EvidenceEntry) -> bool` that identifies entries requiring witness references based on `DecisionKind` (Quarantine, Release, Escalate) and configurable policy thresholds.
3. Implement a validation pass in the evidence emission pipeline that:
   - Checks all high-impact entries for non-empty `witness_references`.
   - Validates each `WitnessRef.integrity_hash` against the referenced witness content (when locally available).
   - Rejects entries with broken or unresolvable witness references via an integrity check failure.
4. Write integration tests at `tests/integration/evidence_trace_witness_linking.rs` covering:
   - High-impact entry with valid witness references passes validation.
   - High-impact entry with empty witness references fails validation.
   - Witness reference with tampered integrity hash fails validation.
   - Witness reference resolves correctly in a replay bundle fixture.
5. Write specification at `docs/specs/witness_reference_contract.md` documenting the `WitnessRef` structure, high-impact classification criteria, and resolution protocol.
6. Produce audit artifact at `artifacts/10.14/witness_link_audit.json` summarizing witness coverage across a test corpus.

## Acceptance Criteria
- High-impact evidence entries include stable trace witness IDs; witness references resolve in replay bundles; broken references fail integrity check.
- All entries with `DecisionKind` in {Quarantine, Release, Escalate} have at least one `WitnessRef`.
- `WitnessRef.integrity_hash` mismatches are detected and reported.
- Entries with unresolvable `replay_bundle_locator` fail validation with a specific error code.
- Non-high-impact entries are not required to have witness references (but may optionally include them).
- Witness link audit artifact shows 100% coverage for high-impact test scenarios.

## Testing & Logging Requirements
- Unit tests: `WitnessRef` serialization roundtrip; `is_high_impact` predicate for each `DecisionKind`; integrity hash computation and verification; `WitnessKind` enum coverage.
- Integration tests: End-to-end flow: create high-impact decision, attach witnesses, emit evidence, validate witness links; replay bundle resolution with fixture data.
- Conformance tests: High-impact entry without witnesses is rejected; witness-bearing entry roundtrips through ledger and snapshot; multi-witness entry preserves ordering.
- Adversarial tests: Tamper with witness hash after attachment; provide witness locator pointing to nonexistent path; attach witness of wrong kind to entry; duplicate witness IDs on same entry.
- Structured logs: `EVD-WITNESS-001` on witness attached; `EVD-WITNESS-002` on witness validation pass; `EVD-WITNESS-003` on broken reference detected; `EVD-WITNESS-004` on integrity hash mismatch. All logs include `entry_id`, `witness_id`.

## Expected Artifacts
- `tests/integration/evidence_trace_witness_linking.rs` — integration tests
- `docs/specs/witness_reference_contract.md` — specification
- `artifacts/10.14/witness_link_audit.json` — witness coverage audit
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-1oof/verification_evidence.json` — machine-readable pass/fail evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-1oof/verification_summary.md` — human-readable summary

## Dependencies
- Upstream: bd-oolt (mandatory evidence emission — witness attachment builds on top of emission)
- Downstream: bd-3epz (section gate), bd-5rh (10.14 plan gate)
acceptance_criteria: High-impact evidence entries include stable trace witness IDs; witness references resolve in replay bundles; broken references fail integrity check.

title: [METAMORPHIC] hash chain order-sensitivity for evidence ledger
description:
Add metamorphic test verifying hash chain order-sensitivity for evidence ledger.

**MR Category:** Permutative (order-sensitive)
**Property:** For distinct entries E1 ≠ E2, the chain tip after append([E1, E2]) must differ from the chain tip after append([E2, E1]).

**Why this matters:** A hash chain's tamper-detection guarantee depends on the chain tip being a function of the full ordered append history. If the chain were order-insensitive, an attacker could reorder evidence without detection.

**Concretely:** prev_entry_hash of the second-appended entry binds to the first-appended entry's content hash. Swapping order produces different prev_entry_hash bindings for the second slot. The metamorphic test asserts:
1. Order sensitivity: snapshot[1].prev_entry_hash differs across append orders
2. Membership commutativity: the multiset of (decision_id, epoch_id) pairs is invariant under reorder
3. First-entry invariant: snapshot[0].prev_entry_hash is empty in both runs

Score: F=4 (catches accidental commutative-hash, weak chaining, missing prev_hash binding) × I=4 (orthogonal to existing canonical-serializer/replay-bundle MRs) / C=1 (cheap, ~ms) = 16.

Files:
- New: crates/franken-node/tests/evidence_ledger_chain_order_metamorphic.rs
close_reason: Metamorphic suite green (4 passed): MR1 chain-head-changes-under-swap, MR2 membership-commutative, MR3 prev-hash-sequence-uniqueness, MR4 PBT order-sensitivity. MR3 was originally over-specified (asserted tail prev_entry_hash uniqueness, but compute_entry_hash deliberately excludes prev_entry_hash to avoid circular dep — corrected to assert sequence-of-prev-hashes uniqueness which holds and still distinguishes all 6 perms). Also fixed build break inherited from 977d9df0 (FleetTransport/FleetTransportError name collisions + missing FleetControlError::internal). Committed in 5088d52d.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/connector/activation_pipeline.rs around lines 151-167
STRUCT: DefaultExecutor (implements StageExecutor trait)

CURRENT CODE:
  pub struct DefaultExecutor;
  impl StageExecutor for DefaultExecutor {
      fn create_sandbox(&self, _config: &str) -> Result<(), String> { Ok(()) }
      fn mount_secrets(&self, refs: &[String]) -> Result<Vec<String>, String> { Ok(refs.to_vec()) }
      fn issue_capabilities(&self, _caps: &[String]) -> Result<(), String> { Ok(()) }
      fn health_check(&self) -> Result<(), String> { Ok(()) }
  }

PROBLEM: All four stage methods are no-ops that always succeed. In production:
  - create_sandbox should actually create an isolated execution environment
  - mount_secrets should resolve secret references and inject them (with cleanup on failure per INV-ACT-NO-SECRET-LEAK)
  - issue_capabilities should provision runtime capabilities to the sandbox
  - health_check should verify the sandbox is operational

With the current code, the activation pipeline always "succeeds" without doing anything, and the transcript records a successful activation that never actually happened.

REQUIRED FIX: This is a significant implementation effort. Consider a phased approach:
  Phase 1: Add validation/precondition checks to each method (verify config is valid JSON, verify secret refs are well-formed, verify caps are recognized)
  Phase 2: Implement actual sandbox creation (may depend on isolation_backend OCI runtime)
  Phase 3: Implement secret mounting and capability issuance

CONSIDERATIONS:
- The trait-based design (StageExecutor) is correct — DefaultExecutor can remain as a test/dev stub, but a ProductionExecutor should be created
- The activate() function at line 174 handles failure correctly (INV-ACT-NO-SECRET-LEAK cleanup) — this cleanup logic will actually matter once stages can fail
- Check who constructs DefaultExecutor — if main.rs uses it unconditionally, it needs a way to select ProductionExecutor based on config/profile
- This may be the largest single task — consider splitting into sub-beads if needed
- The no-op pattern is intentional scaffolding (the comment says "Default executor that simulates successful stages") — the architecture is sound, just needs implementation

title: [REVIEW] verifier SDK seal_session accepts foreign verifier sessions
description: sdk/verifier/src/lib.rs: seal_session() marks a session sealed and computes a final verdict without verifying that session.verifier_identity matches the active VerifierSdk identity. Expected fix: reject seal_session when session.verifier_identity differs from self.verifier_identity, add unit tests for same-verifier success and foreign-session rejection, then rerun rch exec -- cargo check -p frankenengine-node --tests.

**ASSESSMENT COMPLETE: NOT APPLICABLE**

Conformal prediction is inappropriate for ThresholdsConfig:

**No calibration data available:**
- ThresholdsConfig contains static hardcoded thresholds (max_failure_rate=0.05, min_quality_score=0.8, etc.)
- No historical ground truth data exists for calibration
- No evidence collection framework for nonconformity score computation

**Wrong problem type:**
- Current usage: simple binary decisions ()
- Conformal prediction purpose: distribution-free confidence intervals
- No uncertainty quantification needs identified in current codebase

**Simpler approaches sufficient:**
- Static thresholds work for current use cases
- If uncertainty quantification needed: Wilson confidence intervals or Beta-Binomial would suffice
- No complex validity guarantees required for configuration thresholds

**Recommendation:** Close as premature. Conformal prediction belongs in prediction/ML systems with calibration datasets, not static configuration management.

title: [10.20] Implement adversarial contagion simulator for xz-style and multi-stage supply-chain campaigns.
description:
## Why This Exists

The xz-utils backdoor was a multi-stage supply-chain campaign that exploited social engineering, commit access concentration, and transitive trust propagation. Detecting such campaigns before they succeed requires the ability to simulate them against the actual dependency graph. This bead builds the adversarial contagion simulator within DGIS -- a tool that models how supply-chain compromises propagate through the dependency graph under various attacker strategies and policy conditions.

The simulator consumes the topology metrics from bd-t89w to understand graph structure, then runs parameterized campaigns (xz-style social-engineering-to-commit-access, typosquatting, dependency confusion, multi-stage delayed activation) to estimate blast radius, propagation speed, and detection probability. Outputs feed into the immunization planner (bd-2fid) for defensive planning and the economics engine (bd-19k2) for expected-loss estimation.

Within the 9N enhancement map, this is the offensive-analysis complement to the defensive immunization planner. Together they form a red-team/blue-team loop that strengthens DGIS recommendations.

## What This Must Do

1. Implement a contagion simulation engine that propagates compromise through the dependency graph according to parameterized campaign models.
2. Support campaign templates for: xz-style (social engineering + commit access takeover), typosquatting, dependency confusion, multi-stage delayed activation, and supply-chain pivot chains.
3. Model probabilistic branching: at each propagation step, compromise success depends on configurable probability distributions conditioned on node properties (trust level, barrier status, monitoring intensity).
4. Support policy-conditioned propagation: barriers (from bd-1tnu), quarantine zones, and monitoring policies modulate propagation probability.
5. Ensure reproducibility via fixed random seeds and canonical scenario descriptors -- identical seeds + scenarios produce identical simulation traces.
6. Output per-simulation: blast radius (nodes reached), propagation timeline, policy bypass events, and detection/containment opportunities missed.
7. Support batch simulation with parameter sweeps for sensitivity analysis.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Simulator supports campaign templates, probabilistic branching, and policy-conditioned propagation; runs are reproducible via fixed seeds and canonical scenario descriptors.
- At least 4 campaign templates are implemented: xz-style, typosquatting, dependency confusion, multi-stage delayed activation.
- Fixed-seed reproducibility: identical seed + scenario produces byte-identical simulation trace.
- Policy conditioning demonstrably reduces blast radius compared to barrier-free baseline in test scenarios.
- Batch simulation with parameter sweeps produces structured sensitivity analysis output.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: individual campaign template propagation logic; probabilistic branching with seeded RNG verification; policy barrier modulation effects; edge-case handling (isolated nodes, fully-connected subgraphs).
- Integration tests: end-to-end simulation from ingested graph + campaign descriptor to simulation report; reproducibility verification via double-run comparison; sensitivity analysis output validation.
- Structured logging: simulation events with stable codes (DGIS-CONTAGION-001 through DGIS-CONTAGION-NNN); per-step propagation telemetry; policy bypass event logging; trace correlation IDs linking simulation runs to graph snapshots.
- Deterministic replay: canonical scenario descriptors and seeded fixtures checked into repository.

## Expected Artifacts

- `src/security/dgis/contagion_simulator.rs` -- simulator implementation

title: [REALITY] Implement real ops rotate-key or enforce preview boundary
description:
Reality-check gap: `ops rotate-key` validates a key file and emits `actual_rotation_occurred=false`; it does not update signer config or append evidence-ledger state. The current warning is truthful, but the command name is operationally dangerous if users assume rotation occurred.

User outcome: operators need either a real key-rotation workflow that changes the active signer and leaves auditable evidence, or an unmistakable preview-only command that cannot be mistaken for remediation. Prefer implementing real rotation if the config/evidence architecture supports it; otherwise strengthen the preview boundary without deleting the command.

Implementation requirements:
1. First evaluate whether real rotation can be implemented safely in the current config/evidence model.
2. If implementing real rotation: atomically update configured signer state, preserve rollback/backup metadata, append signed evidence-ledger entry, validate old/new fingerprints, and expose dry-run/preview mode separately from apply mode.
3. If deferring real rotation: rename/help/docs/output must make preview-only status unavoidable, automation must receive a non-success or explicit preview status, and operator capability claims must exclude it.
4. In both paths, preserve key validation, fingerprint calculation, JSON/human output, and existing safety warnings; do not remove functionality or hide the current limitation.
5. Fail closed on invalid key material, signer-config write failure, evidence-ledger append failure, mismatched fingerprints, and concurrent/stale config updates.

Testing/logging requirements:
- Unit tests for key parsing, fingerprint stability, invalid key rejection, dry-run/preview behavior, atomic config update, evidence entry fields/signature, rollback metadata, concurrent update rejection, and ledger append failure.
- E2E CLI tests for preview/dry-run, successful apply if implemented, invalid key, write failure using read-only/temp config, and JSON fields consumed by automation.
- Script-level operator test that runs rotate-key in a temp workspace and verifies active signer before/after, evidence ledger state, and failure behavior.
- Structured logs/events for rotate_key_started, key_validated, signer_config_update_started, signer_config_updated, evidence_entry_appended, rotation_preview_only, rotation_failed, and rotate_key_completed; include trace_id, old_fingerprint, new_fingerprint, apply/dry_run, evidence_path, and config_path.
- Verification commands must include rch cargo check/clippy/fmt plus focused ops rotate-key unit/E2E tests.
design:
Design notes for implementation:
- The best user outcome is real rotation if the current config/evidence model can support atomic update and rollback. If it cannot, the second-best outcome is an unmistakable preview command that automation cannot treat as remediation.
- Do an implementation feasibility check first, then choose one of two explicit paths: real apply mode or hardened preview boundary. Do not leave a half-implemented apply path.
- If real apply mode lands, use atomic write/rename or equivalent, parent-dir sync where applicable, backup/rollback metadata, concurrent update guard, and signed evidence append.
- If preview-only remains, consider exit/status semantics carefully: machine output should include a stable non-rotation status that scripts must branch on.
- Keep existing warnings and fingerprint calculation; prior work already fixed preview honesty around old_key_fingerprint, so do not regress that.
- The E2E script should inspect config/evidence before and after command execution so it proves state, not just stdout.
- Estimate: medium; may become large only if signer config ownership is more spread out than expected.
acceptance_criteria: The bead closes only if operators cannot mistake validation for rotation. Either real rotation updates signer state and evidence ledger atomically with tests, or preview-only status is enforced in CLI/help/docs/automation semantics. Existing validation/fingerprint behavior is preserved. Unit, E2E, operator-script, fail-closed, and structured logging coverage are included.

title: [SECAUDIT] ssrf_policy + network_guard: DNS hostnames bypass IP-based blocklist (rebinding-friendly)
description:
LENS: SSRF / DNS rebinding (security-audit-for-saas Operator: ✂ Parser-Diverge — config-time URL validator vs runtime fetcher)
FILE:
  - crates/franken-node/src/security/ssrf_policy.rs:319-560 (check_ssrf), 513-516 (the silent allow path), 269-308 (is_private_ip)
  - crates/franken-node/src/security/network_guard.rs:79-101 (host_matches), 152-167 (EgressPolicy::evaluate)

THREAT MODEL: SsrfPolicyTemplate::check_ssrf and NetworkGuard::process_egress both treat the `host: &str` parameter as ground truth.  Neither resolves the hostname to determine whether the connection target IP falls inside the blocked CIDRs (127/8, 10/8, 169.254/16, 100.64/10, etc.).  An attacker who can supply or influence a hostname can bypass the SSRF block:
  - direct: register `cloudmeta.attacker.com` with an A record at 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata).
  - DNS rebinding: respond first with 1.2.3.4 (passes any allowlist check that resolves), then with 169.254.169.254 on the connect-time resolution.

EXPLOIT SKETCH (path 1 — direct):
  1. `check_ssrf("cloudmeta.attacker.com", 80, Http, ...)`.
  2. parse_ipv4 fails (it's not an IP literal); the function falls to line 515-516: `self.emit_audit(host, port, Action::Allow, None, false, ...); return Ok(Action::Allow)` with the comment "Public IP — allow".  But it isn't a public IP — it's an unresolved DNS name that may resolve to anywhere.
  3. NetworkGuard sees a wildcard `*.attacker.com` allow rule (or no rule, default-deny — the gap is identical when the rule says allow).
  4. Egress proceeds; downstream HTTP client resolves the name and connects to 169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/.

EXPLOIT SKETCH (path 2 — rebinding): same setup but DNS TTL=0; first lookup (e.g., a connectivity preflight by the operator) returns a public IP; second lookup at connect time returns the metadata IP.  No code path in network_guard.rs or ssrf_policy.rs re-checks IP between resolve and connect.

ROOT CAUSE: All matching is string-level.  is_private_ip explicitly returns `false` when the input cannot be parsed as an IPv4 literal (line 303).  host_matches in network_guard does ASCII-case-insensitive suffix/exact matching with no resolution.  The crate currently has no production HTTP client (no reqwest/hyper::Client uses outside test scaffolding — verified via rg) so this is preventative rather than currently-exploited, but the policies are exported and intended to gate any future outbound integration.

MITIGATION:
  1. Make check_ssrf require a resolved IP, not a hostname.  Introduce `check_ssrf_resolved(host: &str, ip: IpAddr, port: u16, ...)` and have callers pass the connect-time IP from a single resolver.
  2. Add a "DNS resolution must be private-safe" wrapper that resolves the hostname once, validates EVERY returned A/AAAA record against the blocked CIDRs (fail-closed if any record matches), and pins the connection to the chosen IP — closing the rebinding window.
  3. For the unresolved-hostname Allow branch (lines 513-516), change the default to `Action::Deny` with a feature flag `allow_unresolved_dns_names` so operators must explicitly opt in.
  4. In NetworkGuard, add a `resolve_and_validate` method that takes the host, performs DNS resolution, and rejects if any IP is private — independent of any name-based rule.

CROSS-REF: Pattern matches the prompt's category "SSRF / SSRF-via-config: URL parsing that trusts the host portion, redirect-following without re-validation, DNS rebinding mitigations? (Resolution → connection gap)."  Distinct from any existing bead.
close_reason: Completed in 458b2e3f: SSRF and network guard now require resolved public IP evidence and fail closed for unresolved/private DNS answers.

title: [10.0] Implement compatibility envelope + divergence ledger.
description:
Master Plan Source: PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_NODE.md
Section: 10.0 — Top 10 Initiative Tracking (Initiative #1, highest priority)
Cross-references: 9A.1, 9B.1, 9C.1, 9D.1

Why This Exists:
The compatibility envelope is the #1 strategic initiative. It creates a deterministic compatibility layer covering high-value Node/Bun behavior while making intentional divergences first-class, policy-visible, and signed. Without this, users cannot trust that franken_node faithfully reproduces expected behavior or understand where/why it intentionally differs.

Task Objective:
Implement the compatibility envelope (the boundary defining which Node/Bun APIs are covered and at what fidelity) together with the divergence ledger (an append-only, signed record of intentional behavioral differences with rationale).

Detailed Acceptance Criteria:
1. Compatibility envelope covers the four bands defined in 10.2: core, high-value, edge, unsafe, each with explicit policy defaults.
2. Divergence ledger stores signed rationale entries for every intentional behavioral difference, with author, timestamp, affected API, severity, and justification fields.
3. Each divergence entry is append-only and tamper-evident (hash-chained or Merkle-backed).
4. Policy-visible: operators can query the ledger to understand all divergences for a given API surface, risk band, or profile.
5. Integration with compatibility modes (strict, balanced, legacy-risky) — divergence handling varies by mode.
6. Shim dispatch overhead profiled and reduced with precompiled decision DAGs where safe (9D.1).
7. Typed-state transition primitives and session-type protocol checks applied to compatibility pathways (9B.1).
8. Proof-carrying compatibility claims: each shim publishes invariance evidence and explicit divergence rationale (9C.1).

Key Dependencies:
- Depends on 10.2 (Compatibility Core) for band definitions and fixture runners.
- Depends on 10.1 (Charter) for split-governance boundaries.
- Depends on 10.N (Normalization) for canonical ownership rules.
- Consumed by 10.3 (Migration) for risk assessment and 10.7 (Verification) for golden corpus.

Expected Artifacts:
- src/conformance/compatibility_envelope.rs — envelope definition and query API.
- src/conformance/divergence_ledger.rs — signed divergence entry storage.
- docs/specs/section_10_0/bd-1qp_contract.md — design rationale, invariants, interface boundaries.
- artifacts/section_10_0/bd-1qp/verification_evidence.json — machine-readable CI gate.
- artifacts/section_10_0/bd-1qp/verification_summary.md — human-readable summary.

Testing and Logging Requirements:
- Unit tests: envelope boundary queries, divergence entry creation/validation, hash chain integrity, mode-dependent divergence handling, band membership queries.
- Integration tests: full workflow from API call -> envelope check -> divergence recording -> ledger query -> policy-visible output.
- E2E tests: operator scenario exercising franken-node verify lockstep with divergence report generation.
- Fuzz tests: malformed divergence entries, hash chain corruption detection.
- Structured logs: stable event codes for COMPAT_ENVELOPE_QUERY, DIVERGENCE_RECORDED, DIVERGENCE_QUERIED, HASH_CHAIN_VERIFIED with trace correlation IDs.

Why This Improves User Outcomes:
- Operators get deterministic, explainable answers about what behavior they can expect from franken_node vs Node/Bun.
- Signed divergence rationale prevents silent behavior drift — every difference is intentional and auditable.
- Policy-visible divergence data enables informed risk decisions during migration and rollout.
- Proof-carrying claims (9C.1) enable external verification of compatibility assertions.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Envelope definition covers >= 95% of high-value Node.js API surface (fs, net, http, crypto, stream, child_process, path, os, events, buffer, url, util, assert, timers) measured by weighted API call frequency in npm-top-1000.
2. Divergence ledger schema captures: API name, divergence type (semantic/signature/missing), severity (breaking/degraded/cosmetic), policy disposition (accepted/mitigated/blocked), signature of approver.
3. Every intentional divergence has a signed entry with rationale, linked mitigation shim (if any), and policy-gate flag.
4. Compatibility score computation is deterministic: same input manifest produces identical score across runs (no floating-point drift, no ordering sensitivity).
5. Ledger entries are cryptographically signed and append-only; tampering detection via hash chain verification.
6. CI gate rejects PRs that reduce overall compatibility score below the 95% category target threshold (Section 3).
7. Divergence ledger is queryable via CLI (`franken-node compat divergences --format json`) and produces machine-readable output for downstream tooling.
8. Replay coverage for envelope validation reaches 100% of catalogued divergences (Section 3 target).
9. Cross-references to enhancement maps 9A.1, 9B.1, 9C.1, 9D.1 verified: each sub-deliverable traceable.
10. Verification evidence artifact contains: compatibility score, divergence count by severity, ledger integrity hash, timestamp.

title: [MOCK] lineage_tracker::verify_snapshot_faithful only compares counts, not edge contents
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/security/lineage_tracker.rs:1830-1834

FINDING: invariants::verify_snapshot_faithful(graph, snapshot) is documented as INV-IFL-SNAPSHOT-FAITHFUL ('the snapshot is a faithful representation of the live lineage graph'), but the implementation only checks three scalar counters and a schema string:
    pub fn verify_snapshot_faithful(graph: &LineageGraph, snapshot: &LineageSnapshot) -> bool {
        snapshot.edge_count == graph.edge_count()
            && snapshot.label_count == graph.label_count()
            && snapshot.schema_version == SCHEMA_VERSION
    }

WHY IT'S A BUG: A snapshot with completely different edges and labels but matching cardinalities will pass this check. The invariant 'faithful' implies that the captured edges/labels are the same as the graph's; a count-only check cannot detect content drift, edge reordering, or label substitution. This is a stub: the function name promises a deep equality check but the body provides only a shallow consistency check. For a security-critical taint-tracking module this is a meaningful gap because an attacker who can perturb the snapshot (e.g. by swapping edges with attacker-influenced ones while preserving counts) would not be detected.

SUGGESTED FIX: Either (a) compare a deterministic hash of the snapshot's serialized edges/labels against a hash computed by graph (length-prefixed canonical encoding, ct_eq-compared); or (b) compare BTreeSet<EdgeKey> equality between snapshot.edges and graph.edges (deterministic O(N log N)); or (c) rename the function to verify_snapshot_count_consistent and add a separate verify_snapshot_content_faithful that does the deep check. Even option (c) — explicit naming — eliminates the false confidence.

EVIDENCE:
1830:     pub fn verify_snapshot_faithful(graph: &LineageGraph, snapshot: &LineageSnapshot) -> bool {
1831:         snapshot.edge_count == graph.edge_count()
1832:             && snapshot.label_count == graph.label_count()
1833:             && snapshot.schema_version == SCHEMA_VERSION
1834:     }

Compare to the doc-comment (one line above):
    /// Verify INV-IFL-SNAPSHOT-FAITHFUL: a snapshot accurately represents the graph.
close_reason: Completed in 2c54f06c: verify_snapshot_faithful now compares snapshot edge and label contents, and exfiltration sentinel scenarios cover edge substitution, edge reordering, and label substitution via the public crate API.

title: [REVIEW] Signed extension manifest decodes unbounded signatures
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/supply_chain/manifest.rs:161
PATTERN: unbounded Vec growth before signature length validation
WHY IT'S A BUG: validate_signature only checks that signature.signature is base64-like and padded, then to_engine_manifest decodes the entire untrusted string into sig_bytes before any Ed25519/threshold signature byte cap. A malicious manifest can force large allocations during validation instead of failing closed on the expected fixed-size signature envelope.\nSUGGESTED FIX: Add a maximum encoded signature length and decoded-byte length check before base64 decode; for Ed25519 require exactly 64 decoded bytes, and for threshold signatures cap by total_signers * 64 plus envelope overhead. Update the negative massive-signature test to require rejection before projection.\nEVIDENCE: git blame -L 155,190 -L 335,397 -L 1152,1164 -- crates/franken-node/src/supply_chain/manifest.rs shows lines 161-165 decode self.signature.signature into a Vec, lines 335-397 perform only base64-shape checks, and the negative_massive_signature_memory_exhaustion test builds a 10MB signature and only asserts no panic.
close_reason: Bounded signed extension manifest signatures before base64 decode; Ed25519 now requires exactly 64 decoded bytes and threshold signatures fail closed above signer-derived envelope budget.

title: [REVIEW] Checker UTF-8 decode errors bypass fail-closed read paths
description:
FILE: scripts/check_policy_approval.py:147; scripts/check_transparency_verifier.py:30; scripts/check_provenance_gate.py:38; scripts/check_device_profile.py:28; scripts/check_quarantine_store.py:27
PATTERN: fallible artifact/source reads only catch OSError/JSONDecodeError, not UnicodeDecodeError
WHY IT'S A BUG: These verification checkers are supposed to turn missing, unreadable, or malformed inputs into structured FAIL evidence. Existing non-UTF-8 content makes Path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") raise UnicodeDecodeError before the helper can return a failed check, so --json and human gate paths can crash with a traceback instead of failing closed.
SUGGESTED FIX: Catch UnicodeDecodeError or UnicodeError alongside OSError in read_utf8/read_required_text/load_json_object helpers, and add temp-file regression coverage with invalid UTF-8 bytes for both text and JSON artifact readers.

title: [10.10] Implement audience-bound token chains for control actions.
description:
Master Plan Source: PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_NODE.md — Section 10.10 (FCP-Inspired Hardening), cross-ref Section 9E.4

## Why This Exists

Enhancement Map 9E.4 mandates capability token delegation chains for migration and control-plane actions. In the three-kernel architecture, control actions (policy updates, migration triggers, zone reconfiguration) must carry cryptographic proof of authorization that is audience-bound — a token issued for one service/kernel cannot be replayed against another. Without audience-bound token chains, the no-ambient-authority invariant (8.5) is violated: any entity with a valid token could escalate its reach across kernel boundaries. This bead implements the product-level token chain system where each delegation step narrows scope, binds to a specific audience, and carries a verifiable chain of custody back to the original authority.

## What This Must Do

1. Define an `AudienceBoundToken` struct containing: issuer identity, audience (target service/kernel/zone), delegated capabilities (explicit allowlist), expiry (epoch-scoped), nonce, parent token hash (for chain verification), and signature over canonical preimage.
2. Implement `TokenChain` — an ordered sequence of delegation tokens where each token's `parent_token_hash` links to its predecessor, capabilities are monotonically narrowing (each delegation can only reduce scope, never widen), and audience fields are non-empty.
3. Provide `issue_token()`, `delegate_token()`, `verify_chain()`, and `check_audience()` APIs for product control-plane code to use when authorizing actions.
4. Enforce that `delegate_token()` rejects any attempt to widen capabilities beyond what the parent token grants — strict attenuation invariant.
5. Integrate audience checking into all control-plane action dispatch points: before executing any control action, the dispatcher verifies that the token chain's terminal audience matches the executing service identity.
6. All token serialization uses the canonical serializer from bd-jjm; all chain verification checks divergence-free state from bd-2ms before accepting tokens from remote nodes.

## Context from Enhancement Maps

- 9E.4: "Capability token delegation chains for migration and control-plane actions"
- 9E.5 (cross-ref): Key-role separation (bd-364) ensures that signing keys used for token issuance are distinct from encryption and operational keys.
- 9E.1 (cross-ref): Canonical object identity (bd-1l5) provides the domain-separation tags used in token type identification.
- 9B.3 (Migration): Migration operations require delegation tokens that prove the migration controller has authority scoped to the specific migration epoch and target.

## Dependencies

- Upstream: bd-2ms ([10.10] Implement rollback/fork detection in control-plane state propagation) — token acceptance requires divergence-free state verification.
- Downstream: bd-364 ([10.10] Implement key-role separation for control-plane signing/encryption/issuance) — key-role separation builds on the token chain to ensure issuance keys are properly scoped.
- Downstream: bd-1jjq ([10.10] Section-wide verification gate) — aggregates verification evidence.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `AudienceBoundToken` includes all required fields (issuer, audience, capabilities, expiry, nonce, parent_hash, signature) with documented invariants.
2. Token delegation strictly attenuates: any attempt to delegate a wider capability set than the parent token grants is rejected with `TOKEN_ATTENUATION_VIOLATION`.
3. Audience mismatch is detected and rejected with `TOKEN_AUDIENCE_MISMATCH` before any control action executes — zero bypass paths verified by code audit.
4. Token chains of depth 10+ verify correctly with sub-millisecond verification time per chain link.
5. Expired tokens (past epoch boundary) are rejected with `TOKEN_EXPIRED` regardless of chain validity.
6. Nonce uniqueness is enforced within an epoch — replaying a token with the same nonce is rejected with `TOKEN_REPLAY_DETECTED`.
7. All token serialization routes through bd-jjm's canonical serializer — verified by golden vector cross-check.
8. Verification evidence JSON includes chain depths tested, attenuation scenarios, and audience mismatch rejection counts.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: Create token chains of depth 1, 5, and 20 and verify correct chain validation. Test strict attenuation: parent grants {read, write, admin}, child attempts {read, write, admin, superadmin} — must reject. Test audience binding: token for "kernel-A" presented to "kernel-B" — must reject. Test expiry at epoch boundary. Test nonce replay detection. Test empty capability set (should be valid — a fully attenuated token grants nothing).
- Integration tests: Simulate a migration workflow where a migration controller issues a scoped token to a worker, the worker delegates a further-narrowed token to a sub-task, and the final action is authorized against the full chain. Verify that token verification checks divergence state (bd-2ms) before accepting remote tokens.
- Adversarial tests: Attempt to forge a token chain by inserting a token with a fake parent_hash. Attempt to widen capabilities in the middle of a chain. Attempt cross-audience token replay. Attempt to use a token after its epoch expires but before garbage collection. Test with corrupted signature bytes.
- Structured logs: `TOKEN_ISSUED` (issuer, audience, capability_count, expiry_epoch, chain_depth). `TOKEN_DELEGATED` (delegator, new_audience, attenuated_capabilities, new_chain_depth). `TOKEN_VERIFIED` (chain_depth, audience_match, verification_duration_us). `TOKEN_REJECTED` (reason, attempted_audience, actual_audience, chain_depth). All events include `trace_id`, `epoch_id`, and `action_id`.

## Expected Artifacts

- docs/specs/section_10_10/bd-1r2_contract.md
- crates/franken-node/src/connector/token_chain.rs (or similar module path)
- scripts/check_token_chain.py with --json flag and self_test()
- tests/test_check_token_chain.py
- artifacts/section_10_10/bd-1r2/verification_evidence.json
- artifacts/section_10_10/bd-1r2/verification_summary.md
acceptance_criteria:
1. Define an AudienceBoundToken struct containing: (a) token_id (TrustObjectId with TOKEN domain), (b) issuer_key_id (TrustObjectId with KEY domain), (c) audience (a list of 1+ TrustObjectId values identifying the intended recipients/zones), (d) action_scope (enum: MIGRATE, ROLLBACK, PROMOTE, REVOKE, CONFIGURE), (e) issued_at (UTC timestamp), (f) expires_at (UTC timestamp), (g) delegation_parent (Option<token_id> for chained delegation, None for root tokens), (h) max_delegation_depth (u8, default 0 = no further delegation).
2. Implement token chain validation: given a chain of tokens [root, delegate1, delegate2, ...], verify: (a) each delegate's delegation_parent matches the previous token_id, (b) chain length <= root's max_delegation_depth + 1, (c) each delegate's audience is a subset of its parent's audience (no audience escalation), (d) each delegate's action_scope is a subset of its parent's action_scope, (e) no token in the chain is expired at the evaluation timestamp.
3. Implement audience binding check: given a token and a requester identity (TrustObjectId), verify the requester appears in the token's audience list. Reject with AudienceMismatch error.
4. Implement scope narrowing: a delegated token MUST NOT grant action_scopes not present in the parent. Return ScopeEscalation error on violation.
5. Reject tokens where issued_at >= expires_at (zero or negative validity window).
6. Reject delegation chains where any intermediate token is expired even if the leaf is not.
7. Unit tests: (a) valid root token creation, (b) valid single-hop delegation, (c) valid multi-hop delegation, (d) audience escalation rejection, (e) scope escalation rejection, (f) depth limit exceeded, (g) expired intermediate rejection, (h) zero-validity rejection, (i) audience mismatch.
8. Golden fixture: a 3-level delegation chain in vectors/audience_bound_tokens.json with known pass/fail cases.
9. Verification: scripts/check_token_chains.py --json, artifacts at artifacts/section_10_10/bd-1r2/.

Task-Specific Clarification:
- The implementation must deliver the exact capability named in the title, with no scope dilution and no silent feature omission.
- Validation artifacts must include capability-specific thresholds, pass/fail criteria, and reproducible evidence bundles tied to this bead ID.
- Program/section verification gates must be able to consume this bead's outputs without manual interpretation.

Why This Improves User Outcomes:
- "[12] Risk control: longitudinal privacy/re-identification" is required to reduce operator error, increase deterministic safety guarantees, and improve time-to-diagnosis for failures in real-world workflows.
- Explicit success/failure evidence for "[12] Risk control: longitudinal privacy/re-identification" prevents false confidence and improves trust in migration/compatibility/security outcomes.
- Detailed unit + integration/E2E + structured logging requirements ensure reproducible quality and faster incident remediation for users.
acceptance_criteria:
RISK: Longitudinal trajectory privacy/re-identification — accumulated behavioral data over time enables re-identification of individual nodes or users.
IMPACT: Privacy violation through trajectory analysis, de-anonymization of supposedly anonymous participants, regulatory exposure.
COUNTERMEASURES:
  (a) Privacy-preserving sketching: behavioral trajectories are represented as lossy sketches (e.g., count-min sketch, HyperLogLog) that prevent exact reconstruction.
  (b) Minimum cohort-size thresholds: no query or aggregation is served if the underlying cohort has fewer than k participants (k >= 50).
  (c) Temporal aggregation: individual time-series data is aggregated into epoch buckets (minimum 1-hour granularity) to prevent fine-grained tracking.
VERIFICATION:
  1. Sketch-based representation: raw trajectories are not stored; only sketches are persisted. Verified by attempting to reconstruct exact trajectory from sketch and confirming failure.
  2. k-anonymity: all query results are filtered by cohort size >= 50; queries on smaller cohorts return empty/error.
  3. Temporal granularity: no stored data has resolution finer than 1-hour epochs.
  4. Re-identification test: given 1000 sketches, an adversary with auxiliary data cannot link > 1% of sketches to individuals.
TEST SCENARIOS:
  - Scenario A: Store 100 trajectories as sketches; attempt to reconstruct any single trajectory; verify failure.
  - Scenario B: Query a cohort of 30 participants; verify response is blocked with 'insufficient cohort size' error.
  - Scenario C: Attempt to store sub-hour-granularity data; verify it is automatically bucketed to 1-hour epochs.
  - Scenario D: Run linkage attack with full auxiliary data on 1000 sketches; verify success rate < 1%.

description:
**Gap:** franken_node has no mutation-testing infrastructure. With 4 fuzz harnesses, 3+ golden tests, 3 conformance harnesses, and 19 metamorphic tests added across recent sessions, we have NO mechanism to verify whether these tests actually catch planted bugs. A passing suite is necessary but not sufficient — mutation testing is the proof that the suite has teeth.

**Approach:**
- Add cargo-mutants as a dev tool (workspace metadata + .config/mutants.toml).
- Start scoped: run on src/security/constant_time.rs, src/observability/evidence_ledger.rs (compute_entry_hash), src/encoding/canonical_serializer.rs — the highest-value security-critical surfaces.

**Why now:** With evidence_ledger_chain_order_metamorphic.rs (bd-1p8y3) just landed, we can immediately validate whether the metamorphic suite catches a planted bug like 'compute_entry_hash returns constant.' If mutants survive on hot security paths, those tests need strengthening before they're trusted.

title: [10.14] Implement cancel-safe eviction saga (upload -> verify -> retire) with deterministic compensations.
description:
## Why This Exists
The L2->L3 artifact lifecycle involves a multi-step saga: upload the artifact to L3, verify the upload succeeded (retrievability proof from bd-1fck), then retire the L2 copy. If any step fails or the process is cancelled (operator interrupt, node crash, network partition), the system must not leave artifacts in a partially-retired state — that would mean the L2 copy is gone but L3 is not confirmed, resulting in data loss. The 9J enhancement map requires a cancel-safe eviction saga with deterministic compensations: every incomplete saga must roll back to a known-good state, and the compensation logic must be provably leak-free (zero orphan states after any failure sequence).

## What This Must Do
1. Implement `EvictionSaga` state machine in `crates/franken-node/src/storage/eviction_saga.rs` (or `src/connector/eviction_saga.rs`) with phases: `Uploading`, `Verifying`, `Retiring`, `Complete`, and `Compensating`.
2. Phase transitions must be persisted to durable storage so that crash recovery can resume or compensate from the last committed phase.
3. Compensation logic: if cancellation or crash occurs during `Uploading`, abort the upload (no L2 change); during `Verifying`, abort and clean up any partial L3 state; during `Retiring`, the L3 copy is confirmed so retirement can proceed on recovery. Compensation must be deterministic — same crash state always produces same recovery action.
4. Require `RemoteCap` capability token (from bd-1nfu) for the upload phase since it involves network-bound operations.
5. Implement leak detection: after saga completion or compensation, verify that no orphan artifacts exist (L2 retired but L3 absent, or L3 present but L2 not retired). Leak detection must run as a post-saga invariant check.
6. Write specification at `docs/specs/eviction_saga.md` covering saga phases, compensation matrix, crash recovery protocol, and leak detection invariants.
7. Produce saga trace artifact at `artifacts/10.14/eviction_saga_trace.jsonl` (JSON Lines format) recording each phase transition with timestamps for audit.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Saga guarantees no partial retire on cancellation/crash; L2 is never retired unless L3 is confirmed retrievable.
- Compensation path is deterministic: identical crash state always triggers identical recovery action.
- Leak tests confirm zero orphan states after any failure sequence (upload failure, verify failure, crash during retire).
- Saga requires RemoteCap for network-bound upload phase.
- Phase transitions are persisted; crash recovery resumes from last committed phase.
- Saga trace (JSONL) records all phase transitions with timestamps, artifact IDs, and outcome codes.

## Testing & Logging Requirements
- **Unit tests**: State machine transition validity (only legal transitions allowed); compensation logic for each crash point; leak detection invariant check with synthetic orphan states.
- **Integration tests**: `tests/integration/eviction_saga_cancel_safety.rs` — full saga success path; saga cancelled during upload (verify L2 intact, L3 cleaned up); saga crashed during verify (verify L2 intact); saga crashed during retire (verify recovery completes retirement); concurrent saga on same artifact (verify mutual exclusion).
- **Leak tests**: Post-saga invariant check that scans all tiers for orphan artifacts; test with injected orphan state to verify detection.
- **Event codes**: `ES_SAGA_START` (saga initiated), `ES_PHASE_UPLOAD` / `ES_PHASE_VERIFY` / `ES_PHASE_RETIRE` (phase transitions), `ES_SAGA_COMPLETE` (success), `ES_COMPENSATION_START` / `ES_COMPENSATION_COMPLETE` (rollback), `ES_LEAK_CHECK_PASSED` / `ES_LEAK_CHECK_FAILED` (post-saga invariant), `ES_CRASH_RECOVERY` (resuming from persisted state).
- **Replay fixture**: Deterministic saga execution with injected failures at each phase boundary.

## Expected Artifacts
- `docs/specs/eviction_saga.md` — specification document
- `tests/integration/eviction_saga_cancel_safety.rs` — integration test suite
- `artifacts/10.14/eviction_saga_trace.jsonl` — saga trace log
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-1ru2/verification_evidence.json` — CI/release gating evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-1ru2/verification_summary.md` — human-readable summary

## Dependencies
- **Depends on**: bd-1fck (retrievability-before-eviction proofs — gate called during verify phase), bd-1nfu (RemoteCap — required for upload phase)
- **Depended on by**: bd-876n (cancellation injection testing), bd-3epz (section gate), bd-5rh (section roll-up)
acceptance_criteria: Saga guarantees no partial retire on cancellation/crash; compensation path is deterministic; leak tests confirm zero orphan states.

description:
## Why This Exists

This is the section-wide verification gate for Section 10.7 (Conformance + Verification). Section 10.7 builds the conformance and verification infrastructure that validates all of franken_node's compatibility, trust, and security claims. It covers golden corpus fixtures, trust protocol vectors, fuzz testing, metamorphic testing, verifier CLI conformance, and external reproduction playbooks.

Section 10.7 is the program's credibility layer. Without rigorous conformance testing and external reproduction, franken_node's claims are unverifiable assertions. This section ensures that every claim is backed by reproducible test fixtures, adversarial test results, and independently executable verification playbooks.

## What This Must Do

1. Aggregate verification evidence from all 6 Section 10.7 beads:
   - bd-2ja: Build compatibility golden corpus and fixture metadata schema
   - bd-s6y: Adopt canonical trust protocol vectors from 10.13 + 10.14 and enforce release/publication gates
   - bd-1ul: Add fuzz/adversarial tests for migration and shim logic
   - bd-1u4: Add metamorphic tests for compatibility invariants
   - bd-3ex: Add verifier CLI conformance contract tests
   - bd-2pu: Add external-reproduction playbook and automation scripts
2. Verify golden corpus coverage: corpus covers all compatibility bands (core, high-value, edge, unsafe).
3. Verify fuzz testing coverage: fuzz tests exercise migration parser, shim logic, and compatibility evaluation.
4. Verify external reproduction: playbook can be executed by an independent party with documented success criteria.
5. Produce deterministic gate verdict.

## Acceptance Criteria

- All 6 section beads must have PASS verdicts.
- Golden corpus covers all defined compatibility bands with documented fixture metadata.
- Fuzz tests have run for minimum configured duration without crashes.
- Metamorphic tests cover all defined compatibility invariants.
- External reproduction playbook is self-contained and executable without franken_node team assistance.
- Gate verdict is deterministic and machine-readable.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Gate self-test with mock evidence.
- Structured logs: GATE_10_7_EVALUATION_STARTED, GATE_10_7_BEAD_CHECKED, GATE_10_7_CORPUS_COVERAGE, GATE_10_7_VERDICT_EMITTED.

title: [10.20] Implement trust barrier primitives and policy wiring (behavioral sandbox escalation, composition firewall, verified-fork pinning, staged rollout fences).
description:
## Why This Exists

The immunization planner (bd-2fid) proposes barrier sets, but those barriers need concrete runtime primitives to enforce. This bead implements the trust barrier primitives and policy wiring layer -- the enforcement mechanisms that actually restrict, sandbox, or fence dependency-graph choke points at runtime.

Four categories of barrier primitives are required: behavioral sandbox escalation (tightening sandbox constraints on high-risk nodes), composition firewall (preventing transitive capability leakage across dependency boundaries), verified-fork pinning (locking dependencies to verified fork snapshots rather than upstream), and staged rollout fences (gating dependency updates through progressive deployment phases).

These primitives must be independently testable, composable (multiple barriers on the same node), and enforceable at designated choke points with deterministic override semantics and audit receipts. The policy engine wires barrier configurations from the immunization planner into runtime enforcement.

Within the 9N enhancement map, this bead provides the enforcement layer that makes DGIS recommendations actionable. Without it, barrier plans are advisory-only.

## What This Must Do

1. Implement behavioral sandbox escalation primitive: dynamically tighten sandbox constraints on nodes flagged as high-risk by the topology metrics engine.
2. Implement composition firewall primitive: prevent transitive capability leakage across dependency boundaries for flagged subgraphs.
3. Implement verified-fork pinning primitive: lock specific dependencies to verified fork snapshots with signature verification on each load.
4. Implement staged rollout fences primitive: gate dependency updates through progressive deployment phases with automatic rollback triggers.
5. Ensure all primitives are independently testable with isolated unit tests.
6. Ensure primitives are composable: multiple barriers can be applied to the same node with well-defined precedence rules.
7. Implement a policy engine that translates barrier plan configurations (from bd-2fid) into runtime enforcement actions at designated choke points.
8. Support deterministic overrides with audit receipts: operators can override barriers with signed justification that is logged for audit.
9. Emit audit receipts for every barrier enforcement action (applied, overridden, expired).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Barrier primitives are independently testable and composable; policy engine can enforce barrier sets at designated choke points with deterministic overrides and audit receipts.
- Each of the 4 barrier types (sandbox escalation, composition firewall, fork pinning, staged rollout) has independent test coverage.
- Composition of 2+ barriers on a single node produces deterministic combined enforcement behavior.
- Override mechanism requires signed justification and emits audit receipt.
- Audit receipts are structured, timestamped, and include the overriding principal identity.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: each barrier primitive in isolation (sandbox escalation enforcement, firewall boundary detection, fork pin verification, rollout fence progression); composition behavior with multi-barrier scenarios; override mechanism with valid/invalid justifications.
- Integration tests: policy engine wiring from barrier plan to runtime enforcement; audit receipt generation and verification; multi-node barrier deployment scenarios.
- Structured logging: barrier enforcement events with stable codes (DGIS-BARRIER-001 through DGIS-BARRIER-NNN); override events with principal attribution; audit receipt emission; trace correlation IDs linking enforcement to barrier plans.
- Deterministic replay: barrier enforcement trace logs (JSONL) enable post-hoc audit and replay.

## Expected Artifacts

- `src/security/dgis/barrier_primitives.rs` -- barrier primitive implementations
- `tests/integration/dgis_barrier_enforcement.rs` -- enforcement test suite
- `artifacts/10.20/dgis_barrier_enforcement_trace.jsonl` -- sample enforcement trace
- `artifacts/section_10_20/bd-1tnu/verification_evidence.json` -- machine-readable CI/release gate evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_20/bd-1tnu/verification_summary.md` -- human-readable verification summary

## Dependencies

None (standalone primitive layer; consumed by bd-2fid immunization planner and bd-2wod quarantine orchestrator)

title: [PERF] Remove full-state recompute and key cloning from anti-entropy reconcile
description: Measurement: TrustState::insert_with_capacity() in crates/franken-node/src/runtime/anti_entropy.rs recomputes the root digest across every record on each accepted insert, while compute_delta() and detect_fork() first clone all record ids into BTreeSets via record_ids() before reconciling. Remediation: keep root maintenance incremental or batched behind a dirty flag, and rewrite delta/fork detection as iterator merges over the existing BTreeMaps instead of materializing full key sets.
