[10.20] Add performance/scale budgets and release claim gates for DGIS-derived security assertions.
description:
## Why This Exists

DGIS makes security claims ("this extension's blast radius is bounded," "this dependency update is safe") that operators rely on for production decisions. These claims are only valid if the underlying computations complete within performance budgets and produce signed evidence artifacts. This bead adds performance/scale budgets and release claim gates for DGIS-derived security assertions.

Without performance budgets, DGIS could timeout on large graphs, silently degrade to partial analysis, or produce stale results -- all of which undermine the trustworthiness of its claims. Without release claim gates, unsigned or uncalibrated DGIS output could be shipped as verified security evidence.

Within the 9N enhancement map, this is the capstone quality gate that ensures DGIS performance and claim integrity before artifacts are released.

## What This Must Do

1. Define p95 and p99 latency budgets for all DGIS computations (graph ingestion, metric computation, contagion simulation, economic ranking) at target graph scales.
2. Implement performance budget enforcement: computations that exceed budgets emit structured timeout/degradation signals rather than silently producing partial results.
3. Define target graph scales for budget validation: node counts, edge counts, and structural complexity parameters that represent real-world ecosystem graphs.
4. Implement release claim gates: the release pipeline blocks topology-security claims that lack signed DGIS evidence artifacts.
5. Verify evidence artifact signatures and completeness before allowing claim propagation.
6. Produce performance budget reports: per-computation latency distribution, budget compliance status, and degradation incidents.

## Acceptance Criteria

- DGIS computation overhead and decision latency remain within p95/p99 budgets at target graph scales; release pipeline blocks topology-security claims lacking signed DGIS evidence artifacts.
- p95/p99 budgets are defined for each major DGIS computation type.
- Budget violations emit structured signals (not silent failures).
- Target graph scales are documented and used in CI performance tests.
- Release pipeline rejects claims without valid signed evidence.
- Performance budget reports are machine-readable.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: budget enforcement logic; timeout/degradation signal generation; evidence signature verification; claim gate accept/reject logic.
- Integration tests: full DGIS pipeline at target graph scale with latency measurement; release claim gate with valid/invalid/missing evidence; performance budget report generation.
- Performance tests at `tests/perf/dgis_budget_gate.rs`: latency distribution measurement at target scale; p95/p99 compliance verification.
- Structured logging: performance events with stable codes (DGIS-PERF-001 through DGIS-PERF-NNN); budget violation telemetry; claim gate decisions; trace correlation IDs.
- CI workflow at `.github/workflows/dgis-claim-gate.yml` for automated release gating.

## Expected Artifacts

- `tests/perf/dgis_budget_gate.rs` -- performance budget test suite
- `.github/workflows/dgis-claim-gate.yml` -- CI release claim gate workflow
- `artifacts/10.20/dgis_release_gate_report.json` -- release gate report
- `artifacts/section_10_20/bd-38yt/verification_evidence.json` -- machine-readable CI/release gate evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_20/bd-38yt/verification_summary.md` -- human-readable verification summary

## Dependencies

None (capstone bead; validates all other 10.20 subsystems)

title: [10.11] Implement anti-entropy reconciliation for distributed product trust state.
description:
Master Plan Source: PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_NODE.md — Section 10.11 (FrankenSQLite-Inspired Runtime Systems), cross-ref Section 9G.10, 9G.9

## Why This Exists

Distributed product trust state (epoch metadata, trust receipts, quarantine verdicts, capability grants) must converge across all nodes participating in a franken_node cluster without requiring full state transfers on every sync cycle. Enhancement Map 9G.10 mandates an O(delta) anti-entropy reconciliation mechanism that exchanges only the missing or divergent portions of the trust state, along with proof-carrying recovery artifacts that let any receiving node verify the authenticity and ordering of each reconciled record. Without this, network partitions or node restarts could leave nodes with stale trust decisions, silently admitting revoked artifacts or rejecting valid ones — a category-defining failure for a product that promises deterministic, evidence-backed trust management.

This bead adapts the append-only marker stream (10.14, bd-126h), fork/divergence detection (10.14, bd-xwk5), and MMR checkpoint primitives (10.14, bd-1dar) into a product-level reconciliation service that operates within the three-kernel architecture, respecting Cx-first control, epoch boundaries, and cancellation protocol semantics.

## What This Must Do

1. Implement an `AntiEntropyReconciler` struct that accepts two trust-state digests (local and remote) and computes the minimal O(delta) diff using Merkle-Mountain-Range prefix comparison from 10.14 primitives.
2. Produce proof-carrying recovery artifacts for each reconciled record: each artifact bundles the record payload, its marker-stream position, an MMR inclusion proof, and the epoch in which it was created.
3. Apply reconciled records through the existing two-phase obligation channel (bd-2ah) so that partial reconciliation failures do not corrupt local state.
4. Enforce epoch-scoped validity: reject any incoming record whose epoch exceeds the local node's current epoch (fail-closed, per 9G.6 / bd-2gr).
5. Emit structured reconciliation events to the append-only decision stream (per 9G.9) including delta size, records accepted, records rejected, and elapsed time.
6. Support cancellation at every await point during reconciliation (per bd-7om cancel-drain-finalize protocol), ensuring partial progress is safely abandoned without state corruption.

## Context from Enhancement Maps

- 9G.10: "O(delta) anti-entropy reconciliation + proof-carrying recovery artifacts"
- 9G.9: "Three-tier integrity strategy + append-only tamper-evident decision stream"
- 9J.12: "Epoch-scoped validity windows for trust artifacts" — reconciled records must respect epoch boundaries.
- 9J.19: "Cancellation-complete protocol discipline with obligation closure proofs" — reconciliation loops must be cancellation-safe.
- Architecture invariant #3 (8.5): Cancellation protocol semantics — all long-running reconciliation must honor cancel signals.
- Architecture invariant #8 (8.5): Evidence-by-default — every reconciliation cycle must produce auditable evidence.

## Dependencies

- Upstream: bd-126h (append-only marker stream), bd-xwk5 (fork/divergence detection), bd-1dar (MMR checkpoints/inclusion proofs), bd-2gr (epoch-scoped validity windows), bd-2ah (obligation-tracked two-phase channels), bd-7om (cancel-drain-finalize protocol)
- Downstream: bd-1jpo (10.11 section-wide verification gate)

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Unit test confirms O(delta) behavior: reconciling two states with N total records and K differing records completes in O(K) comparisons, not O(N).
2. Every reconciled record includes a verifiable MMR inclusion proof that passes independent validation.
3. Records from a future epoch (epoch > local_current) are rejected with a structured error event logged to the decision stream.
4. A crash or cancellation mid-reconciliation leaves local trust state unchanged (atomic rollback via two-phase channel).
5. Structured log events include: `anti_entropy.cycle_started`, `anti_entropy.delta_computed`, `anti_entropy.record_accepted`, `anti_entropy.record_rejected`, `anti_entropy.cycle_completed` — each with trace correlation ID and epoch tag.
6. Reconciliation under simulated 50% packet loss completes correctly (possibly after retries) without data corruption.
7. Verification evidence JSON includes delta_size, records_accepted, records_rejected, proof_verification_pass_rate, and elapsed_ms fields.
8. Fork detection (divergent histories) triggers a structured alert event and halts reconciliation rather than silently merging.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: (a) Identical states produce zero-delta; (b) Single-record divergence produces delta=1; (c) Bulk divergence (1000 records) completes in bounded time; (d) Future-epoch record rejection; (e) Invalid MMR proof rejection.
- Integration tests: (a) Two-node reconciliation through obligation channels with simulated network delay; (b) Three-node transitive convergence (A syncs with B, B syncs with C, verify A and C converge); (c) Reconciliation during concurrent local writes.
- Adversarial tests: (a) Tampered proof payloads are detected and rejected; (b) Cancellation signal mid-reconciliation leaves state clean; (c) Simulated fork/divergence triggers halt-and-alert; (d) Replay of already-reconciled records is idempotent.
- Structured logs: All events use stable event codes (FN-AE-001 through FN-AE-008), include `trace_id`, `epoch`, `delta_size`, and are JSON-formatted for machine parsing.

## Expected Artifacts

- docs/specs/section_10_11/bd-390_contract.md
- crates/franken-node/src/runtime/anti_entropy.rs (or equivalent module path)
- scripts/check_anti_entropy_reconciliation.py (with --json flag and self_test())
- tests/test_check_anti_entropy_reconciliation.py
- artifacts/section_10_11/bd-390/verification_evidence.json
- artifacts/section_10_11/bd-390/verification_summary.md
acceptance_criteria:
AC for bd-390:
1. Implement an anti-entropy reconciliation protocol for distributed product trust state: each node maintains a local trust state (capability grants, epoch bindings, obligation tokens) and periodically synchronizes with peers to detect and resolve divergence.
2. The reconciliation uses a Merkle-tree digest of the local trust state; peers exchange root hashes and, on mismatch, perform a tree-diff to identify the minimal set of divergent entries.
3. Conflict resolution follows a deterministic policy: (a) higher epoch_id wins, (b) within the same epoch, the entry with the later timestamp wins, (c) ties are broken by lexicographic ordering of the node_id. This ensures all nodes converge to the same state without coordination.
4. Reconciliation runs on a configurable interval (default: 30 seconds) and also triggers immediately on epoch transition events (bd-2gr) to accelerate convergence during security-critical transitions.
5. A convergence SLA is enforced: after a state mutation, all nodes must agree within max_convergence_time (configurable, default: 3 reconciliation intervals). A RECONCILIATION_SLA_BREACH event fires if convergence is not achieved within the deadline.
6. The reconciliation protocol is bandwidth-efficient: only divergent entries are transferred, not the full state; a test verifies that reconciling 1 divergent entry out of 10,000 transfers O(log N) data, not O(N).
7. Unit tests verify: (a) identical states produce matching Merkle roots (no false divergence), (b) single-entry divergence is detected and resolved per conflict policy, (c) epoch-based conflict resolution picks higher epoch, (d) immediate reconciliation triggers on epoch transition, (e) SLA breach event fires when convergence deadline is exceeded.
8. Integration test: a 3-node cluster with injected network partition heals after partition removal and converges within the SLA.
9. Structured log events: RECONCILIATION_START / RECONCILIATION_DIVERGENCE_DETECTED / RECONCILIATION_RESOLVED / RECONCILIATION_CONVERGED / RECONCILIATION_SLA_BREACH with node_id, peer_id, divergent_entry_count, and merkle_root_hash.

title: [REVIEW] verifier sdk: transparency log leaf omits authenticated result provenance
description:
Repro:
- In sdk/verifier/src/lib.rs, append_transparency_log() first calls verify_result_belongs_to_current_verifier(), which now checks the private result_origin_nonce to reject detached or forged same-verifier results.
- But the persisted log leaf is still computed from serde_json::to_vec(result) and stored as result_hash, and VerificationResult skips result_origin_nonce during serialization.
- Two different same-verifier SDK instances can therefore produce byte-identical public VerificationResult payloads with different authenticated origin nonces and still land on the same persisted result_hash / merkle_proof chain. A log consumer replaying only stored entries cannot verify that the accepted leaf committed to the authenticated origin that append_transparency_log() actually checked.

Why this is a bug:
- The append path enforces stronger provenance than the log persists. That creates a fail-open gap between admission-time authentication and stored transparency evidence: the log hash commits only to structural public fields, not to the authenticated origin token that made the result acceptable.

Fix suggestion:
- Make the transparency-log leaf commit to the authenticated provenance checked at append time, for example by hashing explicit attestation bytes that include result_origin_nonce (or a replacement signed/private provenance token) instead of hashing the public JSON view alone.
- Add a regression proving two same-verifier results with identical public fields but different authenticated origins do not collide to the same persisted leaf.

Commit refs: 8ef4f688, 43604891

title: [10.21] Define canonical `BehavioralGenome` schema and version-lineage contract for extension phenotypes.
description:
## Why This Exists

Section 10.21 (Enhancement Map 9O) establishes the Behavioral Phenotype Evolution Tracker (BPET), a category-creating capability that tracks longitudinal behavioral evolution of extensions to detect compromise precursors before they manifest as active attacks. The key insight: compromised extensions exhibit behavioral trajectory anomalies (capability creep, dependency pivots, build pipeline changes, maintainer handoffs) that precede the attack payload activation. BPET detects these pre-compromise signals by modeling extension behavior as an evolving phenotype.

This bead defines the foundational BehavioralGenome schema -- the canonical representation of an extension's behavioral phenotype at a given version -- and the version-lineage contract that links phenotypes across versions into an evolution trajectory. Every downstream BPET subsystem (feature extraction, lineage graphs, drift features, regime detection, hazard models, risk scoring) depends on this schema being precise, deterministic, and signed.

Within the Track E frontier context, BPET is the temporal-analysis complement to DGIS's structural analysis (10.20). Where DGIS asks "what is the graph structure now?", BPET asks "how has this extension's behavior changed over time, and does that trajectory resemble compromise precursors?"

## What This Must Do

1. Define the BehavioralGenome schema encoding: capability usage patterns, dependency reach (transitive dependency footprint), API-surface traits (exported/consumed interfaces), resource/network envelopes (CPU, memory, network, filesystem access patterns), complexity signals (code complexity metrics, binary size evolution), maintainer/build events (maintainer changes, CI pipeline modifications), and provenance bindings (build reproducibility, signing key continuity).
2. Ensure serialization is deterministic: identical logical genomes produce byte-identical serialized forms.
3. Implement cryptographic signing of genome snapshots with versioned schema identifiers.
4. Define the version-lineage contract: how genomes at different versions are linked to form evolution trajectories, including handling of version gaps, yanked versions, and fork lineages.
5. Support schema evolution: versioned schema identifiers allow consumers to detect and handle schema changes.
6. Provide golden-vector test fixtures demonstrating: round-trip determinism, signature verification, lineage linking, and schema-version migration.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Schema encodes capability usage, dependency reach, API-surface traits, resource/network envelopes, complexity signals, maintainer/build events, and provenance bindings; serialization is deterministic and signed.
- All 7 genome dimensions (capability, dependency, API, resource, complexity, maintainer, provenance) are explicitly represented in the schema.
- Round-trip serialization produces byte-identical output for at least 3 golden-vector fixtures.
- Signature verification succeeds for unmodified genomes and fails for any single-field mutation.
- Version-lineage contract documents handling for: normal succession, version gaps, yanked versions, and forks.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: per-dimension genome encoding/decoding; deterministic serialization; signature generation and verification; lineage linking with normal/gap/yank/fork scenarios.
- Integration tests: full genome lifecycle (create -> sign -> serialize -> store -> retrieve -> verify -> link to lineage); schema version detection and migration; golden-vector round-trip.
- Structured logging: genome events with stable codes (BPET-GENOME-001 through BPET-GENOME-NNN); schema version telemetry; signature operations; trace correlation IDs.
- Deterministic replay: golden-vector fixtures in `spec/` directory for CI verification.

## Expected Artifacts

- `docs/specs/bpet_behavioral_genome_schema.md` -- human-readable schema specification
- `spec/bpet_behavioral_genome_v1.json` -- machine-readable JSON Schema definition
- `artifacts/10.21/bpet_genome_schema_vectors.json` -- golden-vector test fixtures
- `artifacts/section_10_21/bd-39ga/verification_evidence.json` -- machine-readable CI/release gate evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_21/bd-39ga/verification_summary.md` -- human-readable verification summary

## Dependencies

- bd-1wz (blocks) -- [PLAN 10.17] Radical Expansion Execution Track (9K): provides the extension model whose phenotypes BPET tracks
- bd-cda (blocks) -- [PLAN 10.N] Execution Normalization Contract: ensures no duplicate schema definitions
- bd-ybe (blocks) -- [PLAN 10.20] DGIS Execution Track: BPET consumes DGIS graph data for dependency-reach dimensions
- bd-39a (blocks) -- [PLAN 10.19] Adversarial Trust Commons: provides trust primitives that provenance bindings reference
acceptance_criteria: - Schema encodes capability usage, dependency reach, API-surface traits, resource/network envelopes, complexity signals, maintainer/build events, and provenance bindings; serialization is deterministic and signed.

title: [10.14] Implement anytime-valid guardrail monitor set for security/durability-critical budgets.
description:
## Why This Exists
The franken_node policy engine uses Bayesian posterior diagnostics (bd-2igi) to rank policy recommendations, but statistical recommendations can be wrong — especially with limited data or adversarial conditions. Guardrail monitors provide always-on, anytime-valid bounds that prevent the system from taking dangerous actions regardless of what the Bayesian engine recommends. "Anytime-valid" means the monitors produce valid conclusions at any stopping point (not just at pre-planned sample sizes), which is essential for a continuously-running system that cannot wait for a fixed experiment duration. This is inspired by FrankenSQLite's invariant monitor pattern (9J enhancement map) and directly enforces Section 8.5 Invariant #6 (security/durability budgets are never exceeded) by providing hard upper bounds that no heuristic can override.

## What This Must Do
1. Define the `GuardrailMonitor` trait in `crates/franken-node/src/policy/guardrail_monitor.rs` with:
   - `fn check(&self, state: &SystemState) -> GuardrailVerdict` — returns `Allow`, `Block { reason: String, budget: BudgetId }`, or `Warn { reason: String }`.
   - `fn is_valid_at_any_stopping_point(&self) -> bool` — returns true (required for all monitors; this is a compile-time assertion via the type system).
2. Implement concrete monitors for security/durability-critical budgets:
   - `MemoryBudgetGuardrail` — blocks actions that would exceed memory budget.
   - `DurabilityLossGuardrail` — blocks actions that would reduce durability below threshold.
   - `HardeningRegressionGuardrail` — blocks actions that would regress hardening level (references correctness envelope invariant).
   - `EvidenceEmissionGuardrail` — blocks actions that bypass mandatory evidence emission.
3. Make alert thresholds policy-configurable: each monitor reads its threshold from the policy configuration, but the threshold cannot be set below a minimum defined in the correctness envelope.
4. Implement a `GuardrailMonitorSet` that runs all registered monitors and returns the most restrictive verdict.
5. Write specification at `docs/specs/anytime_valid_guardrails.md` explaining:
   - The anytime-valid property and why it matters.
   - Each monitor's threshold semantics and default values.
   - The relationship between guardrails and the correctness envelope.
6. Write conformance tests at `tests/conformance/anytime_guardrail_monitors.rs` verifying:
   - Each monitor correctly blocks violations of its budget.
   - Each monitor allows actions within budget.
   - Optional stopping property: monitor conclusions are valid at any prefix of the observation sequence.
   - Thresholds are policy-configurable above the minimum.
7. Produce telemetry artifact at `artifacts/10.14/guardrail_monitor_telemetry.csv` with monitor firing rates, verdict distribution, and budget utilization over a test run.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Guardrails are always-on for critical budgets; monitor outputs remain valid under optional stopping; alert thresholds are policy-configurable.
- All four concrete monitors are implemented and registered in the `GuardrailMonitorSet`.
- Each monitor correctly blocks its respective violation scenario.
- Thresholds are configurable but cannot be set below correctness envelope minimums.
- `GuardrailMonitorSet` returns the most restrictive verdict when multiple monitors fire.
- Monitors produce valid conclusions at any stopping point (verified by conformance test with variable-length observation sequences).
- Telemetry artifact contains per-monitor firing counts and verdict distribution.

## Testing & Logging Requirements
- Unit tests: Each concrete monitor with budget-at-limit, budget-exceeded, and budget-within-margin inputs; `GuardrailMonitorSet` combining verdicts from multiple monitors; threshold configuration above and below minimum.
- Integration tests: Full policy decision with guardrail check — action blocked by memory budget; action blocked by durability threshold; action allowed when all budgets are satisfied.
- Conformance tests: Optional stopping — run monitor on observation sequences of length 1, 10, 100, 1000 and verify conclusions are consistent; threshold minimum enforcement — attempt to configure below minimum.
- Adversarial tests: Submit action that exactly hits budget boundary (verify deterministic verdict); rapidly oscillate budget utilization to test hysteresis; attempt to disable a monitor via policy (should be rejected by envelope).
- Structured logs: `EVD-GUARD-001` on monitor check pass; `EVD-GUARD-002` on monitor block (includes `budget_id`, `reason`); `EVD-GUARD-003` on monitor warn; `EVD-GUARD-004` on threshold reconfiguration. All logs include `epoch_id`, `monitor_id`.

## Expected Artifacts
- `crates/franken-node/src/policy/guardrail_monitor.rs` — implementation
- `docs/specs/anytime_valid_guardrails.md` — specification
- `tests/conformance/anytime_guardrail_monitors.rs` — conformance tests
- `artifacts/10.14/guardrail_monitor_telemetry.csv` — telemetry artifact
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-3a3q/verification_evidence.json` — machine-readable pass/fail evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-3a3q/verification_summary.md` — human-readable summary

## Dependencies
- Upstream: bd-sddz (correctness envelope — defines the minimum thresholds that guardrails enforce)
- Downstream: bd-15u3 (guardrail precedence over Bayesian recommendations), bd-1zym (automatic hardening trigger on guardrail rejection), bd-3epz (section gate), bd-5rh (10.14 plan gate)

title: [PROFILE] control_plane/root_pointer.rs: publish_lock_registry global Mutex serializes registry lookup across all root paths
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/control_plane/root_pointer.rs

PATTERN:
`publish_lock_registry()` (L408-411) is a process-global `Mutex<BTreeMap<PathBuf, Arc<Mutex<()>>>>`. Every `publish_lock()` call:

1. Acquires the global registry Mutex (L416-418)
2. Looks up / inserts an Arc<Mutex<()>> for the path
3. Returns the Arc — caller then takes the per-path Mutex separately

L413-424 publish_lock impl. Plus `lock_path.canonicalize()` is invoked inside the critical section (L415) — this performs a syscall (stat/realpath) while holding the global mutex, blocking all other publish operations across all paths during the syscall.

IMPACT:
- All publishes process-wide serialize on the registry mutex during lookup
- Filesystem syscall (canonicalize) inside the critical section magnifies the lock duration
- Particularly impactful when multiple control-plane roots are in flight (multi-tenant or test harness scenarios)

SUGGESTED FIX:
- Move `canonicalize()` outside the critical section: compute it before locking, pass the canonical path in
- Switch the registry to `RwLock` — first read attempts to fetch existing Arc, falls back to write only on miss
- Or use a sharded map (e.g. `dashmap::DashMap`) — eliminates global serialization

EVIDENCE:
- L408-411 process-global Mutex<BTreeMap<...>>
- L413-424 publish_lock acquires global mutex + does canonicalize inside it
- L415 canonicalize() is a filesystem syscall
close_reason: Code landed in e60868c8 with RwLock publish-lock registry, canonicalization outside registry access, and focused RCH validation

title: fix(concurrency): telemetry shutdown ignores drain deadline in ops/telemetry_bridge.rs:492
description: Pattern identified: TelemetryRuntimeHandle::join applies the drain deadline only to the persistence worker; join_connection_workers runs before that and joins all connection workers without a deadline. title: [10.12] Implement verifier-economy SDK with independent validation workflows.
description:
[10.12] Implement verifier-economy SDK with independent validation workflows.

## Why This Exists

Section 9H.3 and Impossible-by-Default principle #10 require that verification is not a privilege of the system operator alone — it must be accessible to independent third parties. The verifier economy is the ecosystem where external auditors, compliance teams, partner organizations, and automated verification agents can independently validate claims made by the franken_node system. This bead provides the SDK — libraries, APIs, and tooling — that makes independent verification easy, reliable, and the default path. Without this SDK, verification requires deep system knowledge and ad-hoc tooling, which makes it effectively impossible for external parties.

## What It Must Do

1. **Verification SDK core library.** Implement a Rust library (`verifier-sdk`) exposing core verification operations:
   - `verify_claim(claim: &Claim, evidence: &Evidence) -> VerificationResult` — verify a single claim against its evidence bundle.
   - `verify_migration_artifact(artifact: &MigrationArtifact) -> VerificationResult` — verify a migration artifact (from bd-3hm) including signature, schema, preconditions, and rollback receipt.
   - `verify_trust_state(state: &TrustStateVector, anchor: &TrustAnchor) -> VerificationResult` — verify a trust state vector's chain of trust back to a known anchor.
   - `replay_capsule(capsule: &ReplayCapsule) -> ReplayResult` — replay a capsule (from 10.17) and verify that the replay produces the claimed output.

2. **Multi-language bindings.** Provide at minimum:
   - Rust (native) — the core library.
   - Python (via PyO3 or FFI) — for scripting and CI integration.
   - CLI tool (`franken-verify`) — for operator and CI usage.
   The Python binding and CLI tool must expose all core verification operations.

3. **Evidence bundle format.** Define the evidence bundle format that accompanies every verifiable claim. The bundle contains: the claim itself, supporting artifacts (signatures, hashes, timestamps), verification procedure reference, and expected outcome. Bundles are self-contained — a verifier needs only the bundle and the SDK to validate.

4. **Independent validation workflows.** Define standard validation workflows for common scenarios:
   - **Release validation**: verify all golden vectors, migration artifacts, and trust state for a release.
   - **Incident validation**: verify the trust state and revocation chain during/after an incident.
   - **Compliance audit**: verify a set of claims against their evidence bundles for regulatory compliance.
   Each workflow is documented with step-by-step instructions and executable scripts.

5. **Verification result format.** All verification operations return a structured `VerificationResult` containing: verdict (pass/fail/inconclusive), confidence score, checked assertions with individual pass/fail, execution timestamp, verifier identity, and cryptographic binding to the verified artifacts. Results are themselves signed by the verifier.

6. **Offline verification.** The SDK must support fully offline verification — no network access required. All necessary data is contained in the evidence bundle. This is critical for air-gapped environments and ensures verification cannot be blocked by network manipulation.

7. **Verification transparency log.** The SDK optionally publishes verification results to a transparency log (append-only, Merkle-tree-backed). This creates a public record of what was verified, by whom, and when. The log format is compatible with RFC 6962 (Certificate Transparency) style structures.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Rust verifier SDK library implemented in `crates/franken-node/src/connector/verifier_sdk.rs` with all four core operations.
2. Python bindings or CLI wrapper expose all core operations with `--json` output.
3. Evidence bundle format defined with JSON Schema at `spec/evidence_bundle_schema.json`.
4. At least 3 standard validation workflows documented with executable scripts.
5. `VerificationResult` format includes verdict, confidence, per-assertion results, and cryptographic binding.
6. Offline verification works without network access (tested in sandboxed environment).
7. Transparency log format defined and append-only property tested.
8. Verification script `scripts/check_verifier_sdk.py` with `--json` flag confirms all criteria.
9. Evidence artifacts written to `artifacts/section_10_12/bd-3c2/`.

## Key Dependencies

- bd-3hm (migration artifact contract) — SDK verifies migration artifacts.
- bd-1l5 (trust object IDs) — claims and evidence reference canonical IDs.
- bd-5si (trust fabric convergence) — SDK verifies trust state vectors.
- 10.17 replay capsules — SDK replays capsules for validation.
- 10.13 stable error namespace — SDK errors use registered codes.
- 10.13 golden vectors — release validation workflow runs golden vector suites.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests for each core verification operation with valid and invalid inputs.
- Integration test executing the release validation workflow against the current codebase.
- Offline verification test in a network-isolated sandbox.
- Round-trip test: generate evidence bundle, verify, check signed result, append to transparency log.
- Fuzz test: mutate evidence bundles and confirm the SDK rejects them.
- Self-test mode that generates a claim, bundles evidence, verifies, and confirms pass.
- Structured logging: `verifier.claim_verified`, `verifier.claim_failed`, `verifier.migration_verified`, `verifier.trust_state_verified`, `verifier.replay_completed`, `verifier.result_signed`, `verifier.transparency_log_appended` events.

## Expected Artifacts

- `docs/specs/section_10_12/bd-3c2_contract.md` — specification document.
- `crates/franken-node/src/connector/verifier_sdk.rs` — Rust SDK implementation.
- `spec/evidence_bundle_schema.json` — evidence bundle JSON Schema.
- `scripts/check_verifier_sdk.py` — verification script.
- `tests/test_check_verifier_sdk.py` — unit tests.
- `artifacts/section_10_12/bd-3c2/verification_evidence.json` — evidence.
- `artifacts/section_10_12/bd-3c2/verification_summary.md` — summary.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Define a VerifierSDK module providing: (a) verify_migration_artifact(artifact_json: &str) -> VerificationResult that validates a MigrationSingularityArtifact (from bd-3hm) without access to the source system, (b) verify_rollback_receipt(receipt_json: &str, public_key: &[u8]) -> VerificationResult that checks receipt signature and deadline, (c) verify_release_gate(manifest_json: &str) -> VerificationResult that validates a ReleaseGateManifest (from bd-1hd).
2. Define VerificationResult as a struct: (a) verdict (PASS, FAIL, INCONCLUSIVE), (b) checked_fields (list of {field_name, check, pass/fail}), (c) verifier_version (SDK semver), (d) verification_timestamp, (e) details (human-readable summary).
3. The SDK MUST be usable as a standalone library with zero runtime dependencies on the franken_node system. It should depend only on cryptographic primitives and JSON parsing.
4. Implement schema validation: the SDK MUST reject artifacts whose schema_version it does not recognize, returning INCONCLUSIVE with a message indicating the required SDK version.
5. Implement independent hash verification: the SDK MUST recompute all hashes (migration_plan_hash, state fingerprints) from the artifact's embedded data and compare against the declared values. Any mismatch produces FAIL.
6. Implement signature verification: the SDK MUST verify all signatures in the artifact using the provided public keys. Support Ed25519 signatures at minimum.
7. Provide a CLI wrapper: `franken-verify <artifact.json> [--public-key <key.pem>]` that prints the VerificationResult as JSON to stdout and exits with code 0 (PASS), 1 (FAIL), or 2 (INCONCLUSIVE).
8. Unit tests: (a) valid artifact passes, (b) tampered hash fails, (c) invalid signature fails, (d) unknown schema version returns INCONCLUSIVE, (e) missing required field returns FAIL, (f) CLI exit codes match verdict.
9. Provide example artifacts in fixtures/verifier_sdk/ with known-good and known-bad samples for third-party testing.
10. Verification: scripts/check_verifier_sdk.py --json, artifacts at artifacts/section_10_12/bd-3c2/.
notes:
Plan-space QA addendum (2026-02-20):
1) Preserve full canonical-plan scope; no feature compression or silent omission is allowed.
2) Completion requires comprehensive verification coverage appropriate to scope: unit tests, integration tests, and E2E scripts/workflows with detailed structured logging (stable event/error codes + trace correlation IDs).
3) Completion requires reproducible evidence artifacts (machine-readable + human-readable) that allow independent replay and root-cause triage.
4) Any implementation PR for this bead must include explicit links to the above test/logging artifacts.

title: [REASONING] root_pointer publish_lock canonicalize fallback collides with main path
description:
LENS: Concurrency / serializability
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/control_plane/root_pointer.rs:413-424 (publish_lock), 408-411 (registry)
CONCERN: publish_lock computes lock_key = lock_path.canonicalize().unwrap_or(lock_path). If canonicalize fails (path doesn't yet exist — common for the very first publish before the lock file is touched), the registry is keyed by the *un-canonicalized* PathBuf. A second concurrent publisher whose call happens after the lock file has been created will canonicalize successfully and key by the canonical path. The two callers then receive distinct Arc<Mutex<()>> handles for the SAME directory, defeating in-process serialization for the first-publish window. This is similar to but distinct from the existing DEADLOCK bead about spelling races; that bead is about equivalent string spellings, this is about the canonicalize fallback creating two different keys for the same physical path across the lifecycle of the lock file.
WHY IT MATTERS: The flock-based file lock at acquire_root_publication_lock still serializes cross-process, but the in-process Mutex is supposed to be the fast path. During system bootstrap (lock file does not exist), two threads can race past the in-process gate, then collide at flock; one will receive a flock error and the bootstrap fails non-deterministically. Worse, if the flock implementation behaves differently when the same process holds the lock from two FDs, behavior is undefined.
SUGGESTED REMEDIATION: Always canonicalize the *parent directory* (which exists) and append ROOT_POINTER_LOCK_FILE to derive lock_key. If parent canonicalize fails, error out instead of falling back to the un-canonicalized path. Add a concurrency test: spawn N threads that race on the very first publish into a fresh tempdir; assert all but one observe the in-process lock contention error before flock is attempted.
close_reason: Covered by 133671a4 / bd-3u81s stable root publication lock key

title: [10.14] Implement epoch-scoped key derivation for trust artifact authentication.
description:
## Why This Exists

Epoch-scoped key derivation ensures that cryptographic keys used for trust artifact authentication are bound to a specific epoch and domain, making cross-epoch key reuse impossible by construction. This is critical for the 9J security model: if a key derived in epoch N could authenticate artifacts in epoch N+1, an attacker who compromises a key could forge future-epoch artifacts, defeating the entire epoch barrier system. This bead directly enforces runtime invariant #7 (epoch barriers are cryptographically hard) and #8 (evidence-by-default: every trust artifact carries epoch-bound authentication). It depends on the monotonic epoch (bd-3hdv) and feeds into the epoch transition barrier (bd-2wsm) which needs epoch-scoped keys to authenticate barrier participation.

## What This Must Do

1. Implement `EpochKeyDerivation` module in `src/security/epoch_scoped_keys.rs` that derives authentication keys from a root secret, epoch value, and domain string using a standard KDF (e.g., HKDF-SHA256).
2. The derivation function signature: `derive_epoch_key(root_secret: &RootSecret, epoch: ControlEpoch, domain: &str) -> DerivedKey` where `DerivedKey` is a fixed-size key type.
3. Enforce by construction that `derive_epoch_key(secret, epoch_a, domain) != derive_epoch_key(secret, epoch_b, domain)` for any `epoch_a != epoch_b` (this is a property of HKDF with distinct info strings, but must be verified by test vectors).
4. Enforce domain separation: `derive_epoch_key(secret, epoch, "marker") != derive_epoch_key(secret, epoch, "manifest")` for any epoch.
5. Publish verification vectors: a JSON file containing `(root_secret_hex, epoch, domain, expected_key_hex)` tuples that any implementation can verify against.
6. Implement `verify_epoch_signature(artifact: &[u8], signature: &Signature, epoch: ControlEpoch, domain: &str, root_secret: &RootSecret) -> Result<(), AuthError>` that derives the key and verifies the signature.
7. Ensure key material is zeroized on drop (use `zeroize` crate or equivalent).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Authentication key derivation binds to epoch and domain; cross-epoch key reuse is impossible by construction; verification vectors are published.
- For any two distinct `(epoch, domain)` pairs, derived keys differ (verified against published vectors with >= 10 test cases).
- `verify_epoch_signature` rejects a signature produced with a different epoch's key.
- `verify_epoch_signature` rejects a signature produced with a different domain's key.
- Key material is zeroized after use (verified by memory inspection test or `zeroize` derive).
- Published verification vectors in `artifacts/10.14/epoch_key_vectors.json` contain at least 10 vector entries with known-answer tests.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: key derivation produces expected output for known inputs (KAT); cross-epoch keys differ; cross-domain keys differ; signature verification succeeds for matching epoch/domain; signature verification fails for mismatched epoch; signature verification fails for mismatched domain; zeroization on drop.
- Integration tests: full sign-verify round trip across epoch transition; key derivation performance (must derive >= 10,000 keys/sec).
- Conformance tests: `tests/conformance/epoch_key_derivation.rs` -- normative test running all published verification vectors.
- Structured logs: `EPOCH_KEY_DERIVED` (epoch, domain, key_fingerprint, trace_id), `EPOCH_SIG_VERIFIED` (artifact_id, epoch, domain, trace_id), `EPOCH_SIG_REJECTED` (artifact_id, epoch, domain, rejection_reason, trace_id). Key material NEVER appears in logs.

## Expected Artifacts

- `src/security/epoch_scoped_keys.rs` -- key derivation and verification implementation
- `tests/conformance/epoch_key_derivation.rs` -- normative conformance tests
- `artifacts/10.14/epoch_key_vectors.json` -- published verification vectors (KAT)
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-3cs3/verification_evidence.json` -- machine-readable CI/release gate evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-3cs3/verification_summary.md` -- human-readable verification summary

## Dependencies

- Upstream: bd-3hdv (monotonic control epoch -- provides `ControlEpoch` type).
- Downstream: bd-2wsm (epoch transition barrier -- uses epoch-scoped keys for barrier authentication), bd-3epz (section gate), bd-5rh (section gate).
acceptance_criteria: Authentication key derivation binds to epoch and domain; cross-epoch key reuse is impossible by construction; verification vectors are published.

title: [10.13 bug] Replace non-empty-token control-channel auth with transcript-bound capability verification
description:
Why this exists:
`crates/franken-node/src/connector/control_channel.rs` still authenticates control traffic with `!token.is_empty()`. That directly contradicts the closed claim that Section 10.13 delivered an authenticated control channel with anti-replay guarantees. Sequence monotonicity without real authenticity is not a secure protocol; it is a replay filter on top of ambient authority.

What this bead must do:
Replace the non-empty-token shortcut with a canonical transcript-bound capability verifier for control-channel frames. The implementation should not invent another ad hoc token format when the repo already contains stronger ingredients: audience/capability token machinery, epoch-scoped signing primitives, remote capability concepts, and canonical serializer infrastructure. The new control-channel auth path should bind identity, audience, session/channel ID, direction, sequence, payload hash, epoch/freshness window, and nonce into a domain-separated transcript that is actually verified. Use the graveyard ideas where they pay rent: attenuated capability tokens or macaroon-like caveats for least-authority control messages, persistent replay filters across restart boundaries, and deterministic counterexample traces for failed auth decisions.

Acceptance criteria:
1. `connector/control_channel.rs` no longer accepts arbitrary non-empty strings as authenticated control traffic; every accepted frame is backed by verified capability/session evidence.
2. Authentication binds at least: issuer/subject, audience, channel/session ID, direction, sequence number, payload commitment, freshness/epoch data, and nonce or equivalent replay salt.
3. Anti-replay state survives restart or is recoverably reconstructed from canonical state so an attacker cannot bypass replay protection with process restarts.
4. Capability attenuation is expressible: a control token/frame can be scoped to direction, action family, tenant/zone, and expiry, and verification enforces those caveats.
5. The implementation reuses canonical key/token/serialization components already present in-repo instead of spawning another incompatible auth mini-stack.
6. Adversarial fixtures cover guessed-token injection, payload swap under reused auth material, cross-channel replay, stale epoch reuse, restart-boundary replay, and caveat-bypass attempts.
7. Add a checker that fails if control-channel auth regresses to token-present / string-shape / opaque-bearer shortcuts.
8. Deliver unit tests, control-protocol replay fixtures, structured logs, and machine-readable evidence proving accepted frames are actually authenticated.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Control-channel authentication must verify transcript-bound capability evidence for every accepted frame and must persist or reconstruct replay state across restart boundaries; arbitrary non-empty bearer strings are never sufficient.
2. Authentication failures are user- and operator-explainable: denials emit stable error and reason codes, retryability hints, recovery hints, and enough transcript facts to debug without leaking secrets.
3. Unit tests cover transcript binding, audience enforcement, direction and action caveats, stale epoch rejection, restart-boundary replay rejection, nonce handling, and regressions against token-present shortcuts.
4. Integration tests exercise normal control traffic, attenuated capability scopes, restart recovery, cross-channel replay attempts, and invalid-token handling using deterministic vectors.
5. At least one deterministic operator E2E shell script under tests/e2e/ reproduces valid control traffic, guessed-token injection failure, replay failure after restart, and capability attenuation failure with detailed logs.
6. Structured logs expose stable CONTROL_AUTH_* event families with required fields: trace_id, channel_id, subject_id, audience, direction, sequence, decision, reason_code, retryable, and freshness_state.
7. Evidence artifacts under artifacts/replacement_gap/bd-3cvu/ include verification_evidence.json, verification_summary.md, protocol_vector_index.json, and any rch offload build IDs used for verification.

title: [REVIEW5] engine_dispatcher: TODO comments in production native engine path
[SECAUDIT] quarantine_controller: signed evidence omits timestamp/nonce/epoch — cross-time replay accepted
description:
LENS: Replay/freshness gap on a high-impact control action (security-audit-for-saas Operator: ⊙ Identity-Chain Trace)
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/security/quarantine_controller.rs:398-415 (sign_evidence), 137-164 (SignedEvidenceEntry / ControlDecision shape)

THREAT MODEL: SignedEvidenceEntry is the audit record that authorizes control actions in {Throttle, Isolate, Quarantine, Revoke}.  The HMAC preimage at lines 401-412 covers principal_id, action, posterior, threshold, policy_version, policy_hash, evidence_count, evidence_hash, scope, and trace_id.  It does NOT cover any monotonic time field, nonce, epoch, or generation id.  The same (principal, action, posterior, threshold, policy, evidence) tuple ALWAYS yields an identical signature.  An attacker who saw a legitimate Revoke decision at time T can replay the exact bytes at T+30 days; the verifier (verify_signature, lines 388-396) recomputes the same MAC and accepts.

EXPLOIT SKETCH:
  1. At time T, an adversary's posterior crosses revoke threshold.  Controller emits a signed Revoke decision; this is published to the audit ledger.
  2. The principal is later rehabilitated, evidence rolled back, posterior drops below all thresholds.
  3. Attacker (or a malicious replay relay, or an adversary with read access to the audit ledger) re-injects the byte-for-byte identical SignedEvidenceEntry at time T+N into a downstream consumer that validates only the signature (the canonical audit-log replay path).
  4. verify_signature passes; the downstream consumer treats the principal as Revoked again, even though current posterior says otherwise — unbounded reuse of a one-shot decision.

ROOT CAUSE: sign_evidence's preimage is purely content-hash-style — every field bound is a stable property of the decision content, none is a freshness/uniqueness token.  trace_id is per-request but not part of any 'consumed'-tracking on the verifier side, and re-using the same trace_id is silently fine.  No `decision_id`, `issued_at_ms`, or `epoch_id` field exists on SignedEvidenceEntry.  This is the same anti-pattern as bd-j587o (threshold_sig omits artifact/connector context) and the OperatorAuthorization replay finding (bd-18q4j — pending), but for the quarantine/revoke surface.

MITIGATION:
  1. Add `decision_id: String` (UUID v7 — already in the dep tree via uuid crate) and `issued_at_ms: u64` to SignedEvidenceEntry.
  2. Include both in sign_evidence's HMAC preimage with length-prefixed framing, BEFORE principal_id.
  3. Introduce a domain-separated bump: change the leading domain tag from `b"quarantine_control_decision_v2:"` to `b"quarantine_control_decision_v3:"` so v2 entries can no longer satisfy v3 verifiers.
  4. Add a new method `QuarantineController::verify_signed_decision(&self, entry: &SignedEvidenceEntry, now_ms: u64, max_age_ms: u64) -> bool` that fail-closes when `now_ms.saturating_sub(entry.issued_at_ms) >= max_age_ms`.
  5. Optionally maintain a bounded LRU of consumed decision_ids for downstream replay-protection (parallel to seen_nonces in audience_token.rs).

CROSS-REF: Distinct from bd-myz81 (sentinel evidence_hash from convenience overload) and bd-99eu8 (HMAC secret stored as plain String).  Same pattern class as bd-j587o (threshold_sig context omission) and bd-18q4j (OperatorAuthorization replay) — confirms a system-wide blind spot: signing preimages capture WHAT was decided but not WHEN or that-it-can-only-be-applied-once.
close_reason: Added v7 decision_id and issued_at_ms freshness binding to SignedEvidenceEntry, bumped quarantine control HMAC domain to v3, added verify_signed_decision age/future checks, and covered freshness/tamper replay regressions.

title: [REVIEW] Barrier warning threshold accepts non-finite f64 config
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/control_plane/epoch_transition_barrier.rs:417
PATTERN: f64 arithmetic without is_finite() guard / missing config validation
WHY IT'S A BUG: BarrierConfig::validate() checks timeout integers but never rejects NaN, infinity, negative, or >1.0 abort_warning_threshold values. abort_warning_time() multiplies global_timeout_ms by that untrusted f64 and casts to u64, and try_commit() also casts the threshold percentage to u32 for audit output, so malformed config can silently clamp/saturate or fire warnings at the wrong boundary instead of failing closed.
SUGGESTED FIX: Make validate() require abort_warning_threshold.is_finite() and 0.0 <= threshold <= 1.0, and make abort_warning_time() avoid raw f64-to-integer casts unless validation has succeeded or use a checked/clamped helper.
EVIDENCE: git blame shows 156ba49a2 at lines 416-417 adding `(self.global_timeout_ms as f64 * self.abort_warning_threshold) as u64`; af1a268fa lines 431-447 validate only integer timeout fields; f6b8c4f6c line 816 casts `(self.config.abort_warning_threshold * 100.0) as u32`.

title: TOCTOU race in proof generator mutex release
description:
TOCTOU race condition in ConcurrentProofGenerator::generate_proof introduced by bd-2js7d concurrency fix.

**Issue:** Between begin_generate_proof() releasing mutex and finish_generate_proof() re-acquiring it, enforce_timeouts() can change request status from Generating to Failed, causing spurious proof generation failures.

**Location:** crates/franken-node/src/vef/proof_generator.rs:714-725

**Attack vector:**
1. Thread A calls generate_proof(), gets to backend.generate() 
2. Thread B calls enforce_timeouts(), times out the request 
3. Thread A's proof succeeds but finish_generate_proof() rejects it due to status != Generating

**Fix:** Add timeout_deadline_millis to proof request state, check in finish_generate_proof() if request was legitimately timed out vs. timed out during generation window. Only reject if proof generation exceeded the deadline.

**Pattern:** Classic TOCTOU - Time-of-Check (begin) to Time-of-Use (finish) race condition.
close_reason: Fixed by deadline-aware proof-generation state and regression coverage; validated proof_generator_timeout_race and all-targets check

title: [BUG-AUDIT] Use canonical bytes for structured Ed25519 signing
description:
Pass-id: review-rotation-2026-05-02-T0340-cod9-relocate-and-audit-atc-crypto

Read-only audit finding in crates/franken-node/src/crypto/signer.rs.

Finding: CryptoSigner::sign_structured promises deterministic structured-data signing, but Ed25519Signer::sign_structured serializes arbitrary T with serde_json::to_vec at signer.rs:105-113. Generic serde_json bytes are not a canonical encoding for all Serialize inputs, especially unordered maps or types whose Serialize implementation can emit map keys in non-stable order. This makes signatures depend on serializer/input ordering rather than the crate's canonical encoding rules, creating hash/canonicalization adjacency risk.

Fix direction: restrict sign_structured to canonicalizable inputs or route through the crate's canonical serializer / an explicitly sorted representation before signing. Add regressions showing logically equivalent map-like data signs to identical bytes and that domain separation still rejects cross-context signatures.

Why filed, not fixed: current pass grants src/crypto/** read-only.
close_reason: fixed in commit 2f68101e - replaced serde_json::to_vec with canonical JSON serialization

title: [10.7] Add verifier CLI conformance contract tests.
description:
## [10.7] Verifier CLI Conformance Contract Tests

### Why This Exists

The verifier CLI (`franken-node verify`) is a public interface used by external verifiers, CI pipelines, and the verifier economy (10.17, 10.12). Its behavior must be stable and predictable across versions — breaking changes to input formats, output schemas, exit codes, or error messages would break downstream consumers silently. This bead establishes contract tests that pin the CLI's observable behavior, detect unintended breaking changes, and require explicit version bumps when intentional breaking changes are made.

### What It Must Do

**Contract definition**: Define the verifier CLI's contract in a machine-readable format (`spec/verifier_cli_contract.toml` or similar). The contract specifies: (1) accepted input formats (file paths, stdin, glob patterns), (2) output JSON schema for success and error cases, (3) exit codes and their meanings (0 = all checks pass, 1 = some checks fail, 2 = invalid input, 3 = internal error), (4) error message format (structured JSON with error code, human message, and remediation hint), and (5) command-line flag inventory with types and defaults.

**Contract test suite**: A test suite that exercises every aspect of the contract with specific, pinned inputs and expected outputs. Tests use snapshot-style assertions — the expected output is stored alongside the test and compared byte-for-byte (after normalization of timestamps and paths). Adding a new flag or output field is non-breaking; removing or changing one is breaking.

**Breaking change detection**: When a contract test fails, the failure message clearly distinguishes between "new field added" (non-breaking, auto-update snapshot) and "existing field changed/removed" (breaking, requires version bump). A `--update-snapshots` flag regenerates expected outputs for non-breaking changes.

**Version enforcement**: The CLI embeds a contract version (semver). Breaking changes increment the major version. The contract test suite validates that the embedded version matches the contract definition's version. If a breaking change is detected without a version bump, the gate fails.

**Backward compatibility layer**: When a major version bump occurs, the CLI supports `--compat-version=<N>` to produce output in the previous format for one major version back, giving consumers time to migrate.

### Acceptance Criteria

1. Verifier CLI contract is defined in a machine-readable file specifying input formats, output schemas, exit codes, error formats, and flag inventory.
2. Contract test suite covers every exit code, every output field, every error code, and every accepted input format with pinned expected outputs.
3. Breaking vs. non-breaking change detection works: new fields pass, changed/removed fields fail with clear breaking-change message.
4. Contract version is embedded in CLI output and validated against the contract definition.
5. `--update-snapshots` regenerates expected outputs for non-breaking changes only.
6. `--compat-version=<N>` produces output in the previous major version's format.
7. Verification script `scripts/check_verifier_contract.py` with `--json` flag validates the contract test suite.
8. Unit tests in `tests/test_check_verifier_contract.py` cover contract parsing, snapshot comparison, breaking change detection, version validation, and compat-version output.

### Key Dependencies

- Verifier CLI implementation (`franken-node verify` subcommand).
- CLI framework from bd-n9r (cli.rs).
- JSON Schema for output validation.
- Existing verification scripts that the CLI orchestrates.

### Testing & Logging Requirements

- Stability test: run contract tests against current CLI, assert all pass.
- Breaking change test: modify an output field, run tests, assert breaking-change failure.
- Non-breaking change test: add a new output field, run tests, assert pass (or auto-update).
- Compat-version test: request previous version output, assert format matches previous contract.
- Structured JSON logs for each contract test execution: test name, expected vs. actual, pass/fail, breaking/non-breaking classification.

### Expected Artifacts

- `spec/verifier_cli_contract.toml` — contract definition.
- `tests/contract/snapshots/` — pinned expected outputs.
- `scripts/check_verifier_contract.py` — verification script.
- `tests/test_check_verifier_contract.py` — unit tests.
- `artifacts/section_10_7/bd-3ex/verification_evidence.json` — gate results.
- `artifacts/section_10_7/bd-3ex/verification_summary.md` — human-readable summary.

### Additional E2E Requirement

- E2E test scripts must execute full end-to-end workflows from clean fixtures, emit deterministic machine-readable pass/fail evidence, and capture stepwise structured logs for root-cause triage.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Verifier CLI exposes at least: verify-module, verify-migration, verify-compatibility, and verify-corpus subcommands.
2. Each subcommand has a conformance contract defined in a spec document under docs/specs/ specifying inputs, outputs, exit codes, and error formats.
3. Contract tests exercise every specified input/output combination including edge cases and error paths.
4. Tests validate that CLI output conforms to the documented JSON schema (no undocumented fields, no missing required fields).
5. Exit codes follow a documented taxonomy: 0=pass, 1=fail, 2=error, 3=skipped.
6. Per Section 3.2 capability #10 (public verifier toolkit): CLI is usable by an external party with no internal knowledge — contract tests verify this by running in an isolated environment with no access to internal state.
7. Contract tests are generated from the spec documents (not hand-written) to ensure spec and tests stay in sync.

title: Emit CAN-006 audit event on resource leak detection in Drop impl (connector/cancellation_protocol.rs:373)
close_reason: Added tracing::warn! with event_code=CAN-006, workflow, leaked_resources count to Drop impl. Uses existing event_codes::CAN_006 constant.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/connector/cancellation_protocol.rs around lines 373-378
CONTEXT: Drop impl for a resource-holding type

CURRENT CODE (in Drop):
  if !self.released && self.resources.has_leaks() {
      // INV-CAN-NO-LEAK: force-release on drop with warning.
      // In production this would emit CAN-006 via the audit channel.
      let _leaked = self.resources.release_all();
      // Leak detected during drop -- CAN-006 would be emitted here.
  }

PROBLEM: When a resource leak is detected during Drop, the code force-releases all resources (correct) but emits NO audit event (incorrect). The CAN-006 event code exists in the event code registry but is never emitted in this code path. This is a safety-critical audit trail gap — resource leaks could happen silently in production with no trace in the audit log.

REQUIRED FIX: Emit a CAN-006 event when leak detection triggers in Drop. Challenges:
1. Drop impls cannot return errors and should not panic
2. The audit channel may not be available in Drop context
3. The existing codebase handles this pattern by using thread-local or static audit sinks

IMPLEMENTATION APPROACH:
- Check how other Drop impls in the codebase emit events (search for Drop + event emission patterns)
- If an audit channel is available via the struct, use it directly
- If not, consider: (a) storing an audit sink reference in the struct, (b) using a module-level static audit sink, or (c) at minimum, using tracing::warn! to produce a structured log entry with the CAN-006 code
- The _leaked return value from release_all() likely contains info about what was leaked — include it in the event payload
- Ensure the event includes: event_code=CAN-006, resource_count, leaked_resource_ids, timestamp

INVARIANTS AFFECTED: INV-CAN-NO-LEAK (partially: force-release works, but audit trail is missing)

title: [10.18] Implement hash-chained receipt stream with periodic commitment checkpoints.
description:
## Why This Exists

Section 10.18 implements the Verifiable Execution Fabric (VEF) — Enhancement Map 9L — delivering proof-carrying runtime compliance for franken_node. This is a Track C (Trust-Native Ecosystem Layer) cornerstone that elevates trust from "we can replay it" to "we can cryptographically prove what executed."

This bead implements the hash-chained receipt stream — the tamper-evident backbone of the VEF data pipeline. Every ExecutionReceipt (defined in bd-p73r) gets appended to a hash chain where each entry's hash incorporates the previous entry's hash, creating an append-only, tamper-detectable log. Periodic commitment checkpoints create reproducible anchor points that proof workers (bd-28u0, bd-1u8m) use to define proof windows, and that verifiers (bd-1o4v) use to validate chain integrity.

Without this component, individual receipts are isolated facts. The hash chain transforms them into a cryptographically ordered, tamper-evident history that forms the substrate for all downstream proofs and adversarial testing (bd-3ptu).

## What This Must Do

1. Implement an append-only receipt stream backed by deterministic hash chaining — each receipt's chain hash incorporates the prior receipt's chain hash plus the current receipt's content hash.
2. Implement periodic commitment checkpoints at configurable intervals (by count and/or time), producing reproducible commitment values that summarize the chain state at that point.
3. Ensure tamper detection is fail-closed: any modification to a past receipt or chain link is detectable and causes immediate rejection with a stable error classification.
4. Support concurrent append operations with linearizable ordering guarantees.
5. Implement chain verification: given a range of receipts and a checkpoint, independently verify chain integrity from scratch.
6. Handle chain initialization (genesis receipt) and recovery (resuming from the latest valid checkpoint after crash/restart).
7. Emit structured commitment log entries for each checkpoint in append-only JSONL format.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Receipt stream is append-only with deterministic chain linkage; checkpoint commitments are reproducible; tamper detection is fail-closed.
- Chain hash computation is deterministic: identical receipt sequences always produce identical chain hashes and checkpoints.
- Checkpoint commitments are reproducible: re-computing a checkpoint from the same receipt window always yields the same value.
- Tamper detection covers: receipt content modification, receipt insertion, receipt deletion, receipt reordering, and checkpoint forgery.
- Chain verification runs independently (no mutable state required beyond the receipts and checkpoints themselves).
- Genesis and crash-recovery scenarios produce correct chain state without data loss or silent corruption.
- Concurrent appends maintain linearizable order and correct chain linkage.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests for chain append, hash linkage verification, and checkpoint computation.
- Tamper detection tests: modify a receipt in the middle of a chain, insert a receipt, delete a receipt, reorder receipts, forge a checkpoint — all must be detected and fail closed.
- Crash recovery tests: simulate crash at various points (mid-append, mid-checkpoint), verify recovery produces correct state.
- Concurrency tests: parallel appends from multiple threads produce a valid chain with correct ordering.
- Performance benchmark: measure append throughput and checkpoint computation latency under load.
- Golden vector tests: committed chain with known receipts, expected chain hashes, and expected checkpoints.
- Structured logging: `VEF-CHAIN-001` (receipt appended), `VEF-CHAIN-002` (checkpoint created), `VEF-CHAIN-003` (chain verified), `VEF-CHAIN-ERR-*` (tamper detected, integrity failure).
- Trace correlation IDs linking chain events to originating receipt IDs.

## Expected Artifacts

- `src/trust/vef_receipt_chain.rs` — hash-chained receipt stream implementation with checkpoint support.
- `tests/conformance/vef_receipt_chain_integrity.rs` — conformance tests for chain integrity and tamper detection.
- `artifacts/10.18/vef_receipt_commitment_log.jsonl` — sample commitment log demonstrating checkpoint format.
- `artifacts/section_10_18/bd-3g4k/verification_evidence.json` — machine-readable CI/release gate evidence.
- `artifacts/section_10_18/bd-3g4k/verification_summary.md` — human-readable summary linking intent to measured outcomes.

## Dependencies

- bd-p73r (blocks) — Canonical ExecutionReceipt schema and deterministic serialization: the chain operates on receipts whose format must already be defined.

Dependents: bd-28u0 (proof-job scheduler needs chain/checkpoints for windowing), bd-3ptu (adversarial test suite for receipt tampering), bd-2hjg (section gate), bd-32p (plan-level tracker).
acceptance_criteria: - Receipt stream is append-only with deterministic chain linkage; checkpoint commitments are reproducible; tamper detection is fail-closed.

close_reason: Replaced HashSignatureVerifier with Ed25519SignatureVerifier using ed25519-dalek. All 50 tests pass.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/security/impossible_default.rs around line 411
STRUCT: HashSignatureVerifier (implements SignatureVerifier trait)

CURRENT CODE:
  impl SignatureVerifier for HashSignatureVerifier {
      fn verify(&self, token: &CapabilityToken) -> bool {
          ct_eq(&token.signature, &token.content_hash())
      }
  }

PROBLEM: This compares the "signature" field against the SHA-256 content hash. This means the signature IS the content hash — anyone who can compute SHA-256 (i.e., everyone) can produce a valid "signature." This provides zero authentication.

REQUIRED FIX: Replace with real Ed25519 signature verification using the ed25519-dalek crate (already a workspace dependency). The verifier needs a public key to verify against. Options:
  1. Store the public key in the CapabilityToken itself (self-contained but needs a trust anchor)
  2. Accept a VerificationKey parameter (requires changing the SignatureVerifier trait)
  3. Look up the key from a trust store based on token.issuer

CONSIDERATIONS:
- Check all callers of SignatureVerifier::verify() to understand key availability
- The CapabilityToken struct already has signature and content_hash fields — understand the expected flow: who signs, who verifies
- The trait is in impossible_default.rs which suggests it was meant as a "this should never ship" default
- ed25519-dalek is already used in the crate (check security/epoch_scoped_keys.rs for patterns)
- Ensure backward compatibility: existing serialized tokens may have hash-based "signatures" — either reject them (preferred, fail-closed) or provide a migration path
- Tests: existing tests that create HashSignatureVerifier must be updated with real key pairs
- The ct_eq usage is correct for timing-safe comparison — keep constant-time comparison in the real implementation

INVARIANTS AFFECTED: Any invariant that assumes signature verification provides authentication of the token issuer.

title: [10.15] Add observability dashboards for region health, obligation health, lane pressure, and cancel latency.
description:
## Why This Exists
The 10 Hard Runtime Invariants from Section 8.5 are only useful in production if operators can observe their health in real time and respond when invariants are under stress. Without observability dashboards, region quiescence failures, obligation leaks, lane starvation, and cancellation latency spikes are invisible until they cause user-facing outages. title: [10.18] Integrate VEF coverage and proof-validity metrics into claim compiler and public trust scoreboard.
description:
## Why This Exists

Section 10.18 implements the Verifiable Execution Fabric (VEF) — Enhancement Map 9L — delivering proof-carrying runtime compliance. This is a Track D (Category Benchmark + Market Capture) integration point: VEF proof coverage and validity metrics must flow into the claim compiler and public trust scoreboard so that franken_node's published security/compliance claims are backed by cryptographic evidence.

This bead integrates VEF coverage and proof-validity metrics into two critical downstream systems: the claim compiler (which assembles and validates security/compliance claims for release) and the public trust scoreboard (which publishes trust posture metrics externally). Without this integration, franken_node could claim "cryptographically verified execution" without actually tracking or publishing whether proofs are current, complete, and valid — undermining the trust-native differentiation.

The claim compiler must be able to require VEF-backed evidence for specific claim categories (e.g., "all high-risk filesystem operations were policy-compliant") and reject claims where VEF coverage is insufficient. The scoreboard must publish real-time VEF coverage/validity statistics with signed evidence links for external consumption.

## What This Must Do

1. Define VEF coverage metrics: percentage of high-risk action classes with current valid proofs, proof freshness (time since last proof), coverage gaps by action class.
2. Define VEF validity metrics: proof verification success rate, verdict class distribution, degraded-mode time fraction.
3. Integrate VEF metrics into the claim compiler so that security/compliance claims can declare VEF evidence requirements.
4. Implement claim compiler gates: claims requiring VEF evidence are blocked when coverage or validity metrics fall below configured thresholds.
5. Integrate VEF metrics into the public trust scoreboard with signed evidence links pointing to specific proofs and verification records.
6. Ensure scoreboard publications are deterministic and reproducible from the underlying evidence.
7. Document the claim-VEF binding semantics, threshold configuration, and scoreboard publication format.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Claim compiler can require VEF-backed evidence for security/compliance claims; scoreboard publishes VEF coverage/validity stats with signed evidence links.
- Claim compiler correctly blocks claims when VEF coverage is below required thresholds.
- Claim compiler correctly passes claims when VEF coverage meets requirements.
- Scoreboard VEF metrics are accurate, up-to-date, and traceable to specific proofs.
- Evidence links in scoreboard publications are verifiable (link -> proof -> receipt window -> chain commitment).
- Coverage gap reporting identifies specific action classes missing proof coverage.
- Threshold configuration is policy-driven and takes effect without code changes.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests for VEF metric computation: coverage percentage, freshness, gap detection.
- Claim compiler gate tests: configure a claim requiring VEF evidence, test with sufficient coverage (pass) and insufficient coverage (block).
- Scoreboard publication tests: generate VEF-backed scoreboard entry, verify all metrics and evidence links are valid.
- Evidence link verification tests: follow links from scoreboard -> proof -> receipt window, confirm chain integrity.
- Threshold boundary tests: coverage at exactly the threshold, just below, just above.
- Structured logging: `VEF-CLAIM-001` (claim VEF check initiated), `VEF-CLAIM-002` (claim passed VEF gate), `VEF-CLAIM-003` (claim blocked by VEF gap), `VEF-SCORE-001` (scoreboard updated with VEF metrics).

title: [MOCK] sdk/verifier_sdk verify_chain has no cryptographic chain linkage
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/sdk/verifier_sdk.rs:673-854

FINDING: VerifierSdk::verify_chain() is documented as the SDK's chain-verification entry point and emits an evidence-bearing VerificationReport whose verdict can be Pass. The actual checks performed are: (1) chain length within capacity, (2) all reports share the same SCHEMA_TAG/API_VERSION, (3) all binding_hash values are non-empty and pairwise-unique, (4) all request_id values pairwise-unique, (5) per-report verdict counts. NO check verifies that report N+1's binding_hash actually commits to report N's outputs (no Merkle/MAC linkage), and no signature on any individual report is verified.

WHY IT'S A BUG: The function name 'verify_chain' and the doc-comment 'verify a chain of verification reports for consistency and integrity' imply a hash/signature-chain integrity check (a la transparency log). What is actually implemented is a uniqueness / schema-consistency sanity check. A malicious aggregator can fabricate a chain of N independent VerificationReport values (e.g. taken from unrelated artifacts or freshly minted with arbitrary verifier_identity strings) and as long as binding_hashes / request_ids are unique and Pass-verdict, the chain will Pass. There is no provenance binding between adjacent reports, so a 'chain' in this SDK is simply a set with uniqueness — it is not a chain in the cryptographic sense.

SUGGESTED FIX:
1. Add an explicit prev_binding_hash field (or hash-chain commitment) to VerificationReport and require reports[i].prev_binding_hash == reports[i-1].binding_hash via constant_time::ct_eq.
2. Require each report carry a detached Ed25519 signature over (binding_hash || prev_binding_hash || verdict_code) signed by verifier_identity, and verify it via connector::verifier_sdk::verify_ed25519_signature_hex.
3. Add a 'genesis' check on reports[0] (e.g. prev_binding_hash must equal a known genesis sentinel).
4. At minimum: rename the public function to verify_report_set_uniqueness and document loudly that this is NOT a chain verifier.

EVIDENCE:
verify_chain (lines 673-854) checks only:
- chain_length, chain_depth_check
- schema_tag_consistent, api_version_consistent
- binding_hashes_present, binding_hashes_unique
- request_ids_unique
- chain_verdict_summary (counts pass vs fail)

NO check on the order: rg 'prev|previous|chain.*hash|merkle' crates/franken-node/src/sdk/verifier_sdk.rs returns nothing relevant. NO signature verification on individual reports inside verify_chain.

External callers: rg 'verify_chain' crates/franken-node/src/ shows only test calls inside verifier_sdk.rs itself — this is the public SDK API for third parties and currently provides only structural consistency, not chain integrity.
close_reason: Retired the in-crate verifier SDK's misleading verify_chain API, renamed the live operation to structural report-set uniqueness validation, added structural-only evidence, and covered the public conformance path with a focused rch regression
