title: [10.14] Implement monotonic hardening mode state machine with one-way escalation semantics.
description:
## Why This Exists
franken_node's integrity assurance level must only increase over time — once the system reaches a higher hardening mode, it should not silently regress to a weaker one. This is the monotonic hardening invariant, directly inspired by FrankenSQLite's one-way journal mode escalation (9J enhancement map). The hardening state machine enforces this by modeling hardening levels as a totally-ordered set with one-way transitions: the system can escalate (e.g., from `Standard` to `Enhanced` to `Maximum`) but cannot de-escalate without an explicit governance rollback artifact that creates an auditable exception. This supports Section 8.5 Invariant #4 (monotonic safety progression) and is a foundational component for the automatic hardening trigger (bd-1zym), rate clamps (bd-1ayu), and retroactive hardening (bd-1daz).

## What This Must Do
1. Implement `HardeningStateMachine` in `crates/franken-node/src/policy/hardening_state_machine.rs` with:
   - `HardeningLevel` enum: `Baseline`, `Standard`, `Enhanced`, `Maximum`, `Critical` — totally ordered.
   - `fn current_level(&self) -> HardeningLevel` — returns current hardening level.
   - `fn escalate(&mut self, target: HardeningLevel) -> Result<(), HardeningError>` — transitions to a higher level. Rejects transitions to same or lower level.
   - `fn governance_rollback(&mut self, target: HardeningLevel, artifact: &GovernanceRollbackArtifact) -> Result<(), HardeningError>` — allows downward transition ONLY with a valid governance artifact.
   - `GovernanceRollbackArtifact` struct: `artifact_id`, `approver_id`, `reason`, `timestamp`, `signature`.
2. Make state transitions durable:
   - Every transition (escalation or rollback) is persisted to disk before it takes effect.
   - State can be reconstructed by replaying the transition log.
3. Make state transitions replayable:
   - `fn replay_transitions(log: &[TransitionRecord]) -> Self` — reconstructs state machine from persisted log.
   - Replay produces identical state as live execution.
4. Reject illegal regressions:
   - Any attempt to call `escalate` with a level <= current is rejected with `HardeningError::IllegalRegression`.
   - Any `governance_rollback` with an invalid or missing artifact is rejected with `HardeningError::InvalidRollbackArtifact`.
5. Write security tests at `tests/security/monotonic_hardening.rs` covering:
   - Forward escalation through all levels.
   - Rejection of backward escalation.
   - Governance rollback with valid artifact succeeds.
   - Governance rollback with invalid artifact fails.
   - Replay produces identical state.
6. Produce state history artifact at `artifacts/10.14/hardening_state_history.json` recording all transitions in a test run.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Hardening transitions are monotonic unless explicit governance rollback artifact is present; state transitions are durable and replayable; illegal regressions are rejected.
- `HardeningLevel` has at least 5 levels with total ordering.
- `escalate` succeeds only for strictly higher levels.
- `governance_rollback` succeeds only with a valid, signed artifact.
- State is persisted before transition takes effect (crash safety).
- `replay_transitions` produces identical state to live execution.
- State history artifact records every transition with timestamp and trigger.

## Testing & Logging Requirements
- Unit tests: Each transition pair (Baseline->Standard, Standard->Enhanced, etc.); rejection of same-level transition; rejection of downward transition; `GovernanceRollbackArtifact` validation (missing fields, invalid signature); replay from empty log; replay from multi-transition log.
- Integration tests: Full lifecycle: Baseline -> Standard -> Enhanced -> governance rollback to Standard -> Standard -> Maximum; persist state, restart, verify level preserved; concurrent escalation attempts (verify serialization).
- Conformance tests: Monotonicity property — no sequence of `escalate` calls ever decreases the level; replay determinism across 100 runs; governance artifact format stability.
- Adversarial tests: Attempt to forge `GovernanceRollbackArtifact` with wrong signature; attempt to escalate past `Critical`; inject corrupted transition log; attempt rollback without artifact.
- Structured logs: `EVD-HARDEN-001` on escalation (includes from/to levels); `EVD-HARDEN-002` on illegal regression rejected; `EVD-HARDEN-003` on governance rollback (includes artifact ID); `EVD-HARDEN-004` on state replayed from log. All logs include `epoch_id`, `current_level`.

## Expected Artifacts
- `crates/franken-node/src/policy/hardening_state_machine.rs` — implementation
- `tests/security/monotonic_hardening.rs` — security tests
- `artifacts/10.14/hardening_state_history.json` — transition history
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-3rya/verification_evidence.json` — machine-readable pass/fail evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-3rya/verification_summary.md` — human-readable summary

## Dependencies
- Upstream: none (foundational component for the hardening subsystem)
- Downstream: bd-1zym (automatic hardening trigger uses state machine), bd-1ayu (rate clamps reference current level), bd-1daz (retroactive hardening writes to state machine), bd-3epz (section gate), bd-5rh (10.14 plan gate)
acceptance_criteria:
1. Hardening state machine defines ordered levels: Baseline, Elevated, Strict, Maximum. Transitions are monotonically increasing (Baseline->Elevated->Strict->Maximum) unless a governance rollback artifact is presented.
2. Monotonic invariant is enforced at the storage layer: any attempt to write a lower hardening level than the current level is rejected with a structured error (HARDENING_REGRESSION_BLOCKED) unless accompanied by a valid governance rollback artifact.
3. Governance rollback artifacts must be: (a) signed by M-of-N governance key holders (threshold configurable per deployment), (b) include explicit justification text, (c) include the target rollback level, and (d) be logged immutably in the evidence ledger.
4. State transitions are durable: persisted to WAL-mode SQLite before acknowledgment. Crash recovery replays to the last durable state.
5. State transitions are replayable: given the same sequence of escalation triggers and rollback artifacts, the state machine produces identical state history.
6. Each hardening level maps to a concrete policy set: Baseline (standard trust checks), Elevated (additional proof requirements), Strict (mandatory multi-party verification), Maximum (all operations require fresh attestations).
7. Escalation triggers include: security incident detection, revocation cascade event, anomalous trust-state change, and operator-initiated escalation via CLI.
8. CLI surface: `franken-node hardening status` (current level + history), `franken-node hardening escalate --level <level>` (with authorization), `franken-node hardening rollback --artifact <path>` (with governance artifact).
9. Health endpoint exposes: current hardening level, time-in-level, last escalation trigger, and last rollback (if any).
10. All state transitions emit structured log events: HARDENING_ESCALATED, HARDENING_ROLLBACK_REQUESTED, HARDENING_ROLLBACK_APPROVED, HARDENING_REGRESSION_BLOCKED with level, trigger, and trace IDs.
close_reason: Completed: 5-level monotonic hardening state machine, governance rollback, replay, 35 Rust tests pass, all artifacts delivered

title: [REVIEW] Extension version metadata lacks length and vector caps
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/supply_chain/extension_registry.rs:83
PATTERN: unbounded string/vector validation and allocation before rejection
WHY IT IS A BUG: VersionEntry includes version, parent_version, content_hash, registered_at, and compatible_with, but register() validates none of those fields and add_version() only checks monotonic order. parse_monotonic_version collects all dot-separated version segments into a Vec before rejecting malformed semver, so a huge dotted version string allocates heavily; compatible_with can also be stored unbounded in each retained VersionEntry.
SUGGESTED FIX: Add MAX_VERSION_LEN, exact content-hash validation, MAX_COMPATIBLE_WITH entries, and per-entry string caps. Parse semver without collecting unbounded segments, or reject overlong strings before splitting.
EVIDENCE: git blame -L 83,111 -L 206,214 -L 720,858 -L 1054,1130 -- crates/franken-node/src/supply_chain/extension_registry.rs shows parse_monotonic_version collecting split parts at line 84, VersionEntry.compatible_with as Vec<String> at line 213, register() only capping trace/name/description/publisher/tags, and add_version() pushing version metadata into ext.versions after only monotonic semver validation.
close_reason: Bounded extension version metadata before registry admission and version append

title: [11] Contract field: change summary
description:

Section: 11 — Evidence And Decision Contracts (Mandatory)

Why This Exists:
Section 11 establishes mandatory evidence contracts for every major subsystem proposal. The 8 required fields are: (1) change summary, (2) compatibility and threat evidence, (3) EV score and tier, (4) expected-loss model, (5) fallback trigger, (6) rollout wedge, (7) rollback command, (8) benchmark and correctness artifacts. title: [REVIEW] MMR inclusion verifier hashes overlong audit paths
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/control_plane/mmr_proofs.rs:348
PATTERN: unbounded proof vector is hashed in verifier without capacity/shape guard
WHY IT'S A BUG: Inclusion proofs generated by this module are logarithmic in tree size, but verify_inclusion() only checks nonzero tree size, matching root tree size, and leaf_index < tree_size before iterating every sibling in proof.audit_path. A forged proof for tree_size=1 can include thousands of siblings and force arbitrary hash work even though the valid path length should be 0.
SUGGESTED FIX: Derive the maximum valid audit path length from proof.tree_size (ceil(log2(tree_size))) and reject proof.audit_path.len() above that bound before hashing; update the massive-audit-path negative test to require fail-closed rejection.
EVIDENCE: git blame shows 10f532f3b lines 312-357 verify_inclusion() looping over `&proof.audit_path` with no length bound; lines 747-758 assert generated proofs are <=14 for 4000 leaves; lines 1135-1165 create a 10000-entry path for tree_size=1 but accept either Ok or Err instead of requiring rejection.
close_reason: Rejected overlong MMR inclusion audit paths before root recompute

title: [10.15] Enforce canonical all-point cancellation injection gate (from `10.14`) for critical control workflows.
description:
## Why This Exists
Hard Runtime Invariant #3 (cancellation protocol semantics) cannot be trusted unless cancellation is injected at every possible suspension point and the system is verified to maintain its invariants (no obligation leaks, no half-commit outcomes, no quiescence violations). Section 10.14 (bd-876n) built the canonical all-point cancellation injection framework that inserts cancellation signals at every await point in a workflow. This bead enforces that canonical injection gate on franken_node's critical control workflows, making it a CI requirement that every high-impact protocol survives cancellation at every await point without violating any runtime invariant.

## What This Must Do
1. Implement `tests/lab/control_cancellation_injection.rs` that:
   - Uses the canonical 10.14 cancellation injection framework (bd-876n).
   - For each critical control workflow (lifecycle, rollout, quarantine, migration, fencing, health-gate), runs the workflow and injects cancellation at every await point (one run per injection point).
   - After each injection, asserts: (a) no obligation leaks (all obligations committed or rolled back), (b) no half-commit outcomes (state is either fully committed or fully rolled back), (c) no quiescence violations (all regions are closed, all child tasks drained).
   - Collects results into a structured report.
2. Generate `artifacts/10.15/control_cancel_injection_report.json` with:
   - Per-workflow, per-injection-point results: injection_point (await site identifier), obligations_status, commit_status, quiescence_status, pass/fail.
   - Summary: total injection points, total passes, total failures, first failure details.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Canonical cancellation injection runs on every critical protocol flow; no obligation leaks, no half-commit outcomes, no quiescence violations.
- The injection gate uses the canonical 10.14 framework, not custom injection logic.
- Every await point in every critical workflow is covered (not just a sample).
- A single failure at any injection point fails the gate.
- The injection report is consumed by the section gate (bd-20eg).

## Testing & Logging Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Validate the injection harness setup with a trivial workflow (one await point, cancel there, assert rollback).
- **Integration tests**: Full injection sweep on lifecycle workflow. Full sweep on rollout workflow.
- **Conformance tests**: Assert the injection framework covers all await points (compare against AST analysis of await points in the workflow).
- **Adversarial tests**: Introduce a workflow with a hidden await point (e.g., inside a utility function); assert the injection framework still finds it. Introduce a workflow that leaks an obligation on cancel; assert the gate catches it.
- **Structured logs**: Event codes `CIN-001` (injection point enumerated), `CIN-002` (cancellation injected), `CIN-003` (post-cancel assertion passed), `CIN-004` (post-cancel assertion failed — obligation leak), `CIN-005` (post-cancel assertion failed — half-commit), `CIN-006` (post-cancel assertion failed — quiescence violation). Include workflow_id, injection_point_id, and trace correlation ID.

## Expected Artifacts
- `tests/lab/control_cancellation_injection.rs`
- `artifacts/10.15/control_cancel_injection_report.json`
- `artifacts/section_10_15/bd-3tpg/verification_evidence.json`
- `artifacts/section_10_15/bd-3tpg/verification_summary.md`

## Dependencies
- **Upstream**: bd-876n (10.14 — canonical all-point cancellation injection framework)
- **Downstream**: bd-20eg (section gate)
acceptance_criteria: - Canonical cancellation injection runs on every critical protocol flow; no obligation leaks, no half-commit outcomes, no quiescence violations.

title: [replacement-gap] Add replacement-critical truthfulness gate for migration/policy/runtime/verifier/extension/control surfaces
description:
Why this exists:
Multiple closed sections currently still have replacement-critical product paths with placeholder or surrogate trust logic. The deeper audit expanded the affected surface beyond migration/policy/runtime/verifier paths: extension admission, trust-card materialization, certification, control-channel auth, and product session-auth still contain security-critical shortcuts that can make the tracker and release story look green while the underlying trust claims are not actually true.

What this bead must do:
Create a replacement-critical truthfulness gate covering migration autopilot/artifacts, compatibility authorization, safe mode, supervision time/budget logic, anti-entropy reconciliation, verifier SDK/economy surfaces, extension registry admission, trust-card/certification derivation, control-channel auth, and product session-auth. The gate should combine static scanning, dynamic adversarial witness corpora, and deterministic evidence emission. It must explicitly block the program success narrative if any critical path still relies on fabricated hashes, signature-present shortcuts, fake duration math, clock stubs, proof-shape checks, decorative signed-looking strings, token-present auth, or asserted trust inputs that bypass verified evidence.

Acceptance criteria:
1. The gate statically scans replacement-critical non-engine surfaces including `migration_pipeline.rs`, `migration_artifact.rs`, `compat_gates.rs`, `compatibility_gate.rs`, `safe_mode.rs`, `supervision.rs`, `anti_entropy.rs`, `verifier_economy/mod.rs`, `connector/verifier_sdk.rs`, `supply_chain/extension_registry.rs`, `supply_chain/trust_card.rs`, `supply_chain/certification.rs`, `connector/control_channel.rs`, `api/session_auth.rs`, plus directly related helpers for banned placeholder markers and trust surrogates.
2. The gate runs a dynamic witness corpus including: forged compatibility receipts, migration inputs whose names previously spoofed heuristics, corrupted/stale trust-state scenarios, burst restart schedules, zero-filled/fake proofs, replay capsules with decorative signatures, forged extension manifests, attestation-chain truncations, caller-injected fake trust-card inputs, guessed control tokens, and decorative session signatures.
3. Any surviving placeholder/surrogate acceptance path fails the gate closed and produces a machine-readable gap report mapping witness -> offending code path -> remediation bead.
4. The gate is wired into replacement-relevant verification so section/program completion cannot stay green while these trust surrogates survive.
5. The gate is deterministic, reproducible, and cheap enough to run in CI on every claim-critical change.
6. Deliver the checker/tests plus JSON and Markdown evidence artifacts with stable schemas and trace IDs.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The truthfulness gate closes only after the root-cause bug beads and the relevant section-level verification gates for 10.0, 10.3, 10.4, 10.5, 10.8, 10.10, 10.11, 10.13, 10.17, and 15 are all green, so no cross-surface replacement claim can bypass comprehensive local unit, integration, and E2E evidence.
2. Static scanning must cover banned placeholder markers, proof-shape shortcuts, decorative signature handling, asserted trust inputs, token-present auth, fake duration math, and related surrogate patterns across all named replacement-critical files plus directly related helpers.
3. Dynamic witness packs must cover at minimum: forged migration receipts, degraded evidence sources, forged compatibility receipts, stale safe-mode frontiers, supervision restart storms, anti-entropy fork or partition cases, forged replay capsules, forged extension manifests, caller-injected trust inputs, guessed control tokens, and decorative session signatures.
4. Gate output must be useful to humans: failures emit stable reason codes, remediation bead mappings, a Markdown summary, and a machine-readable report that ties each failing witness to the exact code path and evidence bundle.
5. At least one deterministic operator E2E shell script under tests/e2e/ runs the truthfulness gate end to end, captures detailed logs for every witness family, and proves deterministic replay on repeated runs.
6. Structured logs expose stable TRUTHFULNESS_GATE_* event families with required fields: trace_id, witness_id, surface, offending_path, decision, reason_code, remediation_bead, and evidence_bundle_id.
7. Evidence artifacts under artifacts/replacement_gap/bd-3tw7/ include verification_evidence.json, verification_summary.md, witness_matrix.json, and any rch offload build IDs used for gate execution or benchmark collection.
8. CI integration must fail closed on missing artifacts, stale artifacts, nondeterministic results, or witness regressions, and the total gate runtime must stay within an explicit CI budget justified by measured data.

title: [10.16] Add substrate conformance gate in CI to block non-compliant feature merges.
description:
## Why This Exists

Substrate integration policies (bd-2owx) are useless without automated enforcement. This bead adds a CI conformance gate that blocks merges of features that violate the substrate policy — for example, a PR that adds raw terminal output in a frankentui-mandatory module, or persists state without going through the frankensqlite adapter in a mandatory domain. The gate provides remediation hints and a waiver path for justified exceptions.

In the three-kernel architecture, franken_node's substrate integrations must be maintained over time as new features are added. Without CI enforcement, policy drift is inevitable — developers will take shortcuts, and the substrate integration will degrade. This gate prevents that decay.

## What This Must Do

1. Create `.github/workflows/adjacent-substrate-gate.yml` containing:
   - A CI workflow that runs on every PR targeting main.
   - Steps:
     1. Parse the substrate policy manifest (`artifacts/10.16/adjacent_substrate_policy_manifest.json` from bd-2owx).
     2. Identify which franken_node modules are modified in the PR.
     3. For each modified module, check compliance with the substrate policy:
        - If module is frankentui-mandatory: verify no raw `println!`/ANSI codes, verify frankentui imports present.
        - If module is frankensqlite-mandatory: verify persistence goes through adapter, no direct file I/O for state.
        - If module is sqlmodel_rust-mandatory: verify typed models are used, no raw SQL strings.
        - If module is fastapi_rust-mandatory: verify endpoints use the skeleton's middleware pipeline.
     4. Check waiver registry (`artifacts/10.16/waiver_registry.json` from bd-159q) for justified exceptions.
     5. Fail with remediation hints if violations found and no valid waiver exists.
     6. Pass if all modified modules comply or have valid unexpired waivers.

2. Create `tests/conformance/adjacent_substrate_gate.rs` containing:
   - Conformance test functions that implement the same checks as the CI workflow but runnable locally.
   - Tests for each substrate's compliance rules.
   - Tests that verify waiver lookup and expiry checking work correctly.

3. Generate `artifacts/10.16/adjacent_substrate_gate_report.json` containing:
   - `checks[]` array with `{module, substrate, rule, status: "pass"|"fail"|"waived", remediation_hint, waiver_id}`.
   - `summary` with `{total_checks, passed, failed, waived}`.
   - `gate_verdict`: `"pass"` or `"fail"`.

4. Create verification script `scripts/check_substrate_gate.py` with `--json` flag and `self_test()`:
   - Validates gate report completeness.
   - Ensures gate verdict is consistent with individual check results.
   - Verifies remediation hints are non-empty for all failures.

5. Create `tests/test_check_substrate_gate.py` with unit tests.

6. Produce evidence artifacts:
   - `artifacts/section_10_16/bd-3u2o/verification_evidence.json`
   - `artifacts/section_10_16/bd-3u2o/verification_summary.md`

## Acceptance Criteria

- CI detects relevant-feature noncompliance with substrate policy; failures include remediation hints and waiver path.
- The CI workflow parses the substrate policy manifest and applies correct rules per module.
- Violations produce actionable remediation hints (not just "failed" — must say what to fix and how).
- Valid unexpired waivers are recognized and do not trigger failures.
- Expired waivers are treated as violations.
- The gate can run both in CI (`.github/workflows/`) and locally (`cargo test` conformance suite).

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- **Unit tests**: Validate policy manifest parsing, module compliance checking, waiver lookup, expiry date comparison, and remediation hint generation.
- **Integration tests**: Simulate PR diffs with policy violations, valid waivers, and expired waivers; verify correct gate verdicts.
- **Event codes**: `SUBSTRATE_GATE_START` (info), `SUBSTRATE_GATE_VIOLATION` (error), `SUBSTRATE_GATE_WAIVED` (info), `SUBSTRATE_GATE_WAIVER_EXPIRED` (warning), `SUBSTRATE_GATE_PASS` (info), `SUBSTRATE_GATE_FAIL` (error).
- **Trace correlation**: PR identifier and gate run ID in all gate events.
- **Deterministic replay**: Gate tests use fixed module content and policy manifests.

## Expected Artifacts

- `.github/workflows/adjacent-substrate-gate.yml`
- `tests/conformance/adjacent_substrate_gate.rs`
- `artifacts/10.16/adjacent_substrate_gate_report.json`
- `scripts/check_substrate_gate.py`
- `tests/test_check_substrate_gate.py`
- `artifacts/section_10_16/bd-3u2o/verification_evidence.json`
- `artifacts/section_10_16/bd-3u2o/verification_summary.md`

## Dependencies

- **bd-2owx** (blocks): The substrate policy manifest must exist before the gate can enforce it.

## Dependents

- **bd-10g0**: Section gate depends on this bead.
acceptance_criteria: - CI detects relevant-feature noncompliance with substrate policy; failures include remediation hints and waiver path.

title: [10.11] Implement BOCPD regime detector for workload/incident stream shifts.
description:
[10.11] Implement BOCPD regime detector for workload/incident stream shifts.

## Why This Exists

Section 9G.5 requires automated detection of regime shifts in operational streams. Workload patterns, incident rates, trust-signal distributions, and error frequencies can shift abruptly due to deployments, attacks, infrastructure changes, or organic growth. Human operators often detect these shifts too late — after SLO violations or security incidents have already occurred. Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection (BOCPD) provides a principled, low-latency mechanism for detecting these shifts as they happen, enabling proactive policy recalibration and early alerting.

## What It Must Do

1. **BOCPD core algorithm.** Implement the Adams & MacKay (2007) Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection algorithm. The implementation must support configurable hazard functions (constant hazard rate is the default, with geometric and custom hazard as options). The posterior over run lengths must be maintained efficiently using the standard message-passing scheme.

2. **Observation models.** Support at least three conjugate observation models:
   - **Gaussian** (normal-inverse-gamma prior): for latency, throughput, and continuous metrics.
   - **Poisson** (gamma prior): for incident counts, error counts, and event rates.
   - **Categorical** (Dirichlet prior): for trust-signal class distributions and error code distributions.
   Each model must support online parameter updates without storing the full history.

3. **Changepoint signaling.** When the posterior probability of a changepoint exceeds a configurable threshold (default: 0.7), emit a `regime_shift_detected` event containing: stream name, timestamp, confidence, old regime summary statistics, new regime preliminary statistics, and recommended actions.

4. **Multi-stream correlation.** Support monitoring multiple streams simultaneously. When changepoints are detected in multiple correlated streams within a configurable time window (default: 60 seconds), emit a `correlated_regime_shift` event that links the individual detections, suggesting a common root cause.

5. **Policy recalibration hooks.** When a regime shift is detected, trigger configurable policy recalibration actions: adjust admission budgets, modify monitoring intervals, escalate alerting thresholds, or trigger diagnostic deep-scans (VOI-budgeted per bd-2nt).

6. **False positive control.** Implement a minimum run-length filter: changepoints are only signaled if the new regime persists for at least `min_run_length` observations (default: 10). This prevents spurious alerts from transient spikes.

7. **Regime history log.** Maintain a bounded history of detected regimes with their start/end timestamps, summary statistics, and confidence scores. This history is queryable for post-incident analysis.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. BOCPD algorithm implemented in `crates/franken-node/src/connector/bocpd.rs` with constant, geometric, and custom hazard functions.
2. All three observation models (Gaussian, Poisson, Categorical) implemented and tested.
3. Changepoint detection correctly identifies regime shifts in synthetic test streams with < 5% false positive rate and < 10% false negative rate on reference benchmarks.
4. Multi-stream correlation links concurrent changepoints within the configured window.
5. Policy recalibration hooks are invoked on regime shift detection.
6. Minimum run-length filter suppresses transient false positives.
7. Regime history log is queryable and bounded (configurable max entries, default: 1000).
8. Verification script `scripts/check_bocpd.py` with `--json` flag confirms all criteria.
9. Evidence artifacts written to `artifacts/section_10_11/bd-3u4/`.

## Key Dependencies

- bd-2nt (VOI-budgeted monitoring) — regime shifts can trigger diagnostic deep-scans.
- 10.13 telemetry namespace — regime shift events must conform to telemetry schema.
- 10.13 stable error namespace — detection errors use registered codes.
- Statistical libraries: `statrs` crate for probability distributions (or equivalent pure-Rust impl).

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests covering each observation model's parameter update and predictive distribution.
- Integration tests with synthetic regime-shift streams (step change, gradual drift, periodic shift).
- Golden vector tests with known changepoint locations and expected detection times.
- Self-test mode that generates a synthetic stream with a known changepoint and confirms detection.
- Structured logging: `bocpd.observation`, `bocpd.changepoint_candidate`, `bocpd.regime_shift_detected`, `bocpd.correlated_shift`, `bocpd.false_positive_suppressed` events.

## Expected Artifacts

- `docs/specs/section_10_11/bd-3u4_contract.md` — specification document.
- `crates/franken-node/src/connector/bocpd.rs` — Rust implementation.
- `scripts/check_bocpd.py` — verification script.
- `tests/test_check_bocpd.py` — unit tests.
- `vectors/bocpd_regime_shifts.json` — golden test vectors.
- `artifacts/section_10_11/bd-3u4/verification_evidence.json` — evidence.
- `artifacts/section_10_11/bd-3u4/verification_summary.md` — summary.
acceptance_criteria:
AC for bd-3u4:
1. Implement a BOCPD (Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection) regime detector that processes streaming workload metrics and incident event streams to detect distributional shifts (regime changes) in real time.
2. The detector maintains a run-length distribution P(r_t | x_{1:t}) updated incrementally with each new observation; the underlying predictive model uses a conjugate-exponential hazard function with configurable prior parameters (hazard_lambda, prior_mean, prior_variance).
3. A regime change is signaled when the posterior probability of run-length r=0 (new regime) exceeds a configurable threshold (default: 0.5); the signal includes the estimated changepoint timestamp, confidence score, and pre/post regime summary statistics.
4. The detector supports multiple concurrent streams (e.g., request_rate, error_rate, latency_p99) with independent run-length distributions; a meta-detector can fuse per-stream signals into a joint regime-change verdict.
5. Detection latency is bounded: the detector must signal a regime change within K observations of the true changepoint (K configurable, default: 10) on synthetic step-function and ramp-function test signals.
6. Memory is bounded: the run-length distribution is truncated at a configurable max_run_length (default: 500) to prevent unbounded growth; truncation error is logged as BOCPD_TRUNCATION_WARNING when the tail probability exceeds 1e-4.

Unit tests verify: (a) step-function changepoint detected within K observations, (b) ramp-function changepoint detected within 2K observations, (c) stationary stream produces no false positives over 10,000 observations, (d) truncation at max_run_length does not cause missed detections on standard test signals, (e) multi-stream fusion correctly requires majority agreement.

title: [10.15] Enforce canonical virtual transport fault harness (from `10.14`) for distributed control protocols.
description:
## Why This Exists
Distributed control protocols (cross-node rollout coordination, remote fencing, epoch barrier participation, distributed saga steps) must be tested under realistic network fault conditions — packet drops, reordering, corruption, and partitions. Section 10.14 (bd-2qqu) built a canonical virtual transport fault harness that simulates these conditions deterministically by seed. This bead enforces that canonical harness on franken_node's distributed control protocols, making it a CI requirement that these protocols produce correct outcomes (or deterministic failures) under all seed-controlled fault scenarios. The product layer must not build its own fault injection — it must adopt the canonical harness.

## What This Must Do
1. Author `docs/testing/control_virtual_transport_faults.md` defining:
   - Which distributed control protocols are tested (remote fencing, cross-node rollout coordination, epoch barrier participation, distributed saga steps).
   - The fault classes injected: DROP (message lost), REORDER (messages arrive out of order), CORRUPT (message bytes altered), PARTITION (bidirectional communication failure).
   - The deterministic seed model: same seed -> same fault injection sequence -> same protocol behavior.
   - Expected protocol behaviors under each fault class (retry, abort, compensate, fail-closed).
2. Implement `tests/harness/control_virtual_transport_faults.rs` that:
   - Uses the canonical 10.14 virtual transport fault harness (bd-2qqu).
   - For each distributed protocol, runs it under each fault class with multiple seeds.
   - Asserts protocol correctness: either the protocol completes correctly despite the fault, or it fails deterministically with an appropriate error and compensation.
   - Captures protocol decisions and failures in a structured report.
3. Generate `artifacts/10.15/control_fault_harness_summary.json` with: per-protocol, per-fault-class, per-seed results (seed, fault_class, protocol_outcome, correctness_assertion, pass/fail).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Canonical harness scenarios are deterministic by seed, adopted by control-plane gates, and reproduce distributed protocol decisions and failures.
- The product layer uses the canonical 10.14 harness, not custom fault injection.
- Every distributed protocol is tested under all four fault classes (DROP, REORDER, CORRUPT, PARTITION).
- Same seed always produces the same protocol outcome.
- The fault harness summary is consumed by the section gate (bd-20eg).

## Testing & Logging Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Validate harness integration with a trivial request/response protocol under each fault class.
- **Integration tests**: Full fault injection on remote fencing protocol. Full injection on epoch barrier protocol.
- **Conformance tests**: Assert the harness covers all distributed protocols identified in the workflow inventory (bd-2177).
- **Adversarial tests**: Run a protocol with a seed that triggers maximum message reordering; assert correct compensations. Run with a partition that splits during an epoch barrier; assert deterministic abort.
- **Structured logs**: Event codes `VTF-001` (fault harness started for protocol), `VTF-002` (fault injected — drop/reorder/corrupt/partition), `VTF-003` (protocol completed correctly under fault), `VTF-004` (protocol failed correctly under fault — deterministic failure), `VTF-005` (protocol produced incorrect result under fault — gate failure). Include protocol_name, seed, fault_class, and trace correlation ID.

- **Downstream**: bd-20eg (section gate)

title: [DEADLOCK] root_pointer publish_lock canonicalize race produces split in-memory mutex keys
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/control_plane/root_pointer.rs:415

FINDING: publish_lock() builds the registry key via lock_path.canonicalize().unwrap_or(lock_path). On the FIRST call to publish_root_internal() for a given dir, the lock file does not yet exist (it is created by acquire_root_publication_lock at line 437-447 which runs AFTER publish_lock). canonicalize() therefore returns Err(NotFound) and the registry key is the non-canonicalized lock path. On a SUBSEQUENT call, the file exists, canonicalize() succeeds, and the key becomes the canonicalized path. If the input dir contains symlinks, .. segments, or is relative, the two keys differ. The registry then stores TWO distinct Arc<Mutex<()>> entries for what is logically the same publication lock, so the in-process mutex no longer serializes intra-process publishers.

SCENARIO:
1. Thread A enters publish_root_internal("./data", ...). publish_lock("./data") computes lock_key = "./data/.root.lock" (canonicalize fails since file does not exist). Inserts M1 into registry. Acquires M1.
2. acquire_root_publication_lock creates the lock file and takes flock-exclusive on fd1. (On Linux, std::fs::File::lock uses flock(2) which is per-OFD, so a second open() in the same process gets a separate lock.)
3. Thread B enters publish_root_internal("./data", ...) concurrently. publish_lock("./data") computes lock_key = "/abs/canonical/data/.root.lock" (canonicalize now succeeds). Lookup misses, inserts M2 into registry. Acquires M2 (no contention with M1).
4. Thread B opens lock file with create(true) (no-op), takes flock-exclusive on fd2 -- succeeds because flock is per-OFD on Linux.
5. Both A and B execute the body of publish_root_internal concurrently: read old root, build new payload, atomic rename. Race on the temp filename and on the auth-record write -- one publisher's atomic rename can clobber the other's, and both can pass the epoch-monotonicity check against the same old_root snapshot, allowing two distinct epochs to share the same predecessor.

SUGGESTED FIX:
- Resolve the lock_key to a stable canonical form BEFORE any acquire path can race. Two safe options:
  a) Pre-create the lock file in publish_lock() (open with create(true) but do not flock), then canonicalize the freshly-created file path so all subsequent callers agree on the same key.
  b) Drop canonicalize entirely and instead canonicalize the *parent dir* (which exists by precondition) and join ROOT_POINTER_LOCK_FILE -- this gives a stable key that does not depend on lock file existence.
- Add a debug_assert / regression test that creates the lock via two threads with different but equivalent dir spellings ("./data" vs canonical absolute) and asserts both map to the same Arc<Mutex<()>>.

EVIDENCE:
crates/franken-node/src/control_plane/root_pointer.rs:413-424
```
fn publish_lock(dir: &Path) -> Result<Arc<Mutex<()>>, RootPointerError> {
    let lock_path = root_publication_lock_path(dir);
    let lock_key = lock_path.canonicalize().unwrap_or(lock_path);  // <-- key splits before/after file exists
    let mut registry = publish_lock_registry()
        .lock()
        .map_err(|_| RootPointerError::LockPoisoned)?;
    Ok(Arc::clone(
        registry
            .entry(lock_key)
            .or_insert_with(|| Arc::new(Mutex::new(()))),
    ))
}
```
crates/franken-node/src/control_plane/root_pointer.rs:663-667
```
let _publication_lock = acquire_root_publication_lock(dir, false)?;  // file-flock first
let publication_mutex = publish_lock(dir)?;                          // then in-memory mutex with bug
let _guard = publication_mutex.lock()...
```

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
GOAL: Make the deterministic timestamp base dynamic instead of hardcoded to 2025-01-01.

FILE: crates/franken-node/src/tools/verifier_toolkit.rs lines 62-63

CURRENT CODE:
  const DETERMINISTIC_TIME_BASE_SECONDS: i64 = 1_735_689_600; // 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z
  const DETERMINISTIC_TIME_WINDOW_SECONDS: u64 = 365 * 24 * 60 * 60;

Used in deterministic_timestamp() (line 92-103):
  Utc.timestamp_opt(DETERMINISTIC_TIME_BASE_SECONDS + offset as i64, 0)

PROBLEM: This creates a one-year window [2025-01-01, 2025-12-31] for deterministic timestamps. The offset wraps modulo DETERMINISTIC_TIME_WINDOW_SECONDS. After the window passes, timestamps appear to be from the past. The function will produce dates in 2025 forever.

OPTIONS (pick one):
  A. Year-relative: Derive base from current year: compute Jan 1 of current year dynamically
     - Pro: Always produces current-year timestamps
     - Con: Non-deterministic across year boundaries (Dec 31 vs Jan 1 produce different bases)
     
  B. Configurable: Add deterministic_time_base to [tools] or [verifier] config section
     - Pro: Operators control the epoch explicitly
     - Con: Requires config update each year
     
  C. Rolling window: Use (current_time - WINDOW) as the base
     - Pro: Always produces recent-looking timestamps
     - Con: Non-deterministic (different runs produce different timestamps)

RECOMMENDATION: Option B (configurable) is most consistent with franken_node's philosophy of explicit operator control. Default to Jan 1 of the current year, allow override via config. The deterministic_timestamp function's contract is that same input produces same output within a deployment — a config-based base preserves this.

IMPLEMENTATION:
  1. Add optional field to config: [tools] deterministic_time_base = "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"
  2. If not set, default to Jan 1 of current year
  3. Parse the config value as RFC 3339 and convert to epoch seconds
  4. Thread through to deterministic_timestamp()
  5. Keep DETERMINISTIC_TIME_WINDOW_SECONDS as-is (365 days is a reasonable window)

title: [ANALYSIS-security-adversarial] middleware: rate limiter allows bypass via instance targeting in distributed deployments
[ALIEN-GRAVEYARD] Implement SWIM-style membership for fleet coordination
description:
Replace current fleet node status polling with SWIM-style distributed membership and failure detection.

**Graveyard Entry:** §13.7 SWIM-Style Membership & Failure Detection [Tier S]  
**EV Score:** 6.67 (Impact: 4, Confidence: 5, Reuse: 3, Effort: 3, Friction: 3)

**Current State:**
- fleet_transport.rs uses file-based node status and manual heartbeats
- Central coordination for fleet health monitoring
- Potential for false positives during GC pauses or network hiccups

**Proposed Implementation:**
- Randomized probe protocol: periodic ping to random peer
- Indirect probes through k=3 peers if direct probe fails  
- Three-state membership: Alive, Suspect, Dead
- Gossip piggyback: attach membership updates to all messages
- Suspicion timeout with refutation (higher incarnation number)

**Protocol Components:**
- Member { addr, incarnation, state: Alive|Suspect|Dead }
- Probe phase: random peer selection, direct ping with timeout
- Indirect probe: PingReq through multiple intermediaries
- Refutation: suspected nodes broadcast higher incarnation
- Gossip: bounded batch of recent updates on all messages

**Adoption Wedge:**
- Boundary: FleetTransport trait methods
- Compatibility: Gradual migration alongside existing file-based transport  
- Rollout: Dual-mode with feature flag, consensus on transition

**Budgeted Mode:**
- Default budget: max 64 nodes, 200ms probe interval, k=3 indirect probes
- On exhaustion: fall back to static configuration

**Files to modify:**
- control_plane/fleet_transport.rs: Add SWIM protocol implementation
- Add: control_plane/swim_membership.rs for core protocol
- Update: node health consumers to use membership events

**Success Criteria:**
- O(log n) convergence time for membership changes
- Reduced false positive rate compared to timeout-based detection
- Scalable membership without centralized coordinator
notes: VERIFIED: Fleet membership is centrally tracked via file-based transport, not P2P. Evidence: (1) Actions stored in central actions.jsonl file (2) Nodes write status to central filesystem (3) File locking for coordination, not distributed consensus (4) No peer-to-peer communication or gossip protocol (5) Single source of truth via shared storage. SWIM is designed for P2P membership and would be premature/overkill for this centralized architecture.

FILE: crates/franken-node/src/supply_chain/extension_registry.rs:1037
PATTERN: unbounded extension registry growth / map insert without capacity guard
WHY IT IS A BUG: SignedExtensionRegistry bounds revocations, audit_log, admission_receipts, and per-extension versions, but the top-level extensions BTreeMap has no MAX_EXTENSIONS guard. Each successful registration inserts a new SignedExtension and content_hash serializes the full map, so an attacker or runaway publisher can grow registry memory and hash/export cost without limit.
SUGGESTED FIX: Add a MAX_EXTENSIONS limit and reject new active registrations once the registry is full, or evict only explicitly terminal/revoked entries under a documented policy. Keep duplicate-name checks and admission receipts bounded.
EVIDENCE: rg -n "MAX_EXTENSIONS|extensions.insert|extensions: BTreeMap" crates/franken-node/src/supply_chain/extension_registry.rs finds no MAX_EXTENSIONS, the extensions map at line 684, and self.extensions.insert(extension_id.clone(), extension) at line 1037; git blame -L 680,700 -L 968,1038 shows no capacity guard around the insertion.
close_reason: Added bounded extension registry capacity guard with integration coverage

title: Fail closed when replay capsules declare extra mismatched expected outputs
description: Why this exists: crates/franken-node/src/sdk/replay_capsule.rs::replay_and_verify() and crates/franken-node/src/sdk/verifier_sdk.rs::verify_capsule() both compare only expected_outputs.first() against the replay hash. validate_capsule() only requires expected_outputs to be non-empty. Result: a capsule can declare multiple expected outputs and still pass if only the first hash matches, silently ignoring mismatched extra outputs. What this task must do: make replay-capsule verification fail closed unless every declared expected output agrees with the deterministic replay hash, keep scope limited to the shared replay capsule + SDK verifier paths, and add focused regressions for extra mismatched outputs. Acceptance criteria: 1. replay_and_verify() rejects a capsule whose second declared expected output hash mismatches the replay hash even if the first matches. 2. VerifierSdk::verify_capsule() yields a failing verdict for the same malformed capsule. 3. Targeted validation uses rch only for cargo-heavy runs and is reported in Agent Mail.

title: [10.11] Add ambient-authority audit gate for product security-critical modules.
description:
Master Plan Source: PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_NODE.md — Section 10.11 (FrankenSQLite-Inspired Runtime Systems), cross-ref Architecture Invariant #10 (8.5)

## Why This Exists

The three-kernel architecture (8.5) establishes invariant #10: no ambient authority. This means no product code may perform security-sensitive operations (signing trust artifacts, issuing capability grants, initiating epoch transitions, dispatching remote effects, modifying quarantine state) by relying on implicit global state, environment variables, thread-local singletons, or any mechanism other than explicitly passed capability tokens. Violations of this invariant silently undermine the entire capability-based security model: a single module that reads a signing key from a global static bypasses all the careful Cx-first control, epoch scoping, and obligation tracking that the rest of the system enforces.

This bead implements an ambient-authority audit gate: a combination of static analysis rules, runtime checks, and CI gate enforcement that detects and rejects ambient authority usage in security-critical product modules. This is the enforcement mechanism that ensures invariant #10 is not merely a guideline but a hard-gated property of the codebase.

## What This Must Do

1. Define the "security-critical module" inventory: enumerate all Rust modules and Python scripts that perform trust artifact signing, capability grant issuance, epoch transition initiation, remote effect dispatch, quarantine state modification, or checkpoint writes. This inventory is maintained as a versioned configuration file.
2. Implement a static analysis pass (clippy custom lint, or a dedicated AST-walking script) that scans security-critical modules for ambient authority patterns: (a) global static mutable access, (b) direct environment variable reads (std::env), (c) thread-local storage access, (d) filesystem access without a path capability, (e) network access without a RemoteCap, (f) clock/time access without an explicit time source parameter.
3. Implement a runtime `AuthorityAuditGuard` that wraps security-critical entry points and asserts that all required capability tokens are present in the `CapabilityContext` before the operation proceeds — missing tokens produce a structured `AmbientAuthorityViolation` error and hard-fail the operation.
4. Implement a CI gate (`scripts/check_ambient_authority.py`) that runs the static analysis on every PR touching security-critical modules and fails the build if any ambient authority pattern is detected.
5. Produce an audit report as a machine-readable artifact listing every security-critical module, its required capabilities, and the pass/fail status of both static and runtime checks.
6. Integrate with the epoch system (bd-2gr): the audit gate must verify that epoch-sensitive operations receive their epoch context from an explicit parameter, not from a global epoch singleton.

## Context from Enhancement Maps

- Architecture invariant #10 (8.5): "No ambient authority" — this bead is the enforcement mechanism for this invariant.
- Architecture invariant #1 (8.5): "Cx-first control" — the audit gate verifies that Cx-first is actually practiced, not just declared.
- 9G.1: "Capability-context-first product runtime APIs" — ambient authority audit ensures the Cx-first APIs are the only path to security operations.
- 9J.10: "Remote effects must be capability-gated, named, idempotent, and saga-safe" — the audit gate verifies the capability-gating requirement.
- 9J.19: "Cancellation-complete protocol discipline" — the audit gate verifies that cancellation tokens are explicitly passed, not ambient.

## Dependencies

- Upstream: bd-2g6r (10.15 Cx-first signature policy — defines the CapabilityContext patterns the audit gate checks for), bd-1nfu (10.14 RemoteCap requirement — defines the remote capability pattern), bd-721z (10.15 ambient-authority audit gate for control-plane — provides the canonical audit pattern that this bead extends to product services)
- Downstream: All 10.11 security-sensitive beads are gated by this audit (bd-2gr epoch operations, bd-3hw remote sagas, bd-24k bounded masking Cx requirement), bd-1jpo (10.11 section-wide verification gate)

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Security-critical module inventory is a versioned TOML/JSON file listing every module path and its required capabilities; adding a new security-critical module without updating the inventory fails CI.
2. Static analysis detects at least the following ambient patterns: global mutable static, std::env::var, thread_local!, direct filesystem open without path capability, direct TcpStream without RemoteCap, SystemTime::now() without explicit time source.
3. Static analysis produces zero false positives on the current codebase (verified by running against known-clean modules).
4. Runtime AuthorityAuditGuard blocks an operation missing required capabilities with a structured `AmbientAuthorityViolation` error within 1ms (no hanging).
5. CI gate fails the build on any new ambient authority pattern introduced in a PR touching a security-critical module.
6. Audit report artifact includes: module_path, required_capabilities, static_analysis_pass (bool), runtime_check_pass (bool), violations (list), and timestamp.
7. A deliberately introduced ambient authority violation (e.g., adding `std::env::var("SECRET")` to a security-critical module) is caught by both the static analysis and the CI gate.
8. Verification evidence JSON includes modules_audited, static_violations_found, runtime_violations_found, audit_pass_rate, and ci_gate_executions fields.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: (a) Static analyzer detects global mutable static in a test module; (b) Static analyzer detects std::env::var in a test module; (c) Static analyzer passes a clean module with only explicit capability usage; (d) AuthorityAuditGuard passes with correct CapabilityContext; (e) AuthorityAuditGuard fails with missing capability.
- Integration tests: (a) Full CI gate run on a PR with a clean change — verify pass; (b) Full CI gate run on a PR with an introduced ambient violation — verify fail with diagnostic; (c) Audit report generation for all security-critical modules — verify completeness; (d) AuthorityAuditGuard on a real product endpoint (e.g., trust artifact signing) with and without capabilities.
- Adversarial tests: (a) Ambient authority hidden behind a macro — verify static analyzer expands macros or flags them; (b) Ambient authority in a dependency crate — verify the analysis scope includes transitive dependencies of security-critical modules; (c) Runtime capability spoofing (forged CapabilityContext) — verify cryptographic verification in AuthorityAuditGuard; (d) Module removed from inventory but still performing security operations — verify runtime guard still catches it.
- Structured logs: Events use stable codes (FN-AA-001 through FN-AA-008), include `module_path`, `trace_id`, `violation_type`, `required_capability`, `audit_result`. JSON-formatted.

## Expected Artifacts

- docs/specs/section_10_11/bd-3vm_contract.md
- crates/franken-node/src/runtime/authority_audit.rs (or equivalent module path)
- config/security_critical_modules.toml (module inventory)
- scripts/check_ambient_authority.py (with --json flag and self_test())
- tests/test_check_ambient_authority.py
- artifacts/section_10_11/bd-3vm/verification_evidence.json
- artifacts/section_10_11/bd-3vm/verification_summary.md
acceptance_criteria:
AC for bd-3vm:
1. A static-analysis or init-time audit gate scans all product security-critical modules and flags any use of ambient authority (global mutable state, unscoped file/network access, raw syscalls not routed through a CxHandle).
2. The gate produces a machine-readable AuditReport JSON listing every ambient-authority site found, with module path, line number, and violation category.
3. The gate returns exit code 0 (pass) only when zero ambient-authority violations exist; any violation returns exit code 1 with structured error output.
4. CI integrates the gate as a mandatory pre-merge check; PRs introducing new ambient authority are blocked until a CxHandle refactor or an explicit exception annotation is added.
5. Exception annotations (e.g., #[allow_ambient(reason = "...")]) are tracked in the audit report and require review sign-off; the total exception count is emitted as a metric.
6. Unit tests verify: (a) a clean module passes the gate, (b) a module with raw std::fs::read (no CxHandle) fails, (c) an annotated exception is reported but does not fail the gate, (d) removing a CxHandle wrapper from a previously-clean call causes regression failure.
7. Structured log events use stable codes AMBIENT_AUDIT_PASS / AMBIENT_AUDIT_VIOLATION / AMBIENT_AUDIT_EXCEPTION with module path context.
notes:
Plan-space QA addendum (2026-02-20):
1) Preserve full canonical-plan scope; no feature compression or silent omission is allowed.
2) Completion requires comprehensive verification coverage appropriate to scope: unit tests, integration tests, and E2E scripts/workflows with detailed structured logging (stable event/error codes + trace correlation IDs).
3) Completion requires reproducible evidence artifacts (machine-readable + human-readable) that allow independent replay and root-cause triage.

title: [PROFILE] control_plane/fleet_transport.rs: read-shaped Asupersync ops take exclusive lock + clone whole Vec for record_event side effect
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/control_plane/fleet_transport.rs

PATTERN:
Every nominally-read operation on AsupersyncFleetTransport acquires the inner Mutex *as a writer* purely to call `record_event`, then clones the entire actions/nodes Vec while holding the lock:

- L865-871 `list_actions`: `let mut state = self.network.lock()?;` (write borrow), then `state.actions.clone()` returned. lock held across the clone.
- L893-899 `list_node_statuses`: same pattern, clone of state.nodes Vec.
- L901-926 `read_shared_state`: clones BOTH actions and nodes Vec, then sorts both Vecs, all under the same lock.

`record_event` (L809-816) pushes a `AsupersyncFleetControlEvent` (with formatted strings) onto state.control_events for every read, inflating the Vec and forcing every reader to be a writer.

IMPACT:
- All readers contend on a single Mutex even when no actual mutation is needed
- Vec clones occur under the lock, lengthening the critical section linearly with state size
- The "audit every read" pattern doubles the lock scope and turns reads into writes

SUGGESTED FIX:
- Switch to `RwLock<AsupersyncFleetNetworkState>` and split `state.control_events` into its own `Mutex` (or atomic-ring buffer) so reads never block other reads
- Or move `record_event` to a fire-and-forget channel (mpsc::Sender) — readers don't block on event recording
- Move the `clone()` outside the lock by snapshotting an `Arc<Vec<...>>` (interior mutability with arc_swap or similar)

EVIDENCE:
- L729-740 AsupersyncFleetNetworkState shape
- L865-871 list_actions full clone under lock
- L893-899 list_node_statuses full clone under lock
- L901-926 read_shared_state two clones + two sorts under one lock
- L809-816 record_event mutation triggered by every read

title: [VALAUTO.4] Model bounded RCH retry budgets and worker quarantine advice
description:
## What
Extend validation-autopilot planning with bounded RCH retry policy and worker-health recommendations derived from normalized RCH evidence.

## Why
Several current blockers are not product failures; they are RCH stale-progress, timeout, or dependency-convergence failures. Agents need a repeatable policy for when to retry, switch target dirs, lower priority, quarantine/drain a worker, or stop and preserve the blocker.

## How
Use scripts/normalize_rch_evidence.py output as the input contract. Define retry budgets by blocker class: product diagnostics reached means stop and fix product code; remote timeout/stale progress may allow one bounded retry with a fresh CARGO_TARGET_DIR and low priority; repeated worker-specific failures should recommend worker quarantine/drain coordination; dependency resolver errors should create/refresh a dependency-convergence bead.

## Risks
Do not launch RCH from this planner. Do not recommend local cargo fallback. Preserve command lines exactly, including env vars, target dirs, and first blocker text.

## Success Criteria
Fixtures cover repeated timeout on one worker, stale progress with cancellation, dependency resolver error, product compile error, and clean success. The output includes retry_allowed, retry_budget_remaining, recommended_rch_command, worker_action, and stop_reason fields with deterministic labels.

title: [10.18] Implement degraded-mode policy for proof lag/outage (`restricted`, `quarantine`, `halt`) with explicit SLOs.
description:
## Why This Exists

Section 10.18 implements the Verifiable Execution Fabric (VEF) — Enhancement Map 9L — delivering proof-carrying runtime compliance. This is a Track C (Trust-Native Ecosystem Layer) resilience component that ensures franken_node degrades safely when the proof pipeline cannot keep up or suffers an outage.

This bead implements the degraded-mode policy for VEF proof lag and outage scenarios. In production, proof generation may fall behind (due to resource constraints, backend failures, or burst workloads) or become entirely unavailable (backend crash, network partition). Without explicit degraded-mode policies, the system would either silently continue without proofs (violating the trust model) or halt entirely (violating availability). This bead defines the middle ground: tiered degraded modes (`restricted`, `quarantine`, `halt`) with explicit SLOs, mandatory audit events, and recovery receipts.

This is the safety net that makes VEF production-viable. It ensures that operators understand the trust posture at all times and that transitions between modes are deterministic, auditable, and recoverable.

## What This Must Do

1. Define degraded-mode tiers with clear semantics:
   - `restricted`: proof pipeline is lagging but within SLO tolerance; actions proceed with enhanced monitoring and audit trail.
   - `quarantine`: proof pipeline lag exceeds SLO threshold; high-risk actions are blocked, low-risk actions proceed with warnings.
   - `halt`: proof pipeline is down or critically lagged; all VEF-gated actions are blocked until recovery.
2. Implement deterministic mode transition logic based on proof lag metrics (time since oldest unproven window, backlog depth, error rate).
3. Define explicit SLOs for each tier: maximum proof lag duration, maximum backlog depth, maximum error rate before escalation.
4. Emit mandatory audit events on every mode transition (including rationale: which metric triggered the transition).
5. Emit recovery receipts when the system transitions back from a degraded mode to normal operation.
6. Make SLO thresholds and tier behavior policy-configurable without code changes.
7. Integrate with the proof-job scheduler (bd-28u0) metrics for lag detection and with the verification gate (bd-1o4v) for enforcement.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Proof pipeline lag/outage triggers deterministic degraded mode by policy tier; mode transitions emit mandatory audit events and recovery receipts.
- Mode transitions are deterministic: identical metric sequences always trigger identical transitions.
- SLO thresholds are configurable per policy tier and action class.
- Audit events include: current mode, target mode, triggering metric, metric value, SLO threshold, timestamp, correlation ID.
- Recovery receipts include: degraded-mode duration, actions affected, recovery trigger, proof pipeline health at recovery.
- No silent mode transitions: every transition is logged and auditable.
- Mode enforcement is consistent across all VEF-gated control points.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests for each mode transition path: normal -> restricted, restricted -> quarantine, quarantine -> halt, and all reverse paths.
- SLO threshold tests: configure various thresholds, inject metrics at boundary values, verify correct transitions.
- Determinism tests: replay identical metric sequences, verify identical mode transition traces.
- Audit event tests: verify all required fields are present in transition events.
- Recovery receipt tests: simulate degradation and recovery, verify receipt contains correct duration and action impact.
- Integration tests: combine with mock scheduler metrics and verification gate, verify end-to-end degraded-mode behavior.
- Structured logging: `VEF-DEGRADE-001` (mode transition), `VEF-DEGRADE-002` (SLO breach detected), `VEF-DEGRADE-003` (recovery initiated), `VEF-DEGRADE-004` (recovery complete), `VEF-DEGRADE-ERR-*` (transition failures).
- Trace correlation IDs linking degraded-mode events to proof pipeline metrics and affected action contexts.

## Expected Artifacts

- `docs/specs/vef_degraded_mode_policy.md` — mode tier definitions, SLO specifications, transition rules, audit event format.
- `tests/security/vef_degraded_mode_transitions.rs` — security tests for all mode transition paths and enforcement.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
2026-07-24 CrimsonCrane, verified by reading. security/sandbox_policy_compiler.rs:67. level() is Strict=0..Permissive=3, documented 'higher = more permissive'. is_downgrade_to(target) returns target.level() < self.level(), i.e. TRUE when the target is more RESTRICTIVE. The gate at :262 is 'if is_downgrade_to(new) && !allow_downgrade { Err(DowngradeBlocked) }'. Net effect: TIGHTENING a connector's sandbox needs the override flag; LOOSENING it does not. ProfileTracker::new(.., Strict).change_profile(Permissive, .., allow_downgrade=false) returns Ok, after which is_capability_allowed(fs_write|process_exec|network_access) all return Allow — a connector pinned to the strictest profile relaxes itself to full ambient authority with the override off.

NOT patched blind, and this is the important part: the current semantics are DELIBERATELY test-pinned, not a slip. tracker_downgrade_blocked (:494), tracker_downgrade_with_override (:509), the direction asserts at :384-396, and test_security_downgrade_bypass_attempts (:1024) with its explicit comment 'from Permissive (most permissive, level 3) moving to the more-restrictive Moderate (level 2) is itself a downgrade and must not succeed without an explicit override' all encode it. So the module means 'downgrade' = numeric level decreasing, and guards tightening as the operator-intent action (plausibly an availability guard against silently breaking a connector).

The real defect is therefore not just the predicate direction: LOOSENING has no gate at ALL. Deciding between (a) flip to target.level() > self.level() and re-bless ~8 assertions, or (b) keep the tightening guard and add a separate, stricter gate for permission-increasing transitions, is a product call that needs the inline-test lane runnable (blocked by bd-3mj98). Both module-header text ('Downgrades are blocked') and the enum's 'ordered from most to least restrictive' comment currently describe the opposite of what is computed, so whichever way it goes the docs need fixing too.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: 2026-07-28 CrimsonCrane — FIXED per operator decision (AskUserQuestion: 'Guard both directions'). The bead's real finding stands: is_downgrade_to(target) = target.level() < self.level() means DOWNGRADE here = TIGHTENING, so change_profile's allow_downgrade flag guarded the direction that REMOVES authority, while the direction that GRANTS it (Strict -> Permissive, under which fs_write/process_exec/network_access all compile to AccessLevel::Allow) had no gate at all. Both the module header ('Downgrades are blocked') and the enum comment described the opposite of what was computed. Rather than flip the predicate and re-bless ~8 assertions that encode the tightening guard as a deliberate availability control, relaxation now has its own explicit entry point. NEW: SandboxProfile::is_relaxation_to(); SandboxError::RelaxationBlocked (SANDBOX_RELAXATION_BLOCKED); ProfileTracker::relax_profile(target, operator_justification, timestamp), which refuses anything that is not actually a relaxation so it cannot be used to bypass the tightening guard. change_profile now refuses relaxation outright — passing allow_downgrade: true does NOT authorize it, because the two directions are guarded for different reasons and one flag cannot express both intents. Well-formedness (empty reason/timestamp) is validated BEFORE the direction gate so malformed requests still report CompileError. Module header and doc comments rewritten to match the code. [INSIGHT] Cancellation protocol timing windows create potential race condition attack surface
description: ADVERSARIAL FINDING: While franken_node has exemplary memory/crypto hardening, the cancellation protocol (bd-1cs7) creates logic-level attack opportunities. Attack vector: Adversary can exploit timing windows between phase transitions (REQUEST→DRAIN→FINALIZE) to cause resource leaks or state inconsistency. Example: docs/specs/cancellation_protocol_contract.md defines per-workflow timeouts (5000ms lifecycle_shutdown, 3000ms rollout_cancel), but concurrent cancellation requests could race. Gap: Current hardening focuses on constant-time crypto, bounded collections, but not on state machine race conditions. Recommendation: Add formal verification of cancellation state machines or implement atomic phase transitions.
