title: [10.14] Add cancellation injection at all await points for critical control workflows in lab tests.
description:
## Why This Exists

Async Rust workflows can be cancelled at any await point via task cancellation or timeout. If a critical control workflow (like epoch transition, marker write, or evidence commit) is cancelled mid-execution, it could leave the system in an inconsistent state: a half-written marker, a partially-committed epoch, or leaked resources. Cancellation injection testing systematically cancels workflows at every await point to verify that the system maintains its invariants under all possible cancellation timings. This directly enforces runtime invariant #7 (epoch barriers survive cancellation without partial state) and #9 (deterministic verification: cancellation safety is proven, not assumed). The 10.15 cancellation injection gate (bd-3tpg) and the deterministic lab runtime (bd-145n) consume this capability.

## What This Must Do

1. Implement a cancellation injection framework in `tests/lab/cancellation_injection_control_workflows.rs` that can cancel a workflow at every identified await point.
2. Identify all await points in critical control workflows: epoch transition barrier (bd-2wsm), marker stream append (bd-126h), root pointer publication (bd-nwhn), evidence commit, and cancel-safe eviction saga (bd-1ru2).
3. For each workflow, generate a test matrix where each test case cancels at a different await point. The matrix is `(workflow, await_point_index)`.
4. For each cancellation test case, verify two invariants: (a) leak-free: no resources (file handles, locks, memory allocations) are leaked after cancellation, (b) half-commit-free: no partial state is visible to other components after cancellation (e.g., no half-written marker, no partially-advanced epoch).
5. Implement leak detection: track resource allocations before workflow start and after cancellation; any delta is a leak.
6. Implement half-commit detection: read all relevant state (epoch, marker stream head, root pointer) before and after cancellation; any unexpected change is a half-commit.
7. Produce a cancel injection matrix document listing all workflows, their await points, and test results.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Critical workflows are instrumented for all-point cancellation injection; leak-free and half-commit-free invariants hold under injected cancellations.
- Every await point in the epoch transition barrier workflow is cancellation-tested.
- Every await point in the marker stream append workflow is cancellation-tested.
- Every await point in the root pointer publication workflow is cancellation-tested.
- Zero resource leaks detected across all cancellation points (verified by resource tracker).
- Zero half-commits detected across all cancellation points (verified by state comparison).
- Cancel injection matrix document lists >= 20 distinct `(workflow, await_point)` test cases with pass/fail results.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: cancellation at each await point for a simple 3-await-point workflow (smoke test of framework); leak detection for known-leaky vs clean workflows; half-commit detection for known-inconsistent vs clean workflows.
- Integration tests: full cancel injection matrix for epoch transition barrier, marker append, and root publication; combined cancellation with concurrent operations; cancellation during force transition (bd-1vsr).
- Conformance tests: `tests/lab/cancellation_injection_control_workflows.rs` -- the full cancel injection matrix.
- Structured logs: `CANCEL_INJECTED` (workflow, await_point_index, trace_id), `CANCEL_LEAK_CHECK` (workflow, await_point_index, leaked_resources, trace_id), `CANCEL_HALFCOMMIT_CHECK` (workflow, await_point_index, state_delta, trace_id), `CANCEL_MATRIX_COMPLETE` (total_cases, pass_count, fail_count, trace_id).

## Expected Artifacts

- `tests/lab/cancellation_injection_control_workflows.rs` -- cancel injection matrix tests
- `docs/testing/cancel_injection_matrix.md` -- cancel injection matrix document
- `artifacts/10.14/cancel_injection_report.json` -- injection report with per-case results
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-876n/verification_evidence.json` -- machine-readable CI/release gate evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-876n/verification_summary.md` -- human-readable verification summary

## Dependencies

- Upstream: bd-2wsm (epoch transition barrier -- primary workflow under test), bd-1ru2 (cancel-safe eviction saga -- another workflow under test).
- Downstream: bd-3tpg (10.15 canonical cancellation injection gate), bd-145n (10.15 deterministic lab runtime), bd-3i6c (conformance suite), bd-3epz (section gate), bd-5rh (section gate).
acceptance_criteria: Critical workflows are instrumented for all-point cancellation injection; leak-free and half-commit-free invariants hold under injected cancellations.

title: Add blocked-bead first-blocker freshness audit
description:
## What
Add a fixture-backed audit that checks blocked beads for fresh, exact first-blocker evidence: command line, first real error string, external owner/repo when applicable, and a timestamped comment or notes field.

## Why
Several current blocked lanes are valid blockers, but they are easy to lose or overwrite during repeated triage. Examples: bd-f5b04.2.6 is blocked on sibling franken_engine real hostcall producer; bd-famte is blocked on RCH remote timeout after dependency convergence; bd-rjc2m.21 is blocked by broad inline-test compile health. The project benefits when blocked beads remain precise and auditable.

## How
Implement as a source/test checker that accepts a Beads JSON snapshot and emits stale/fresh classifications. It should not modify beads itself; agents can use the report to decide whether to comment, coordinate, reopen, or leave blocked.

## Risks
Avoid false certainty: the checker should flag missing evidence for human review rather than auto-unblocking. Do not treat old comments as fresh just because a bead is blocked. Preserve exact blocker strings in outputs.

## Success Criteria
- Tests cover fresh blocker, stale blocker, missing command, missing first-error string, and external-repo blocker cases.
- Report has stable JSON fields suitable for future doctor/readiness integration.
- Documentation names the policy for when an agent should refresh a blocker comment.

title: Implement validation proof cache store and fail-closed lookup
description:
## Scope
Implement the proof cache store and lookup primitives behind the spec. Keep the code behavior-preserving for existing validation flows until integration beads wire it in.

## Implementation Notes
Prefer a focused module such as `crates/franken-node/src/ops/validation_proof_cache.rs` exported through `ops::mod`. Use structured serde types and atomic file persistence patterns already used by validation receipts and fleet transports. Avoid compatibility shims.

## Required Behavior
- Compute cache keys from canonical validation broker request/receipt material.
- Persist cache entries under a canonical artifact root without overwriting unrelated files.
- Validate receipt digest, command digest, input digests, freshness expiry, dirty-state policy, feature flags, target-dir policy, and environment policy before returning a hit.
- Reject corrupted or malformed entries with stable error codes instead of panicking.

title: [10.16] Add cross-substrate contract tests validating end-to-end behavior (`frankentui` -> service -> persistence).
description:
## Why This Exists

Individual substrate integrations (frankentui, frankensqlite, sqlmodel_rust, fastapi_rust) are tested in isolation by their respective beads. But the real-world operator experience spans all four planes: an operator interacts through the TUI (presentation), triggers a service endpoint (service), which persists state through typed models (model) into frankensqlite (persistence). This bead adds cross-substrate contract tests that validate these end-to-end flows work correctly across plane boundaries.

In the three-kernel architecture, franken_node is the integration nexus — it is the only kernel that touches all four adjacent substrates simultaneously. Cross-substrate bugs (e.g., a TUI displaying stale data because the service endpoint read from a cache instead of frankensqlite, or a typed model mismatch causing a silent persistence failure visible only through the TUI) can only be caught by E2E tests that exercise the full stack.

## What This Must Do

1. Create `tests/e2e/adjacent_substrate_flow.rs` containing representative end-to-end test scenarios:
   - **Operator status flow**: TUI renders node status -> status data fetched via fastapi_rust endpoint -> endpoint queries frankensqlite via sqlmodel_rust model -> TUI displays result. Verify data consistency from persistence to display.
   - **Lease management flow**: TUI accepts lease operation -> fastapi_rust fleet-control endpoint processes request -> fencing token written to frankensqlite -> TUI shows confirmation. Verify ACID semantics across layers.
   - **Audit log flow**: Operator action via TUI -> fastapi_rust endpoint -> action logged to frankensqlite audit table -> verifier endpoint retrieves audit entry -> TUI displays audit trail. Verify replay determinism.
   - **Error propagation flow**: Invalid request via TUI -> fastapi_rust returns structured error (RFC 7807) -> TUI renders error with error code from error_code_registry -> audit log records the error event. Verify error fidelity across all layers.
   - **Concurrent access flow**: Multiple simulated operators performing simultaneous operations -> verify no data corruption, correct fencing, and consistent TUI display.

2. Add cross-layer trace verification:
   - Each E2E test verifies that trace-context (W3C Trace Context) propagates from the TUI event through the service endpoint to the persistence layer and back.
   - Trace spans must form a connected tree with no orphaned spans.

3. Add replay determinism verification:
   - Record the event sequence from an E2E test run.
   - Replay the sequence and verify identical final state in frankensqlite and identical TUI output.

4. Generate `artifacts/10.16/adjacent_substrate_e2e_report.json` containing:
   - `scenarios[]` array with `{name, planes_exercised[], trace_verified: bool, replay_deterministic: bool, status}`.
   - `trace_coverage` with `{total_spans, connected_spans, orphaned_spans}`.
   - `replay_results` with `{scenarios_replayed, state_matches, display_matches}`.

5. Create verification script `scripts/check_cross_substrate_e2e.py` with `--json` flag and `self_test()`:
   - Validates all required scenarios are present and passing.
   - Checks trace coverage has zero orphaned spans.
   - Verifies replay determinism passes for all replayed scenarios.

6. Create `tests/test_check_cross_substrate_e2e.py` with unit tests.

7. Produce evidence artifacts:
   - `artifacts/section_10_16/bd-8l9k/verification_evidence.json`
   - `artifacts/section_10_16/bd-8l9k/verification_summary.md`

## Acceptance Criteria

- End-to-end tests cover representative operator flows and replay determinism; failure includes cross-layer trace.
- At least 5 E2E scenarios covering all four substrate planes.
- Trace-context propagates across all layers with zero orphaned spans.
- Replay determinism verified for at least the operator status and audit log flows.
- Error propagation preserves error codes from persistence through service to presentation without loss of fidelity.
- Concurrent access scenario demonstrates correct fencing and data consistency.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- **Unit tests**: Validate E2E report JSON schema, trace tree connectivity checker, and replay comparison logic.
- **Integration tests**: Full stack E2E tests with all four substrates running (frankentui in test-backend mode, fastapi_rust on localhost, frankensqlite in tempfile DB, sqlmodel_rust typed models).
- **Event codes**: `E2E_SCENARIO_START` (info), `E2E_SCENARIO_PASS` (info), `E2E_SCENARIO_FAIL` (error), `E2E_TRACE_ORPHAN_DETECTED` (error), `E2E_REPLAY_MISMATCH` (error), `E2E_CONCURRENT_CONFLICT` (warning).
- **Trace correlation**: Scenario name and trace root ID in all E2E events.
- **Deterministic replay**: All E2E tests use fixed seeds, mock clocks, and tempfile-backed databases.

## Expected Artifacts

- `tests/e2e/adjacent_substrate_flow.rs`
- `artifacts/10.16/adjacent_substrate_e2e_report.json`
- `scripts/check_cross_substrate_e2e.py`
- `tests/test_check_cross_substrate_e2e.py`
- `artifacts/section_10_16/bd-8l9k/verification_evidence.json`
- `artifacts/section_10_16/bd-8l9k/verification_summary.md`

## Dependencies

- **bd-2owx** (blocks): Substrate policy contract must be in place to define which substrate is required where.

## Dependents

- **bd-10g0**: Section gate depends on this bead.
acceptance_criteria: - End-to-end tests cover representative operator flows and replay determinism; failure includes cross-layer trace.

[10.18] Integrate VEF verification state into high-risk control transitions and action authorization.
description:
## Why This Exists

Section 10.18 implements the Verifiable Execution Fabric (VEF) — Enhancement Map 9L — delivering proof-carrying runtime compliance. This is a Track C (Trust-Native Ecosystem Layer) integration bead that wires VEF verification into the actual control-plane decisions that govern high-risk actions.

This bead integrates the VEF verification gate (bd-1o4v) into high-risk control transitions and action authorization flows. Without this integration, the VEF proof infrastructure exists but does not actually influence runtime behavior — proofs are generated and verified but nothing enforces them. This bead closes the loop: high-risk actions (network access, filesystem operations, process spawning, secret access, policy transitions, artifact promotion) must present valid VEF verification state before proceeding.

The integration must support both strict mode (proof required, no exceptions) and graded mode (proof preferred, downgrade with audit trail), and all gate decisions must be auditable and replayable for incident response and compliance review.

## What This Must Do

1. Identify all high-risk control transitions and action authorization points in the franken_node control plane that require VEF verification state.
2. Integrate VEF verification gate checks at each identified point — the gate verdict (from bd-1o4v) must be consulted before the action proceeds.
3. Implement strict mode: proof required, action denied without valid proof regardless of other trust signals.
4. Implement graded mode: proof preferred, action permitted with downgrade and mandatory audit trail when proof is unavailable or stale.
5. Make mode selection policy-configurable per action class and workload tier.
6. Ensure all gate decisions (permit, deny, downgrade) emit auditable decision records with full context: action, actor, policy, proof status, verdict, mode, timestamp.
7. Ensure gate decisions are replayable: given the same inputs (action context, proof state, policy), the same decision is always reached.
8. Document the integration points, mode semantics, and decision audit format.

## Acceptance Criteria

- High-risk actions require configured VEF verification state; policy can enforce strict/graded modes; gate decisions are auditable and replayable.
- All identified high-risk action classes have VEF integration points.
- Strict mode correctly denies actions without valid proof — no bypass path.
- Graded mode correctly downgrades with audit trail — no silent pass-through.
- Mode switching (strict <-> graded) is policy-driven and takes effect without restart.
- Decision records contain sufficient context for independent replay and audit.
- No performance regression beyond the agreed VEF overhead budget for control-plane hot paths.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Integration tests for each high-risk action class: valid proof -> permit, invalid proof -> deny (strict), invalid proof -> downgrade (graded).
- Mode switching tests: change policy from strict to graded mid-execution, verify behavior changes correctly.
- Bypass resistance tests: attempt to skip VEF check in strict mode through various code paths — all must enforce the gate.
- Audit record tests: verify decision records contain all required fields and are sufficient for replay.
- Replay tests: replay decision records and confirm identical outcomes.
- Performance tests: measure control-plane latency impact of VEF integration at p95/p99.
- Structured logging: `VEF-GATE-001` (VEF check initiated), `VEF-GATE-002` (action permitted), `VEF-GATE-003` (action denied), `VEF-GATE-004` (action downgraded), `VEF-GATE-ERR-*` (integration errors).
- Trace correlation IDs linking gate decisions to action contexts, proof IDs, and verification records.

## Expected Artifacts

- `docs/integration/vef_control_plane_integration.md` — integration point inventory, mode semantics, decision audit format.
- `tests/integration/vef_high_risk_action_gating.rs` — integration tests for all action classes and modes.
- `artifacts/10.18/vef_control_gate_decisions.json` — sample gate decision records demonstrating audit format.
- `artifacts/section_10_18/bd-8qlj/verification_evidence.json` — machine-readable CI/release gate evidence.
- `artifacts/section_10_18/bd-8qlj/verification_summary.md` — human-readable summary linking intent to measured outcomes.

## Dependencies

- bd-1o4v (blocks) — Proof-verification gate API: provides the verification verdicts that this integration consumes.

Dependents: bd-2hjg (section gate), bd-32p (plan-level tracker).
acceptance_criteria: - High-risk actions require configured VEF verification state; policy can enforce strict/graded modes; gate decisions are auditable and replayable.

title: [10.14] Implement per-class symbol-size/overhead/fetch policy with benchmark-derived defaults.
description:
## Why This Exists
Different object classes in the FrankenSQLite storage layer have radically different performance profiles. A critical marker is a small, latency-sensitive artifact that must be fetched in microseconds; a replay bundle can be megabytes and tolerates higher latency; telemetry artifacts are write-heavy but rarely re-read. Without per-class tuning of symbol size, encoding overhead, and fetch priority, the system either over-provisions for the common case (wasting resources) or under-provisions for the critical case (risking control-plane stalls). The 9J enhancement map requires that these defaults be derived from actual benchmark data, not guesswork, so that policy overrides have a defensible baseline.

## What This Must Do
1. Implement `ObjectClassTuning` policy engine in `crates/franken-node/src/policy/object_class_tuning.rs` that reads object-class definitions from the registry (bd-2573) and applies class-specific defaults for: `symbol_size_bytes`, `encoding_overhead_ratio`, `fetch_priority` (enum: Critical/Normal/Background), and `prefetch_policy` (enum: Eager/Lazy/None).
2. Derive default values from benchmark data — create a benchmark suite under `benchmarks/object_class_tuning/` that measures encode/decode throughput and fetch latency for each class at varying symbol sizes (e.g., 256B, 1KB, 4KB, 16KB, 64KB).
3. Store benchmark-derived defaults in a structured format (`artifacts/10.14/object_class_policy_report.csv`) linking each class to its optimal symbol size, measured overhead, and recommended fetch policy.
4. Implement a runtime policy override path that is audited — any override must be logged with event code `OC_POLICY_OVERRIDE_APPLIED` including before/after values.
5. Policy engine must reject nonsensical overrides (e.g., symbol_size = 0, overhead_ratio > 1.0) with stable error codes.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Policy engine applies class-specific defaults at runtime; each of the four canonical classes has distinct tuning parameters.
- Defaults are justified by benchmark data stored in `artifacts/10.14/object_class_policy_report.csv` with columns: class_id, symbol_size_bytes, overhead_ratio, fetch_priority, p50_encode_us, p99_encode_us, p50_decode_us, p99_decode_us.
- Policy override path is audited: structured log emitted on every override with before/after values.
- Invalid overrides (zero symbol size, negative overhead, unknown class) are rejected with stable error codes.
- Benchmark suite is reproducible — running it twice on the same hardware produces results within 10% variance.

## Testing & Logging Requirements
- **Unit tests**: Default policy lookup for each canonical class returns expected values; override application modifies returned policy; invalid override rejection for each invalid-input class (zero, negative, unknown).
- **Benchmark tests**: `benchmarks/object_class_tuning/bench_encode_decode.rs` measuring throughput at multiple symbol sizes; `benchmarks/object_class_tuning/bench_fetch_latency.rs` measuring fetch latency by priority class.
- **Integration tests**: End-to-end test that modifying TOML config changes runtime fetch behavior; test that policy engine correctly reads from registry dependency.
- **Event codes**: `OC_POLICY_ENGINE_INIT` (startup with loaded defaults), `OC_POLICY_OVERRIDE_APPLIED` (runtime override), `OC_POLICY_OVERRIDE_REJECTED` (invalid override), `OC_BENCHMARK_BASELINE_LOADED` (benchmark data ingested).
- **Replay fixture**: Deterministic policy resolution sequence with known inputs and expected outputs.

## Expected Artifacts
- `crates/franken-node/src/policy/object_class_tuning.rs` — policy engine implementation
- `benchmarks/object_class_tuning/` — benchmark suite (bench_encode_decode.rs, bench_fetch_latency.rs)
- `artifacts/10.14/object_class_policy_report.csv` — benchmark-derived policy report
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-8tvs/verification_evidence.json` — CI/release gating evidence
- `artifacts/section_10_14/bd-8tvs/verification_summary.md` — human-readable summary

## Dependencies
- **Depends on**: bd-2573 (object-class profile registry — provides class definitions this policy engine reads)
- **Depended on by**: bd-27o2 (profile tuning harness), bd-3epz (section gate), bd-5rh (section roll-up)
acceptance_criteria: Policy engine applies class-specific defaults at runtime; defaults are justified by benchmark data; policy override path is audited.

title: [meta] Closer-discipline initiative: prevent fake-evidence false closes
description:
Initiative bead from the 2026-05-12 audit follow-up session.

The 2026-05-11 audit pass found 18 of 2,944 closed beads (2.4%) were genuinely false-closed.
All 18 share an anti-pattern: closer marks bead closed with close_reason "done" / "Completed"
AND drops a fabricated artifacts/.../verification_evidence.json claiming "20/20 PASS" — but
the underlying source file the artifact attests to does not exist in the tree.

Full analysis + recommendations: beads_compliance_audit/closer_discipline_memo.md

Three concrete deliverables, ordered by leverage:

1. Closer checklist in AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md — define exactly what a valid close_reason
   looks like (commit SHA + file:line + test names). One-paragraph minimum. Reject "done"
   alone.

2. Pre-commit guard at scripts/check_close_reason_quality.py — runs on every bead JSONL
   update; rejects empty / thin / fabricated-artifact closes BEFORE the commit lands.

3. CI gate at .github/workflows/closer-discipline-gate.yml — runs the same check on push;
   blocks PRs with thin closes from merging to main.

The tuned scorer at beads_compliance_audit/scripts/score-bead-tuned.py will detect the
anti-pattern automatically in future audit passes; this bead is the SOURCE-SIDE fix that
prevents the anti-pattern from accumulating in the first place.

See:
- beads_compliance_audit/closer_discipline_memo.md
- beads_compliance_audit/audit-policy.yaml (P-thin-close-reason patterns added 2026-05-12)
- beads_compliance_audit/passes/2026-05-11T17-36-47Z/full_recalibration_report.md
acceptance_criteria:
- AGENTS.md and/or CLAUDE.md has a "Closing beads" section requiring close_reason to include commit SHA, file:line citations, and test names that newly pass.
- scripts/check_close_reason_quality.py exists with --warn-only / --strict / --ci modes and rejects thin close_reasons.
- Pre-commit hook in .git/hooks/pre-commit invokes the check in --warn-only mode for 7 days then flips to --strict.
- .github/workflows/closer-discipline-gate.yml gates pushes to main via the check in --ci mode.
- After 30 days of strict enforcement, run the LLM recalibration of the next audit pass and verify the new TFC rate is less than 0.5% (vs the 2.4% baseline from 2026-05-11).
close_reason:
Implemented all 3 deliverables of the closer-discipline initiative.

(A) Guard script landed at scripts/check_close_reason_quality.py (303 LOC). 5 detection rules: R1 empty reason, R2 thin reason (matches done|Completed|fixed alone), R3 short reason (<80 chars), R4 missing commit-SHA or PR# or file:line citation for bug/feature/task beads (R4b warns on missing test name for bug/feature), R5 fabricated verification_evidence.json citing source paths absent from git ls-files. Modes: --staged for pre-commit, --since <ref> for ranged, --all for backward audit, --self-test for smoke. Modes: --warn-only / --strict / --ci. --self-test passes 5/5 rule cases.

(B) AGENTS.md updated with a new 'Closer Discipline' section between Workflow Pattern and Key Concepts. Mandatory close_reason format documented with REJECTED / WARN / ACCEPTED examples. Cross-references the guard script and the bd-8vo8v initiative bead.

(C) Pre-commit hook landed at .git/hooks/hooks.d/pre-commit/60-close-reason-quality.py (54 LOC). Plugs into the existing chain-runner pre-commit. Currently --warn-only; date-based ramp flips to --strict on 2026-06-15. Tested locally: exit 0 when no .beads/issues.jsonl in staged diff.

(D) CI workflow landed at .github/workflows/closer-discipline-gate.yml. Triggers on PR and push touching .beads/issues.jsonl. Same date-based --warn-only/--strict ramp as the pre-commit hook. Emergency-skip via SKIP_CLOSER_DISCIPLINE_CHECK repo secret.

title: Implement deterministic validation recovery planner for RCH failures
description:
Epic: bd-i9m9u. Depends on recorder artifacts and broker receipt links; should also account for proof-coalescer admission/capacity outputs when available.

Purpose:
Turn a classified failed or stalled validation attempt into a deterministic next action so agents do not improvise inconsistent retries.

Scope:
- Add a recovery planner input that includes recorder timeline, `RchAdapterOutcome`, validation broker request/receipt/status, proof priority, bead priority, capacity snapshot when available, dirty-state policy, and timeout budget.
- Emit stable decisions such as `retry_remote_same_worker`, `retry_remote_different_worker`, `queue_until_capacity`, `drain_worker_then_retry`, `wait_for_existing_proof`, `use_source_only_blocker`, and `fail_closed`.
- Keep behavior priority-aware without starving lower-priority proofs: P0/P1 can preempt more aggressively, but all queue growth remains bounded.
- Never retry product compile/test failures as worker infra.
- Treat RCH-E104, worker missing toolchain, filesystem pressure, local fallback refusal, contention, and stale progress as separate cases.

Acceptance:
- Planner decisions are deterministic for identical inputs.
- Every decision has reason_code, event_code, operator message, required_action, fail_closed flag, and freshness timestamp.
- Retry loops are bounded by attempt count, worker diversity, timeout budget, and stale queue age.
- Unit tests cover success/no-op, RCH-E104 retry, worker drain, missing toolchain, disk pressure, local fallback refusal, contention deferral, compile failure fail-closed, and source-only blocker.

Verification expected:
- Focused Rust tests via `rch exec -- cargo test -p frankenengine-node <planner-test-target>`.
- `rustfmt`, `git diff --check`, and `ubs` on changed Rust files.

title: [10.11] Add checkpoint-placement contract in all long orchestration loops.
description:
Master Plan Source: PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_NODE.md — Section 10.11 (FrankenSQLite-Inspired Runtime Systems), cross-ref Section 9G.2, 9G.9

## Why This Exists

Long orchestration loops in franken_node — iterating over hundreds of trust artifacts for migration, scanning thousands of quarantine entries for promotion, replicating large batches of state across regions — must be resumable after crashes or cancellations without restarting from the beginning. Enhancement Map 9G.2 (cancellation protocol) implies that cancelled loops need to record their progress, and 9G.9 (three-tier integrity strategy) requires that progress records are tamper-evident and part of the append-only decision stream. The checkpoint-placement contract formalizes this: every long orchestration loop must place checkpoints at defined intervals, each checkpoint records the loop's progress state, and the loop can resume from the last valid checkpoint after restart.

This bead adds a checkpoint-placement contract that mandates and enforces checkpoint discipline in all long orchestration loops, providing both the checkpoint infrastructure and a compile-time/runtime gate that rejects loops exceeding a configurable iteration count without a checkpoint.

## What This Must Do

1. Implement a `CheckpointWriter` that accepts a serializable progress state and atomically writes it to the checkpoint store using the bounded masking helper (bd-24k) to prevent cancellation during the atomic write.
2. Implement a `CheckpointReader` that loads the latest valid checkpoint for a given orchestration ID, enabling resumption from the last checkpointed state.
3. Define the checkpoint-placement contract: every orchestration loop must call `checkpoint()` at least once per `max_iterations_between_checkpoints` (configurable, default 100 iterations) or once per `max_duration_between_checkpoints` (configurable, default 5 seconds), whichever comes first.
4. Implement a `CheckpointGuard` that wraps orchestration loops and monitors compliance with the placement contract — if the loop exceeds the configured limits without checkpointing, the guard emits a structured warning and (in strict mode) aborts the loop.
5. Record each checkpoint as an event in the append-only decision stream (per 9G.9), including: orchestration_id, iteration_count, progress_state_hash, wall_clock_time, and epoch.
6. Ensure checkpoint data is integrity-protected: each checkpoint includes a hash chain linking it to the previous checkpoint for the same orchestration, enabling tamper detection.

## Context from Enhancement Maps

- 9G.2: "Cancellation as a strict protocol for all long-running orchestration tasks" — checkpoints enable safe resumption after cancellation.
- 9G.9: "Three-tier integrity strategy + append-only tamper-evident decision stream" — checkpoints are part of the integrity stream.
- 9J.19: "Cancellation-complete protocol discipline with obligation closure proofs" — checkpoint state is included in obligation closure proofs for cancelled orchestrations.
- Architecture invariant #3 (8.5): Cancellation protocol semantics — checkpoints are the mechanism for making cancellation non-destructive.
- Architecture invariant #8 (8.5): Evidence-by-default — checkpoint history is auditable evidence of orchestration progress.

## Dependencies

- Upstream: bd-24k (bounded masking for atomic checkpoint writes), bd-7om (cancel-drain-finalize — checkpoint integrates with drain phase), bd-126h (10.14 append-only marker stream for checkpoint recording), bd-2ah (obligation channels — checkpoint state referenced in obligation closure proofs)
- Downstream: bd-390 (anti-entropy reconciliation loop uses checkpoints for resumable reconciliation), bd-1jpo (10.11 section-wide verification gate)

## Acceptance Criteria

1. `CheckpointWriter` atomically writes checkpoint state; a crash during write does not corrupt the checkpoint store (verified by kill-during-write test).
2. `CheckpointReader` correctly loads the latest valid checkpoint; corrupted checkpoints are detected via hash chain and skipped with a structured alert.
3. `CheckpointGuard` in strict mode aborts a loop that exceeds 2x `max_iterations_between_checkpoints` without checkpointing, with a clear `CheckpointContractViolation` error.
4. `CheckpointGuard` in warn mode logs a structured warning but allows the loop to continue.
5. Checkpoint events in the decision stream include orchestration_id, iteration_count, progress_state_hash, previous_checkpoint_hash, and epoch.
6. Resumption from checkpoint: an orchestration loop that is killed and restarted resumes from the last checkpoint, processing only the remaining iterations (verified by counting total work done).
7. Hash chain integrity: tampering with a checkpoint's progress_state produces a chain verification failure on the next checkpoint read.
8. Verification evidence JSON includes checkpoints_written, checkpoints_resumed_from, checkpoint_contract_violations, hash_chain_verifications_passed, and avg_iterations_between_checkpoints fields.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: (a) CheckpointWriter serialization round-trip for various progress state types; (b) CheckpointReader loads latest checkpoint correctly; (c) Hash chain verification detects tampered checkpoint; (d) CheckpointGuard triggers on iteration limit; (e) CheckpointGuard triggers on duration limit.
- Integration tests: (a) Full orchestration loop with periodic checkpoints and successful completion; (b) Orchestration loop killed at iteration 150 (checkpoint at 100), restarted, resumes from iteration 100; (c) Checkpoint placement within cancel-drain-finalize lifecycle — checkpoint written during drain phase; (d) Concurrent orchestration loops with independent checkpoint streams.
- Adversarial tests: (a) Power-kill during checkpoint write — verify atomic write prevents corruption; (b) Checkpoint store full — verify graceful degradation with structured error; (c) Extremely fast loop (1M iterations/sec) — verify checkpoint overhead is bounded; (d) Forged checkpoint with valid hash but wrong epoch — verify epoch validation catches it.
- Structured logs: Events use stable codes (FN-CK-001 through FN-CK-008), include `orchestration_id`, `trace_id`, `iteration_count`, `checkpoint_hash`, `contract_status`. JSON-formatted.

## Expected Artifacts

- docs/specs/section_10_11/bd-93k_contract.md
- crates/franken-node/src/runtime/checkpoint.rs (or equivalent module path)
- crates/franken-node/src/runtime/checkpoint_guard.rs
- scripts/check_checkpoint_placement.py (with --json flag and self_test())
- tests/test_check_checkpoint_placement.py
- artifacts/section_10_11/bd-93k/verification_evidence.json
- artifacts/section_10_11/bd-93k/verification_summary.md
acceptance_criteria:
AC for bd-93k:
1. Every long orchestration loop (defined as any loop that may execute more than N iterations or exceed T wall-clock seconds, where N and T are configurable) must contain at least one checkpoint call that persists recoverable state.
2. A CheckpointContract trait is defined with methods: save_checkpoint(state) -> CheckpointId, restore_checkpoint(id) -> State, and list_checkpoints() -> Vec<CheckpointMeta>.
3. A compile-time or lint-time contract checker verifies that all orchestration loops annotated with #[long_orchestration] contain at least one checkpoint call; missing checkpoints cause a build warning (or error in strict mode).
4. Checkpoints are idempotent: calling save_checkpoint with identical state produces the same CheckpointId (content-addressed).
5. On crash recovery, the orchestration loop resumes from the latest valid checkpoint rather than restarting from scratch; a test demonstrates this by injecting a panic mid-loop and verifying resumed iteration count.
6. Checkpoint storage is pluggable (in-memory for tests, persistent for production) via a CheckpointBackend trait.
7. Unit tests verify: (a) checkpoint save/restore round-trip, (b) idempotent checkpoint ID stability, (c) loop resumption after simulated crash, (d) missing-checkpoint lint fires on unannotated loop.
8. Structured log events use stable codes CHECKPOINT_SAVE / CHECKPOINT_RESTORE / CHECKPOINT_MISSING with loop identifier and iteration count context.

title: BUG: verifier facade validate_bundle accepts foreign verifier bundles
description: Fresh-eyes audit of sdk/verifier/src/lib.rs found that VerifierSdk::validate_bundle() only calls bundle::verify(bundle) and returns Ok(()) without enforcing verify_bundle_belongs_to_current_verifier(). In the same facade, verify_migration_artifact() and verify_trust_state() do enforce verifier ownership. Impact: a verifier-scoped SDK instance can treat a structurally valid replay bundle from a different verifier identity as accepted during preflight validation, creating a fail-open ownership bypass and inconsistent policy surface. Fix should require validate_bundle() to reject bundles whose verifier_identity does not match self.verifier_identity and add regression coverage for foreign-bundle rejection.

title: EPIC — franken_node performance optimization (profiling rounds 1+2)
description:
# franken_node performance optimization — derived from /profiling-software-performance rounds 1 + 2

This epic captures all optimization work derived from two consecutive
profiling rounds (2026-05-20) on the franken_node Rust workspace
(crates/franken-node/). It is **self-contained**: nothing in here
should require a reader to fetch the original markdown artifacts to
make a decision. The artifacts still live at
`tests/artifacts/perf/20260520T214003Z_franken_node_perf/` (round 1)
and `tests/artifacts/perf/20260520T231041Z_franken_node_perf_r2/`
(round 2), and the cross-round index is at
`tests/artifacts/perf/HISTORY.md` — read those if you want raw
flamegraphs / heaptrack data, otherwise this epic's children carry
everything needed to execute.

## Why the work matters

franken_node is a trust-native JS/TS runtime *product layer* over
franken_engine. It ships signed receipts on every decision, runs a
fleet quarantine state machine across zones, and exposes a verifier
SDK for independent third-party verification. The hot paths are the
ones that touch every signed artifact, every trust-card update, every
replay-bundle export. Constant-factor wins on those paths show up on
every customer's machine.

These optimizations are NOT speculative. Each hotspot below is backed
by:
- Criterion wall-time numbers (round-1 BASELINE.md)
- perf record flat profiles (round-1 + round-2 /profiles/*.perf.flat.txt)
- heaptrack allocation traces for the alloc-bound candidates
- source-code line-citations confirming the root cause

Each child task names the exact files + line numbers, the equivalence
proofs to preserve, the recommended fix shape, and the expected
re-baseline target.

## Host / build provenance (round 1 + 2 share the same)

- Host: AMD EPYC 7282 16-Core × 2 sockets, 64 logical CPUs, NUMA-2,
  251 GiB RAM, ext4 on NVMe (/dev/nvme0n1p4), Linux 6.17.0-22-generic
- Toolchain: rustc 1.97.0-nightly (f53b654a8 2026-04-30), edition 2024
- Build profile used for profiling (must be re-added before any
  perf rerun — concurrent agents have shown they will revert it):

  ```toml
  # workspace Cargo.toml
  [profile.release-perf]
  inherits = "release"
  opt-level = 3
  lto = "thin"
  codegen-units = 1
  debug = "line-tables-only"
  strip = false
  ```

  Build with: `RUSTFLAGS="-C force-frame-pointers=yes" rch exec -- cargo build --profile release-perf -p frankenengine-node --benches`

- Kernel tuning applied (sysctl): `perf_event_paranoid=1`,
  `kptr_restrict=0`, `nmi_watchdog=0`, `perf_event_mlock_kb=32768`.
  Revert with: `sudo sysctl -w kernel.perf_event_paranoid=4 kernel.kptr_restrict=1 kernel.nmi_watchdog=1`
- `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` is in both lib.rs and main.rs — no
  optimization may introduce unsafe.

## Unified hotspot ranking (cross-round)

See `tests/artifacts/perf/HISTORY.md` for the table. Score =
Impact × Confidence / Effort (each 1-5, Effort: 5 = hardest).
Recommended attack order (lowest effort first; this is intentional —
quick wins build measurement confidence before invasive changes):

| # | Hotspot                                              | Score | Bead       |
|---|------------------------------------------------------|------:|------------|
| 1 | threshold_sig preparsed keys (already bench-proven)  | 15.0  | T1 (bd-98xo5.1) |
| 2 | Ed25519Scheme key cache                              | 12.5  | T2 (bd-98xo5.2) |
| 3 | cuckoo insert cliff policy decision                  | 10.0  | T3 (bd-98xo5.3) |
| 4 | trust_card deep-clone restructure                    |  6.3  | T4 (bd-98xo5.4) |
| 5 | DGIS String NodeId → u32 interning                   |  4.0  | T5 (bd-98xo5.5) |
| 6 | replay_bundle_event_size vec_len → streaming         |  5.0  | T6 (bd-98xo5.6) |
| 7 | fleet_transport canonicalize_json_value path cleanup |  5.0  | T7 (bd-98xo5.7) |

Plus measurement-gap tasks (round-3 work; no optimization until
the bench exists):
- T8 vef::proof_generator + receipt_chain Criterion benches
- T9 migration tree-sitter on real corpora
- T10 DGIS contagion_simulator::step on a large graph

Plus infrastructure / cross-cutting tasks:
- T11 Persist release-perf profile against agent reverts
- T12 Sentinel frames + HDR histograms for the four hot paths
- T13 Cross-round perf-budget contract update (after T1–T10 land)
- T14 Document the 25-30 % Criterion-bootstrap CPU band
- T15 Cross-cutting test infrastructure (shared harness, log schema,
  CI gate). EVERY major optimisation task has a test-suite subtask
  (Tx.tests) that uses the T15 harness.
- T16 Schema-version bump runbook — opened ONLY if T4 forces a
  trust-card canonical schema bump.

## Methodology guard-rails for every child task

- Treat `artifacts/performance_budgets/bd-ncwlf_hot_path_budget_evidence.json`
  as the existing perf-budget contract. New budgets land alongside the
  measured change.
- Goldens under `tests/golden/` must remain byte-identical unless a
  schema_version is intentionally bumped — see T16 for the runbook.
- Re-baseline on a quiet host (`rch queue` should show <3 active builds).
- One lever per commit. Bundle nothing.
- All cargo builds via `rch exec --` per repo policy.
- **ubs gate**: `ubs $(git diff --name-only --cached)` before every
  commit. Exit 0 required.

## Concurrent-agent coordination protocol

Multiple swarm agents will pick up beads in parallel. Race protection:

1. **Claim atomically before working**:
   `br update bd-98xo5.X --claim --actor <your-agent-name>`
   This sets `assignee=<actor>` and `status=in_progress` in one
   write — no two agents can claim the same bead.
2. **File reservation** (MCP Agent Mail), reserve the surface paths
   the bead names BEFORE starting:
   `file_reservation_paths(project_key=<repo>, agent_name=<you>,
   patterns=["crates/franken-node/src/<module>/**"],
   ttl_seconds=3600, exclusive=true, reason="bd-98xo5.X")`
3. **Announce thread**: send a Mail message with
   `thread_id="bd-98xo5.X"` so progress is visible to other agents.
4. **Per-AGENTS.md Closer Discipline** when closing:
   ≥ 80-char `close_reason` including (a) a commit SHA, (b) a PR
   reference or `file:line` citation, and (c) for bug/feature beads
   at least one passing-test name. Empty / thin / "done" close
   reasons are NOT acceptable.
5. **Release reservations + send completion mail** when closing.

## Test-logging standard (apply to every Tx.tests subtask)

Each task's test-suite subtask (T15 owns the shared harness) MUST
emit a JSONL log under `tests/artifacts/perf/<bead-id>_test_log.jsonl`
with one line per test phase. Each line is canonical JSON with
this minimum field set:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-05-21T14:22:31.118Z",
  "level": "info|warn|error",
  "event_code": "TEST-START|TEST-CASE|TEST-PASS|TEST-FAIL|TEST-SUMMARY|PERF-MEASUREMENT",
  "bead_id": "bd-98xo5.X.tests",
  "trace_id": "<run-id>",
  "phase": "build|unit|property|fuzz|e2e|baseline",
  "test_name": "<descriptive_name>",
  "duration_ms": <number>,
  "extra": { ... per-test detail ... }
}
```

Event codes are stable; future tooling (`scripts/render_perf_test_summary.py`)
parses them.

## Cross-cutting policy for every optimisation PR

Required by reviewers before merge:
- [ ] Unit-test parity proves byte-identical outputs before/after.
- [ ] Property test (proptest) covers the full input envelope.
- [ ] Fuzz harness added if the surface produces canonical bytes or
      signatures (see fuzz/ directory; mirror the existing
      replay_bundle_adversarial_fuzz pattern).
- [ ] Criterion regression bench updated with the new post-fix
      numbers.
- [ ] perf-budget contract updated (T13 once all batched).
- [ ] e2e shell script under `tests/perf_beads/<bead-id>.sh` that
      builds, runs, and validates the change end-to-end, emitting
      structured JSONL logs per the standard above.
- [ ] ubs clean on all changed files.
- [ ] Closer Discipline-compliant `close_reason` on the bead.

## Rejections (do NOT optimize these — measured, not hot)

- `observability::evidence_ledger::append` — 16.62 µs / large entry,
  well under any reasonable audit-log budget.

title: T1 — threshold_sig preparsed VerifyingKey plumbing (score 15.0)
description:
# Task T1 — threshold_sig preparsed VerifyingKey plumbing

Parent: bd-98xo5 (epic). Recommended starting point — lowest effort,
proven win already lives in the benchmark.

## Background

`security::threshold_sig::verify_threshold` is a k-of-n Ed25519 quorum
verifier. Today it re-decodes hex strings into `VerifyingKey` for
every signer on every `verify` call. That's a wasted parse + Edwards
point validation per verify.

The `threshold_sig_verify_bench` already documents a working fix as a
bench-local helper. Numbers (round-1
`tests/artifacts/perf/20260520T214003Z_franken_node_perf/criterion_raw/threshold_sig_verify.txt`):

| Variant       | 8 signers  | 32 signers | speedup |
|---------------|-----------:|-----------:|--------:|
| current       | 433.6 µs   | 1 778 µs   | 1.00×   |
| preparsed_keys| 396.4 µs   | 1 611 µs   | 0.91× (~10 % saved) |

The bench scaffolding lives at
`crates/franken-node/benches/threshold_sig_verify_bench.rs:87-108` as
`struct PreparsedThresholdConfig { threshold, verifying_keys: BTreeMap<String, VerifyingKey> }`.
The bench's `verify_threshold_preparsed` (lines 110-159) shows the
verification loop with cached keys.

## perf profile evidence

Round 1 `tests/artifacts/perf/20260520T214003Z_franken_node_perf/profiles/threshold_sig_verify_32.perf.flat.txt`:

| % cycles | symbol |
|---------:|--------|
| 17.73 % | curve25519_dalek FieldElement2625x4 AVX2 ops |
| 13.51 % | FieldElement51::pow2k |
|  6.92 % | FieldElement2625x4 AVX2 ops |
|  6.55 % | vartime_double_base spec_avx2::mul::_impl_mul |
|  1.82 % | FieldElement51::Mul |
|  0.63 % | frankenengine_node::security::threshold_sig::verify_threshold |

50 % of cycles are in dalek field math (irreducible without
`verify_batch` — separate research item). The user code accounts for
0.63 %. The +10 % preparsed_keys win is essentially THE available
user-code lever.

## Equivalence proof requirement

Quorum **decisions** (accept/reject) for every existing signature
artifact must be byte-identical before and after. The bench's
`current` path and `preparsed_keys` path are designed to return
identical pass/fail; the production migration must preserve that.

## Recommended fix shape

1. Promote `PreparsedThresholdConfig` from a bench-only struct to a
   public type in `crates/franken-node/src/security/threshold_sig.rs`.
   Public API: `PreparsedThresholdConfig::from(&ThresholdConfig)` +
   `verify_threshold_preparsed(&PreparsedThresholdConfig, &PublicationArtifact, trace_id, timestamp) -> VerifyResult`.

2. Find every production caller of `verify_threshold(&ThresholdConfig, ...)`
   and convert the call site to cache one `PreparsedThresholdConfig`
   per `ThresholdConfig` instance (which is itself usually
   long-lived). Likely call sites:
   - `crates/franken-node/src/security/threshold_sig.rs` inline tests
   - any caller in `connector/`, `supply_chain/`, `extensions/registry/`,
     `vef/` (search: `verify_threshold\(`).

3. Preserve `verify_threshold` as a thin wrapper that builds a
   `PreparsedThresholdConfig` once and calls
   `verify_threshold_preparsed`, so callers that don't want to cache
   keep working. The cost is the same as today; the new path is for
   callers that DO want caching.

4. Cache invalidation: the `PreparsedThresholdConfig` is keyed by the
   `signer_keys` Vec inside `ThresholdConfig`. Any rotation event
   that mutates `signer_keys` must invalidate the cache. Simplest:
   require callers to construct a new `PreparsedThresholdConfig` after
   any config change; document the invariant.

5. Re-run the round-1 baseline:
   `./target/release-perf/deps/threshold_sig_verify_bench-<hash> --bench`
   and confirm `preparsed_keys/{8,32}` numbers haven't drifted from
   396.4 µs / 1611 µs respectively (±10 % envelope).

## Out of scope for this task

- `ed25519_dalek::verify_batch` — batched verification across signers
  is a separate research item (see the round-3 task on this epic).
- Promoting the same pattern to `crypto::Ed25519Scheme` — that's a
  separate task (T2) because the trait surface is different.

## Subtasks

Will be created as child beads with `--parent` = this task and
explicit `blocks` deps between them.

# T1.5 — Comprehensive test suite for threshold_sig preparsed API

Parent: T1 (bd-98xo5.1). Owns ALL the test deliverables that the
T1 sibling implementation subtasks reference. Uses the T15 harness
(`scripts/run_perf_bead_test.sh`) for structured JSONL logging.

## Files this bead delivers

1. **Unit tests** (inline) at
   `crates/franken-node/src/security/threshold_sig.rs` under
   `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` — extend the existing module, do not
   create a new one:
   - `parity_with_legacy_at_8_signers` — same artifact through
     both `verify_threshold` (legacy) and
     `verify_threshold_preparsed` returns identical VerifyResult.
   - `parity_with_legacy_at_32_signers` — same at the larger size.
   - `parity_under_missing_signers` — when k-of-n condition is
     not met, both paths reject identically.
   - `parity_under_duplicate_key_id` — both paths reject duplicate
     key_id identically (the existing BTreeSet dedup must hold).
   - `parity_under_malleable_signature` — both paths reject
     malleable / non-canonical-s signatures (verify_strict).
   - `preparsed_from_config_rejects_invalid_hex` — PrepConfig
     construction surfaces hex-decode errors instead of silently
     producing a partially-populated map.
   - `preparsed_from_config_rejects_short_pubkey` — same for
     32-byte length check.
   - `preparsed_send_sync_bounds` — `PreparsedThresholdConfig:
     Send + Sync` (compile-time bound check).

2. **Property tests** (inline) using `proptest` (already a
   workspace dev-dep):
   - `prop_parity_random_config(n in 1usize..=64, k in 1usize..=n)`
     generates random keys, random message payloads up to 4 KiB,
     and asserts both paths agree on accept/reject for 5000
     random inputs.
   - `proptest-regressions/threshold_sig_parity.txt` carries the
     persistent seed file (proptest writes this automatically on
     a finding; commit it).

3. **Fuzz harness** at `fuzz/fuzz_targets/threshold_sig_parity.rs`,
   following the existing `replay_bundle_adversarial_fuzz` pattern:
   - takes a structured input that yields a (ThresholdConfig,
     PublicationArtifact) pair.
   - asserts `verify_threshold(...) == verify_threshold_preparsed(...)`.
   - panics on divergence (which `cargo fuzz` flags as a finding).
   - Add to `fuzz/Cargo.toml` `[[bin]]` list.
   - Run for 30 minutes minimum in CI nightly.

4. **e2e shell script** at
   `tests/perf_beads/bd-98xo5.1.tests.sh`:
   - Sources `scripts/run_perf_bead_test.sh`.
   - Build phase: `cargo build --profile release-perf --bench threshold_sig_verify_bench` and a CLI smoke build.
   - Unit phase: `cargo test --lib security::threshold_sig`.
   - Property phase: `cargo test --lib threshold_sig_parity_property --release -- --nocapture`.
   - Fuzz phase: `cargo +nightly fuzz run threshold_sig_parity -- -max_total_time=60`
     (short, just to confirm the harness builds; nightly CI runs
     long).
   - Baseline phase: invoke the bench binary, extract
     `preparsed_keys/{8,32}` p95 numbers, call
     `perf_test_measurement` for each, assert under budget.
   - Cleanup: print final summary.

5. **Logging**: every phase + every case emits a JSONL event per
   the T15 schema. The log lands at
   `tests/artifacts/perf/test_runs/bd-98xo5.1.tests_<ts>/test_log.jsonl`.
   `scripts/render_perf_test_summary.py --ci <log>` is the gate.

## Acceptance criteria

- All 8 inline unit tests pass.
- `prop_parity_random_config` runs 5000 iterations without
  finding a divergence.
- Fuzz harness builds under `cargo +nightly fuzz build`.
- e2e shell script exits 0 on the reference host.
- Test log JSONL is schema-valid (`render_perf_test_summary.py
  --ci` returns 0).
- Bench p95 numbers match expectation:
  - `preparsed_keys/8` ≤ 436 µs (round-1 was 396.4 µs; +10 % envelope)
  - `preparsed_keys/32` ≤ 1 772 µs (round-1 was 1 611 µs)

## Why this is a separate bead

The implementation subtasks (T1.1, T1.2, T1.3) churn code; the
test suite is a single bundled deliverable that gates the merge.
Splitting it lets a different agent author tests in parallel
with the implementation, and lets the test bead carry its own
specific close_reason (test names that newly pass per
AGENTS.md Closer Discipline).

  migrated, the integration-test path of the e2e script can't
  exercise real callers.
- T15.3 (template available) — copy the template as starting
  point.

title: T10 — Round-3 DGIS large-graph contagion_simulator::step bench
description:
# Task T10 — Round-3 measurement: DGIS contagion_simulator::step on a large graph

Parent: bd-98xo5 (epic). Closes the round-2 hypothesis-revisit
gap: the round-1 static read claimed `step()` is a hotspot due to
per-tick `build_in_edges` rebuild + `BTreeSet::clone`. Round-2
profile rejected that — but the rejection came from a workload of
tiny fixtures (xz_style, dependency_confusion, typosquat profiles
with ≤ a few hundred nodes). On a large graph, `step` may still be
hot.

## Background

`crates/franken-node/src/dgis/contagion_simulator.rs:235-305` is
the per-tick function. Round-2 measurement
(`tests/artifacts/perf/20260520T231041Z_franken_node_perf_r2/profiles/dgis_contagion.perf.flat.txt`)
shows `step` at 0.45 % of cycles on a 200x integration-test loop.
The function is small but has three potentially-O(V+E) operations
per tick:

1. L247: `let in_edges = build_in_edges(graph);` rebuilds the
   reversed adjacency map per step — O(E).
2. L250: `let mut next_infected: BTreeSet<NodeId> = state.infected.clone();`
   deep-clones the infected set — O(|infected|) String allocations
   today, O(|infected|) integer copies after T5 (NodeId u32
   interning).
3. L252-298: iterate over `graph.nodes()`, with per-node BTreeMap
   lookup into in_edges and BTreeSet membership check.

At ≤ a few hundred nodes these are invisible. At 10 000 nodes ×
100 steps × a heavily-infected state vector, they should dominate.

## Recommended bench shape

New file `crates/franken-node/benches/dgis_large_graph_bench.rs`:

```rust
fn bench_step(c: &mut Criterion) {
    let mut group = c.benchmark_group("dgis_large_graph");
    group.measurement_time(Duration::from_secs(10));
    group.sample_size(20);

    for (n_nodes, n_steps, sparsity) in [
        (1_000usize, 100usize, 0.001f64),  // 1k nodes
        (10_000,     100,       0.0001),    // 10k nodes
        (50_000,     50,        0.00005),   // 50k nodes
    ] {
        let graph = build_random_graph(n_nodes, sparsity);
        let initial_infected = pick_seeds(&graph, n_nodes / 100); // 1 % seeded
        let config = SimulatorConfig::default();
        group.bench_with_input(BenchmarkId::new("simulate", format!("{}n_{}s", n_nodes, n_steps)),
            &(graph, initial_infected, config),
            |b, (g, ii, cfg)| b.iter(|| {
                black_box(simulate(black_box(g), black_box(ii), black_box(cfg), black_box(n_steps)))
            }));
    }
}
```

Use a deterministic random graph generator (existing
`ContagionGraph::generate_deterministic` may already produce a
suitable input).

## Acceptance

A baseline run produces wall-time + perf-record numbers for
1 k / 10 k / 50 k node graphs. Decide:

(A) `step` shows up at > 5 % on the large-graph profile: the
    round-1 hypothesis was right after all (just measured wrong
    in round 2). File a new bead under this epic for the
    `build_in_edges` cache + `BTreeSet::clone` reduction.

(B) `step` stays < 1 % even at 50 k nodes: round-2 rejection
    holds. Document the bench numbers in HISTORY.md as
    confirmation; close the round-1 hypothesis permanently.

## Dependency on T5

This task should run AFTER T5 lands (NodeId u32 interning),
because:
- If we measure before T5, we conflate "step is hot because of
  String NodeIds" with "step is hot for other reasons".
- After T5, any remaining hotness in step IS the structural
  issue (build_in_edges rebuild, infected.clone, etc.).

## Out of scope

- Optimising step itself in this task. Decision (A) above files a
  new optimisation bead; (B) closes the question.

title: T11 — Persist [profile.release-perf] against concurrent-agent reverts
description:
# Task T11 — Persist [profile.release-perf] against concurrent-agent reverts

Parent: bd-98xo5 (epic). Infrastructure — feeds every future
profiling round.

## Background

During round 1, the profiling skill added a `[profile.release-perf]`
section to the workspace `Cargo.toml`. A concurrent agent (within
the multi-agent swarm working on this repo) reverted it. The
profile had to be re-added at the start of round 2 — and may have
been reverted again by the time you're reading this.

This is a stability problem for future profiling rounds: every
fresh run starts by needing the profile, building once with
`opt-level=3 + lto=thin + codegen-units=1 + debug=line-tables-only
+ strip=false`, then risks losing it before the next run.

## Why it can't just live in Cargo.toml forever

The repo's policy under AGENTS.md "No File Proliferation" + the
multi-agent swarm dynamics mean random additions to top-level
files get cleaned up. The release-perf profile is "measurement
infrastructure" — useful only when actively profiling — and looks
like profile bloat the rest of the time.

## Recommended fix shape

Two complementary moves:

1. **Document the profile prominently** so any agent reverting
   it sees a strong "don't" signal:
   - Add a section "Profiling Build Profile" to
     `docs/dev/profiling.md` (new doc) or to CONTRIBUTING.md.
   - The doc body MUST include the exact profile block, the
     reasoning ("debug = line-tables-only is required for samply /
     perf frame attribution"), and a "DO NOT REMOVE WITHOUT READING
     `tests/artifacts/perf/HISTORY.md`" warning.
   - Link the doc from the workspace `Cargo.toml` via a comment
     immediately above the profile section:

     ```toml
     # See docs/dev/profiling.md before removing this profile.
     # It is referenced by every profile run under
     # tests/artifacts/perf/<run-id>/.
     [profile.release-perf]
     ...
     ```

2. **Add a CI sanity check** that fails loudly if the profile is
   missing when the run is invoked with `PROFILING_HARNESSED=1`:
   - A small Python check under `scripts/check_release_perf_profile.py`
     that opens `Cargo.toml`, asserts the `[profile.release-perf]`
     header exists, and that all four required keys (lto,
     codegen-units, debug, strip) match the canonical values.
   - Wire it into a new minor workflow
     `.github/workflows/release-perf-profile-gate.yml` that only
     triggers when files under `tests/artifacts/perf/**` change.

## Acceptance

- `docs/dev/profiling.md` exists and explains the profile.
- The comment above `[profile.release-perf]` references that doc.
- The Python checker exists and exits non-zero when the profile
  is removed or mutated.
- Workflow runs green on this exact repo state.

## Out of scope

- Adding the profile to a separate file (e.g. `.cargo/config.toml`)
  is technically possible but couples the build behaviour to
  filesystem state that's NOT versioned the same way. Stay in
  Cargo.toml.

Both design-time (docs warning) and runtime (CI gate) backstops are now in place; concurrent-agent reverts of [profile.release-perf] will trip the workflow gate at PR time and the test suite locally. No additional EPIC-level code needed beyond the two child commits.

title: T11.2 — Add scripts/check_release_perf_profile.py + CI workflow gate
description:
Python checker at `scripts/check_release_perf_profile.py`:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Assert workspace [profile.release-perf] exists with canonical values.

Run with --ci to exit non-zero on any mismatch. Run without args for
a friendlier warning that prints what's missing.
"""
import sys, tomllib, pathlib

WANT = {
    "inherits": "release",
    "opt-level": 3,
    "lto": "thin",
    "codegen-units": 1,
    "debug": "line-tables-only",
    "strip": False,
}

def main():
    root = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "Cargo.toml"
    with root.open("rb") as f:
        data = tomllib.load(f)
    profile = data.get("profile", {}).get("release-perf")
    if profile is None:
        print("FAIL: [profile.release-perf] missing from Cargo.toml.")
        print("See docs/dev/profiling.md for the canonical block.")
        return 1
    missing = {k: v for k, v in WANT.items() if profile.get(k) != v}
    if missing:
        print(f"FAIL: [profile.release-perf] has wrong values: {missing}")
        return 1
    print("OK: release-perf profile is canonical.")
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

CI workflow `.github/workflows/release-perf-profile-gate.yml`:

```yaml
name: release-perf-profile-gate
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - 'Cargo.toml'
      - 'tests/artifacts/perf/**'
      - 'docs/dev/profiling.md'
      - 'scripts/check_release_perf_profile.py'

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: python3 scripts/check_release_perf_profile.py --ci
```

Add a matching test under `tests/` so the project's existing
Python-gate-script test pattern catches us if the checker itself
breaks.

title: T12 — Sentinel frames + HDR histograms on four hot paths (Phase-4 plan)
description:
# Task T12 — Sentinel frames + HDR histograms for the four hot paths (Phase-4 plan)

Parent: bd-98xo5 (epic). Round-1 Phase-4 INSTRUMENTATION.md
explicitly deferred this to "the next skill". It's instrumentation
infrastructure that makes EVERY future profile easier to interpret.

## Background

Round-1 INSTRUMENTATION.md catalogued:
- 24 source files use `tracing::*` (event-style, with stable
  `event_code` fields).
- 0 source files use `#[tracing::instrument]` (span-style).
- 0 source files use `hdrhistogram::Histogram` (no latency tails
  captured).
- 0 source files use sentinel `#[inline(never)] fn _profile_*()`
  no-ops (so the flamegraph can't show pipeline stages as distinct
  bars).
- The `PerformanceBudgetGuard` machinery (4 683 LOC across
  `policy/perf_budget_guard.rs` + `connector/perf_budget_guard.rs`)
  is a CONSUMER of measurements; nothing in `src/` actually
  produces the measurements.

The /profiling-software-performance skill's `INSTRUMENTATION.md`
template recommends FOUR layers of instrumentation, all of which
should be gated behind `FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE=1` so production
pays nothing:

1. **Sentinel `_profile_*` frames** — no-op `#[inline(never)]`
   functions that show up as distinct bars on flamegraphs.
2. **HDR histograms** — `hdrhistogram::Histogram::<u64>::new_with_bounds(1, 60_000_000, 3)`
   per hot path, periodically flushed as `perf.profile.span_summary`
   events with cumulative_us, count, p50_us, p95_us.
3. **`#[tracing::instrument]` spans** on the hot-path entry
   points so cumulative_us × count rollups are computable.
4. **`perf.profile.*` structured logging contract** — a stable
   JSON schema so `scripts/render_hotspot_table.py` (provided by
   the profiling skill) can ingest the output directly.

## Why this is round-2-or-later work

It changes EVERY future round's data quality:
- Round 1 had to fall back to perf's binary-symbol attribution; a
  sentinel `_profile_canonicalize_value_current()` would have
  made the flame bar self-labelled.
- HDR histograms inside the function give us p99 / p99.9 / p99.99
  tails that Criterion's 100-sample default misses entirely.
- The `perf.profile.span_summary` events are what
  `extreme-software-optimization` will look for to rank candidates
  in future rounds.

## Scope

Four hot paths the four child tasks below cover, one each:

- T12.1: `trust_card_canonical::canonicalize_value_current` (or
  whatever T4 names the new streaming encoder).
- T12.2: `crypto::Ed25519Scheme::{sign_raw, verify_raw}` (and the
  new `Ed25519PreparsedSigner::sign_raw` from T2).
- T12.3: `security::threshold_sig::verify_threshold` (and the new
  `verify_threshold_preparsed` from T1).
- T12.4: `observability::evidence_ledger::EvidenceLedger::append`.

Each subtask follows the same template — they're functionally
identical except the function names.

## Acceptance

After T12.1-T12.4 land:
- `FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE=1 ./benchmark` emits stable
  `perf.profile.span_summary` JSONL lines that
  `scripts/render_hotspot_table.py` (from the
  /profiling-software-performance skill) can parse directly.
- Flamegraphs from samply/perf show the four `_profile_*` sentinel
  bars distinctly even at codegen-units=1 + thin LTO.
- Production builds (NOT the bench builds) pay zero cost: the
  histograms are behind `if cfg!(debug_assertions) || option_env!("FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE").is_some()`
  and elided by LLVM.

## Out of scope

- Wiring the histograms to a metrics exporter (Prometheus, etc.).
  That's a separate observability work item; this task just emits
  structured log events.

title: T12.1 — Instrument trust_card_canonical_canonicalize_value with sentinel + HDR histogram + span
description:
Surface: crates/franken-node/src/connector/canonical_serializer.rs::write_canonical_value (post-T4) or the existing CanonicalSerializer::serialize_value

Add three pieces of measurement-only instrumentation, ALL gated by
the env flag `FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE=1` so production builds pay zero
cost. Use `option_env!("FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE")` so the gate is
compile-time-resolvable and LLVM elides the dead branch.

## 1. Sentinel frame

```rust
#[inline(never)]
fn _profile_trust_card_canonicalize() {
    std::hint::black_box(());
}
```

Call the sentinel at the very start of the function body so
flamegraph attribution shows the bar self-labelled.

## 2. HDR histogram (lazy_static or OnceCell)

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "profiling")]  // or env-gated equivalent
static trust_card_canonical.us: OnceLock<Mutex<Histogram<u64>>> = OnceLock::new();

#[cfg(feature = "profiling")]
fn record_us(elapsed: Duration) {
    let h = trust_card_canonical.us.get_or_init(|| {
        Mutex::new(Histogram::<u64>::new_with_bounds(1, 60_000_000, 3).unwrap())
    });
    h.lock().unwrap().record(elapsed.as_micros() as u64).ok();
}
```

Capture elapsed time around the function body. On every Nth call
(e.g. N=10 000) OR on a Drop hook at process exit, flush a
`perf.profile.span_summary` event with the histogram's current
p50/p95/p99/cumulative.

## 3. tracing instrument span

```rust
#[tracing::instrument(skip_all, fields(...))]
pub fn surface_method(...) -> ... {
    ...
}
```

The `skip_all` is important — the function's arguments are large
and we don't want them auto-logged. Add only the small fields
(counts, sizes) that are interesting per-call.

## 4. Structured log event

The histogram-flush should emit a JSON line matching the profiling
skill's contract:

```json
{
  "event_code": "perf.profile.span_summary",
  "span_name": "trust_card_canonical.us",
  "cumulative_us": <number>,
  "count": <number>,
  "p50_us": <number>,
  "p95_us": <number>,
  "p99_us": <number>,
  "category": "CPU",
  "evidence": "crates/franken-node/src/connector/canonical_serializer.rs::write_canonical_value (post-T4) or the existing CanonicalSerializer::serialize_value"
}
```

So that `scripts/render_hotspot_table.py` from the profiling
skill can ingest it directly.

## Tests

Inline tests under #[cfg(test)]:
- When FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE is unset, the instrumented function
  must produce IDENTICAL outputs as today (no observable
  side-effect).
- When FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE=1, a single call records one
  histogram sample.
- The histogram bound-check (1 µs .. 60 s) must not panic on
  zero-elapsed or large-elapsed inputs.

## Cost when profile disabled

LLVM must elide both the sentinel and the histogram record path.
Confirm by checking the disassembly: `objdump -d
target/release/.../<binary> | grep "_profile_trust_card_canonicalize"` should
return zero matches in the non-profiling build.

the env flag `FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE=1` so production builds pay zero
cost. Use `option_env!("FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE")` so the gate is
compile-time-resolvable and LLVM elides the dead branch.

## 1. Sentinel frame

```rust
#[inline(never)]
fn _profile_threshold_sig_verify() {
    std::hint::black_box(());
}
```

Call the sentinel at the very start of the function body so
flamegraph attribution shows the bar self-labelled.

## 2. HDR histogram (lazy_static or OnceCell)

```rust
#[cfg(feature = "profiling")]  // or env-gated equivalent
static threshold_sig_verify.us: OnceLock<Mutex<Histogram<u64>>> = OnceLock::new();

#[cfg(feature = "profiling")]
fn record_us(elapsed: Duration) {
    let h = threshold_sig_verify.us.get_or_init(|| {
        Mutex::new(Histogram::<u64>::new_with_bounds(1, 60_000_000, 3).unwrap())
    });
    h.lock().unwrap().record(elapsed.as_micros() as u64).ok();
}
```

Capture elapsed time around the function body. On every Nth call
(e.g. N=10 000) OR on a Drop hook at process exit, flush a
`perf.profile.span_summary` event with the histogram's current
p50/p95/p99/cumulative.

## 3. tracing instrument span

```rust
#[tracing::instrument(skip_all, fields(...))]
pub fn surface_method(...) -> ... {
    ...
}
```

The `skip_all` is important — the function's arguments are large
and we don't want them auto-logged. Add only the small fields
(counts, sizes) that are interesting per-call.

## 4. Structured log event

The histogram-flush should emit a JSON line matching the profiling
skill's contract:

```json
{

  "span_name": "threshold_sig_verify.us",
  "cumulative_us": <number>,
  "count": <number>,
  "p50_us": <number>,
```

title: T12.5 — Test suite for sentinel-frame + HDR-histogram instrumentation
description:
# T12.5 — Test suite for sentinel-frame + HDR-histogram instrumentation

Parent: T12 (bd-98xo5.12). The four T12.1-T12.4 subtasks each add
instrumentation to one hot path. T12.5 is the consolidated
test-suite bead that verifies the whole instrumentation system.

## Files this bead delivers

1. **Unit tests** in each instrumented module
   (`schemes.rs`, `threshold_sig.rs`, `evidence_ledger.rs`,
   `connector/canonical_serializer.rs`):
   - `instrumentation_disabled_produces_identical_output_to_uninstrumented` —
     when `FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE` is unset, the instrumented function
     behaves byte-identically to a fresh build without the
     instrumentation. (This is the "production pays zero cost"
     invariant.)
   - `instrumentation_enabled_records_one_sample_per_call` — when
     `FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE=1`, a single call appends exactly one
     histogram sample.
   - `instrumentation_handles_zero_elapsed` — fast-path call
     completing in < 1 µs doesn't crash the bounds-checked HDR
     histogram (lower bound is 1 µs).
   - `instrumentation_handles_large_elapsed` — artificial slow
     call (sleep + manual record) at the upper bound (60 s)
     records cleanly.
   - `instrumentation_histogram_flush_emits_structured_event` —
     after N (e.g. 10 000) recorded samples, a
     `perf.profile.span_summary` event fires with the correct
     event_code, span_name, cumulative_us, count, p50/p95/p99.

2. **Compile-time elision audit** at
   `crates/franken-node/tests/instrumentation_zero_cost_audit.rs`:
   - Builds the library WITHOUT the profile flag.
   - Greps the resulting binary (via `nm` + symbol filter) for
     any `_profile_*` sentinel symbol.
   - Asserts the sentinel symbols are NOT present (LLVM should
     have elided the dead branch).
   - Same for the histogram statics (they should be missing or
     marked dead-code).
   - If the elision fails, the integration test fails LOUDLY
     with the offending symbol name.

3. **Flamegraph attribution integration test** at
   `crates/franken-node/tests/instrumentation_flamegraph_attribution.rs`:
   - Builds the bench under release-perf WITH the profile flag.
   - Runs a 10-second perf record on a representative bench
     (e.g. trust_card_canonical at medium_3x8).
   - Asserts each of the four `_profile_*` sentinel symbols
     appears in the perf flat profile at > 0.1 % (i.e. the
     sentinel IS visible on the flame as a distinct bar).
   - This is the "flame bars are self-labelled" gate.
   - SKIP with reason if `perf` is not in PATH.

4. **e2e shell script** at `tests/perf_beads/bd-98xo5.12.tests.sh`:
   - Build twice (with + without `FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE` env).
   - Diff the symbol counts; assert the profile-enabled build
     has 4 more `_profile_*` symbols than the disabled build.
   - Run a small workload through each instrumented function
     with profile enabled.
   - Assert the resulting JSONL stream contains exactly the
     expected event_codes (`perf.profile.span_summary` with the
     right span_names).
   - Pretty-print the histogram summaries.
   - Cleanup.

5. **Logging**: per T15 schema.

## Acceptance

- All 5 unit tests pass per module (20 tests total).
- Zero-cost audit passes (sentinel symbols absent in release build).
- Flamegraph attribution test passes OR SKIPs cleanly when perf
  is absent.
- e2e shell exit 0.

## Blockers

- T12.1, T12.2, T12.3, T12.4 — all four instrumentation
  subtasks must land first.
- T15.3 (template).

## Why this matters

The T12 instrumentation is meant to make EVERY FUTURE profiling
round more interpretable. If the zero-cost invariant breaks,
production pays ongoing overhead for our diagnostics. If the
flame-bar visibility breaks, the next round's hotspot ranking
falls back to symbol-table archaeology again. Both gates protect
the value of T12 itself.

title: T14 — Document the Criterion bootstrap-band CPU+alloc overhead
description:
# Task T14 — Document the Criterion bootstrap-band CPU overhead

Parent: bd-98xo5 (epic). Infrastructure — feeds future profiling
rounds. Cheap to do.

## Background

Across all three perf-record profiles in round 1 + 2
(trust_card_canonical, threshold_sig_verify_32,
crypto_scheme_sign64, evidence_ledger, dgis_contagion,
proof_generator) the top symbol band is ALWAYS the same:

| Symbol                                                | % cycles  |
|-------------------------------------------------------|----------:|
| `__ieee754_exp_fma`                                   | 27-36 %   |
| `exp@@GLIBC_2.29`                                     | 7-10 %    |
| `rayon::iter::plumbing::bridge_producer_consumer`     | 3-7 %     |
| `crossbeam_deque::Stealer::steal`                     | 1-2 %     |
| `crossbeam_epoch::Global::try_advance`                | 1-2 %     |

Combined: **25-30 % of cycles in every Criterion bench profile**.
This is Criterion's bootstrap-resampling estimator computing
confidence intervals in parallel via rayon's work-stealing queue.
It's pure scaffolding — has NOTHING to do with the function being
benched.

A naive reading of any perf flat profile would say "exp() is the
hottest function!" That's wrong. Excluding this band is mandatory
for any user-code hotspot ranking on a Criterion-driven workload.

heaptrack has the SAME problem on the alloc side: in the round-2
evidence_ledger bench, 1 005 881 / 1 158 614 allocations (87 %)
came from `criterion::stats::univariate::bootstrap` — NOT from
the evidence_ledger code. Anyone reading raw heaptrack alloc
counts must filter this band first.

## Why this matters for future rounds

Without explicit documentation, every fresh profiling agent will
re-trip on the same misreading. The round-1 + round-2 reports
both have a section calling this out, but those are tucked inside
hotspot_table.md / hypothesis.md — easy to miss.

## Recommended fix shape

1. **Update the `/profiling-software-performance` skill's
   `references/PATTERNS-ENCYCLOPEDIA.md`** with a named pattern:
   "Criterion bootstrap-band CPU + alloc overhead is 25-30 % of
   any short-iteration bench profile; exclude before ranking."
   Include the symbol list above and link to the round-1 +
   round-2 fingerprint.json files as concrete examples.

   Surface: `~/.claude/skills/profiling-software-performance/references/PATTERNS-ENCYCLOPEDIA.md`
   (the skill itself is global; this edit benefits every project,
   not just franken_node).

2. **Add a project-local note** in
   `docs/dev/profiling.md` (created by T11) under a "Reading the
   profiles" section, explaining the bootstrap band and the
   `awk` filter pattern used in round-1 / round-2 to skip it:

   ```bash
   # Filter out bench scaffolding from a perf flat report:
   awk '/^\s+[0-9]+\.[0-9]+%/ {
       sym=$0
       sub(/^.*\] /, "", sym)
       if (sym !~ /^(__ieee754_exp_fma|exp@@GLIBC|__exp_finite|rayon::|crossbeam_)/)
         printf "%6s %s\n", $1, substr(sym,1,100)
   }' profiles/foo.perf.flat.txt | head -20
   ```

3. **Optional: post-processor script** at
   `scripts/render_perf_clean.py` that takes a `*.perf.flat.txt`
   and outputs the user-code-only top-N table. Keep it simple
   (the awk version above is enough for most users).

## Acceptance
