title: [PERF] anti_entropy root digest recompute is quadratic on inserts
description: Measurement: `TrustState::insert_with_capacity()` in `crates/franken-node/src/runtime/anti_entropy.rs:525-560` recomputes the full root digest after every insert. A 2048-record load triggers sum(1..2048)=2098176 record-digest hash updates and 2048 full-map walks, versus about 2048 digest updates for a one-shot or incremental root maintenance path. That is orders of magnitude above the 5 percent bar on the insert hot path. Remediation: keep deterministic ordering and precedence semantics but add batch or incremental root maintenance for reconciliation loads so root hashing happens once per accepted batch instead of once per insert; also gate `anti_entropy_insert_bench` behind the required feature set so default `cargo bench` can prove the win.

title: [IDEA] Create one evidence verification spine across SDK provenance and capsules
description:
Idea-wizard Phase 5 output.

Why this exists:
Open beads show a repeated failure mode: SDK/provenance/evidence surfaces advertise verification while trusting producer-set flags, self-referential hashes, plain SHA-256 pseudo-signatures, or missing chain linkage. Fixing each leaf is necessary, but future drift needs one spine-level contract that says what a verified evidence object means across capsules, provenance links, SDK chains, and verifier-facing APIs.

Existing leaves this bead coordinates:
- bd-j3eip: EvidenceCapsule::verify_all trusts producer-set verified flag.
- bd-n74uz: AttestationLink.signature is plain SHA-256, not a real signature.
- bd-2ycxk: SDK modules advertise Ed25519 verification but perform no signature checks.
- bd-3gpya: verifier_sdk verify_chain has no cryptographic chain linkage.
- bd-2f8zc: verify_artifact hash check is self-referential, not content-based.

What this bead must do:
1. Define a small canonical verification contract for evidence objects: content digest, signer key id, signature algorithm, chain parent binding, and producer-independent verified verdict.
2. Add golden negative fixtures: tampered content, swapped key id, missing parent link, producer-set verified=true with invalid signature.
3. Wire the contract into the SDK/provenance/capsule call sites after prerequisite leaf fixes.
4. Add a registered integration test that runs the same fixture matrix through all public verification surfaces.
5. Document the contract in docs/specs or an artifact so future call sites cannot invent parallel semantics.

Acceptance criteria:
- Every coordinated surface rejects producer assertion without independent verification.
- Fixture matrix covers positive and negative cases with stable JSON evidence.
- `rch`-based focused validation passes or reports exact external blockers.

title: [MEDIUM] Incomplete tenant isolation in RevocationScope and FleetAction
[PROFILE] connector/obligation_tracker.rs: O(n) scans on every reserve/try_reserve via reserved_count_for_flow / evict_oldest_terminal
description:
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/connector/obligation_tracker.rs

PATTERN:
Multiple O(n) full-map walks per single `reserve()` operation while holding the global tracker Mutex:

1. L277-282 `reserved_count_for_flow`:
   `self.obligations.values().filter(|o| o.state == Reserved && &o.flow == flow).count()`
   Called on every `try_reserve` (L428).

2. L284-310 `evict_oldest_terminal_obligation`:
   `self.obligations.iter().filter(...).min_by_key(...)` — O(n) scan + O(n) min, called whenever `obligations.len() >= MAX_OBLIGATIONS` on every reserve attempt (L355).

3. L312-322 `mark_expired_reserved_as_leaked`:
   Filter + clone all leaked IDs, called from `ensure_capacity_for_reserve` periodically.

All three execute while holding `inner: Arc<Mutex<TrackerState>>` (L663). This is a shared single-mutex tracker on the connector hot path.

IMPACT: With MAX_OBLIGATIONS in the multi-thousand range, each reserve at-or-near capacity does O(n) per call (potentially O(3n) when all three trip). Combined with mutex-serialized access this caps single-tracker throughput at roughly `1 / (n * per-entry-cost)` reserves per second.

SUGGESTED FIX:
- Maintain `reserved_per_flow: HashMap<ObligationFlow, usize>` updated on insert/commit/rollback — turns `reserved_count_for_flow` into O(1)
- Maintain `terminal_obligations: BTreeMap<(resolved_at_ms, reserved_at_ms, id), ObligationId>` so `evict_oldest_terminal_obligation` is O(log n) front-pop
- Maintain `reserved_by_deadline: BTreeMap<u64, BTreeSet<ObligationId>>` so leak sweep only walks expired entries (O(k) for k expired, not O(n))

EVIDENCE:
- L277-282 reserved_count_for_flow O(n)
- L284-310 evict_oldest_terminal_obligation O(n)
- L312-322 mark_expired_reserved_as_leaked O(n)
- L373-416 reserve calls ensure_capacity_for_reserve which can trip both eviction and leak sweep
- L663 single Mutex<TrackerState>
close_reason: Completed: obligation tracker reserve hot path now maintains per-flow, deadline, and terminal indexes instead of scanning all obligations.

title: [AUDIT-LOGIC] capability admission lacks trust card validation integration
description:
**Logic Gap**: Capability admission process doesn't validate trust card status, creating potential for revoked extensions to retain valid capability contracts.

**Flow Breakdown**:
1. **Capability Admission**: extensions/artifact_contract.rs:AdmissionGate.evaluate() validates capability contracts against trusted signers (lines 329-628)
2. **Trust Validation**: main.rs:evaluate_run_trust_preflight() checks trust cards via registry.read() (lines 16078-16284) 
3. **Revocation**: Trust cards can be revoked via supply_chain/trust_card.rs:RevocationStatus::Revoked (lines 796-798)

**Gap**: AdmissionGate signature validation (artifact_contract.rs:623) only checks if signer is in config.trusted_signers list, but never cross-references trust card revocation status. If an extension's trust card gets revoked, its previously-admitted capability contract remains valid.

**Attack Scenario**: 
1. Extension gets capability contract admitted (valid signer)
2. Extension's trust card gets revoked due to security incident  
3. Extension retains cached/admitted capability contract despite being untrusted
4. Extension could execute with stale permissions until next admission cycle

**Impact**: Revoked extensions may retain capability permissions longer than intended, defeating revocation-based security controls.
close_reason: 0ac2fd7b extensions/artifact_contract.rs:334-402 AdmissionGate.evaluate() trust validation + test_admission_denies_revoked_trust_card test_admission_denies_quarantined_trust_card test_admission_denies_missing_trust_card_fail_closed test_admission_denies_no_trust_registry_provided_fail_closed

title: [REVIEW] verifier sdk: VerificationResult lost public JSON deserialization
description:
Module: sdk/verifier/src/lib.rs

Finding:
`VerificationResult` now derives `Serialize` but not `Deserialize`, while `sdk/verifier/tests/conformance_harness.rs:1763-1780` still constructs a `VerificationResult` from public JSON using `serde_json::from_value`. That makes the checked-in public JSON surface write-only and breaks harnesses or consumers that need to ingest serialized verifier results.

Why this is a real bug:
- The public JSON shape still advertises `VerificationResult` fields as API-contract data.
- Removing `Deserialize` breaks round-trip use of the public result schema without any replacement type.
- The private `result_origin_nonce` is already hidden with `#[serde(skip, default)]`, so deserialization can remain safe without exposing internal provenance state.

Repro:
1. Serialize a `VerificationResult` with `serde_json::to_value`.
2. Attempt `serde_json::from_value::<VerificationResult>(...)`.
3. Observe failure because `VerificationResult` no longer implements `Deserialize`.

Suggested fix:
Restore `Deserialize` for `VerificationResult` while keeping `result_origin_nonce` skipped/defaulted so public JSON remains round-trippable without leaking the private nonce.

Refs:
- sdk/verifier/src/lib.rs:218
- sdk/verifier/tests/conformance_harness.rs:1763
- sdk/verifier/tests/public_api_contract.rs:285-303
close_reason: Completed

title: [MOCK-AUDIT] verifier public API fixtures encode impossible live values
description:
Module: sdk/verifier/tests/fixtures/public_api/*.json

Finding:
Several verifier public API fixture files now encode values that the live SDK would reject or never emit, which means the frozen JSON set has drifted into placeholder/mock territory.

Evidence:
- `sdk/verifier/tests/fixtures/public_api/facade_result.json:18,20` uses `verifier_identity: "test-verifier-deterministic"` and an `ed25519:` verifier signature, while the live facade requires `verifier://...` identities (`sdk/verifier/src/lib.rs:967-983`) and computes `verifier_signature` with `bundle::hash(&payload)` (`sdk/verifier/src/lib.rs:772-798`).
- `sdk/verifier/tests/fixtures/public_api/transparency_entry.json:4-8` uses `verifier_id: "test-verifier-deterministic"` plus three raw hash strings in `merkle_proof`, while the live transparency format requires `root:...`, `leaf_index:...`, `tree_size:...`, then `left:/right:` siblings (`sdk/verifier/src/lib.rs:200-202,857-893`).
- `sdk/verifier/tests/fixtures/public_api/bundle_canonical.json:13,61` uses a bare verifier name and `signature.algorithm: "ed25519"`, while live bundle verification requires `verifier://...` identities (`sdk/verifier/src/bundle.rs:555-575`) and canonical bundles are sealed with `signature.algorithm = REPLAY_BUNDLE_HASH_ALGORITHM` (`sdk/verifier/src/bundle.rs:397-398`).

Why this is a real bug:
- These files are still documented as frozen public API references, but they now describe impossible outputs rather than the actual verifier surface.
- Any docs/audit/regeneration flow that trusts them will learn the wrong contract.

Suggested fix:
- Regenerate the fixture set from live serializer output and live bundle sealing code, then gate it with executable fixture-based tests.
close_reason: Completed

title: Epic: RCH validation flight recorder and recovery planner
description:
Idea-wizard output: make remote validation proof failures replayable and actionable for large agent swarms.

Background:
- `validation_broker` already models requests, queue entries, receipts, timeout classes, and proof status.
- `rch_adapter` already classifies RCH-E104, missing toolchains, local fallback, filesystem pressure, and contention.
- `validation_proof_coalescer` now covers pre-admission capacity snapshots and lease coalescing.
- Recent work still blocked on opaque remote proof stalls/timeouts, where the operator has to reconstruct worker, queue, timeout, target-dir, and retry context from terminal history.

Goal:
Add a validation flight recorder and deterministic recovery planner that turns each RCH validation attempt into a bounded, redacted, schema-checked artifact with enough context for doctor/readiness/closeout to say what happened and what to do next.

Non-goals:
- Do not replace proof coalescing or admission control. This epic begins after a validation attempt is admitted or running.
- Do not require live RCH in tests. Use replayable captured fixtures and unit/integration coverage.
- Do not treat retryable worker infra failures as product failures or green proof.

Desired user impact:
Operators running many agents get deterministic next actions instead of vague timeouts: reuse an existing proof, wait behind capacity, retry on a different worker, drain/quarantine a worker, switch to source-only blocker evidence, or fail closed with a precise reason.

Acceptance at epic close:
- Flight recorder schemas and fixtures exist and are checked.
- RCH adapter outcomes and validation broker receipts can link to attempt timelines.
- Recovery planning is deterministic and priority-aware.
- Doctor/readiness/closeout output exposes the flight recorder and next action.
- Test coverage includes unit tests, fixture replay, and an E2E-style logged harness with no live remote dependency.

title: [REVIEW] verifier session-step fixture freezes impossible digest formats
description:
Module: sdk/verifier/tests/fixtures/public_api/session_step.json

Finding:
The checked-in SessionStep fixture still encodes pre-hardened digest formats that the live verifier SDK no longer emits.

Evidence:
- session_step.json currently sets artifact_binding_hash to sha256:a1b2... and step_signature to sha256:session-step-signature-fixture.
- sdk/verifier/src/lib.rs stores artifact_binding_hash directly from VerificationResult, and session_step_signature() is derived through bundle::hash(...), which returns bare 64-hex digests without a sha256: prefix.
- public_api_contract only enforces that the fields are strings/non-empty, so this stale fixture can drift indefinitely while still passing current contract checks.

Why this is a real bug:
- The repo presents session_step.json as a public API golden, but it currently shows values the live SDK would never emit.
- Downstream readers and future harness work will inherit the wrong wire format from the frozen fixture.

Suggested fix:
- Refresh session_step.json to use live bare-hex digest/signature formats.
- Strengthen public API fixture checks so session-step goldens validate semantic digest shape, not just serde shape.
close_reason: Completed

title: tests/oracle/n_version_semantic_oracle.rs has 7 dead tests — never registered in Cargo.toml
description:
The integration test file at `tests/oracle/n_version_semantic_oracle.rs` (156 lines, 7 tests for bd-al8i N-version semantic oracle) is NOT wired into the test runner:

  - `crates/franken-node/Cargo.toml:6` sets `autotests = false` — no auto-discovery
  - No `[[test]]` entry in `crates/franken-node/Cargo.toml` references the file
  - No shim file in `crates/franken-node/tests/` uses `#[path]` or `include!` to pull it in
  - Verified by `grep -rnE "tests/oracle|n_version_semantic_oracle"` across both Cargo.toml files and crates/franken-node/tests/ — zero matches

Result: the 7 tests (report_identity_fields_are_correct, report_summary_counts_are_consistent, report_contains_expected_event_codes, report_contains_expected_error_codes, divergence_contract_flags_are_all_true, invariants_include_core_set, checks_are_nonempty_and_well_formed) have never executed in CI or local `cargo test`. The bd-al8i acceptance was claimed without the integration test surface actually running.

Fix (single-line change in crates/franken-node/Cargo.toml):

```toml
[[test]]
name = "n_version_semantic_oracle"
path = "../../tests/oracle/n_version_semantic_oracle.rs"
```

(matches the pattern of other `../../tests/...`-targeted `[[test]]` entries in the same file, e.g. `signed_lineage_graph_builder`, `dgis_immunization_planner`, `security_economy_integration`.)

title: [AUDIT-LOGIC] rollback execution lacks success verification - rollback claims success without validating actual state restoration
description:
**Logic Gap**: Migration rollback execution claims success without verifying actual system state restoration.

**Flow Breakdown**:
1. **Pipeline Rollback**: migration_pipeline.rs:rollback() changes stage to Rollback but only records state transition (lines 754-771)  
2. **Rollback Execution**: operator_intelligence.rs:execute_rollback() calls proof.verify() and logs events (lines 892-914)
3. **Proof Verification**: RollbackProof.verify() only checks structural correctness - empty specs, hash differences, spec format matching (lines 241-261)

**Gap**: No verification that rollback actually succeeded in restoring system to pre_state_hash. RollbackProof.verify() validates proof structure but never confirms the actual system state matches the expected pre_state_hash after rollback execution.

**Attack Scenario**:
1. Migration rollback initiated due to verification failure
2. Rollback proof passes structural validation  
3. Rollback execution reports success without state verification
4. System remains in corrupted/partial state while claiming successful rollback
5. Next migration cycle may build on corrupted baseline

**Impact**: Failed rollbacks can be masked as successful, leaving system in undefined state and compromising migration pipeline integrity.

title: Preserve fleet safe-start invariant at request boundary
description:
Why this exists:
`crates/franken-node/src/api/fleet_quarantine.rs` documents `INV-FLEET-SAFE-START` and the manager methods correctly reject mutation operations while unactivated, but the request-path owner currently calls `mgr.activate()` immediately before every mutation handler (`quarantine`, `revoke`, `release`, `reconcile`). That means the public request boundary silently bypasses the read-only safe-start invariant instead of enforcing it.

What this bug must do:
1. Remove request-path auto-activation from the shared owner so mutation handlers fail closed while the manager is still in safe-start.
2. Preserve read-only `status` behavior before activation.
3. Add focused handler tests that prove mutation handlers reject while unactivated.
4. Add or adjust focused tests that show handler mutation succeeds only after explicit activation in test setup, rather than implicit activation as a side effect of the request.
5. Run focused Rust validation through `rch` only.

Acceptance criteria:
1. `handle_quarantine`, `handle_revoke`, `handle_release`, and `handle_reconcile` no longer activate the manager implicitly.
2. Unactivated handler calls return an error carrying `FLEET_NOT_ACTIVATED` instead of succeeding.

title: Fix audit chain signature exclusion in approval_workflow — tamper-evident hash ignores signature field
[REASONING] EvidenceCapsule::verify_all trusts producer-set 'verified' flag
description:
LENS: Data-flow / type-driven
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/vef/evidence_capsule.rs:118-158 (verify_all), 40-48 (VefEvidence)
CONCERN: VefEvidence is a public struct with 'pub verified: bool' set by the producer of the capsule. EvidenceCapsule::verify_all counts evidence as 'passed' iff ev.verified is true and the commitment/proof_id strings are non-empty. There is no re-derivation against receipt_chain_commitment, no signature check, no replay against the proof_type. A capsule producer that marks every entry verified=true and supplies any non-empty commitment string trivially satisfies INV-EVIDENCE-CAPSULE-VERIFIABLE.
WHY IT MATTERS: This is the classic 'trust the producer's claim' anti-pattern. Anyone holding a serialized EvidenceCapsule can hand-craft one with verified=true; consumers calling verify_all get a CapsuleVerificationResult { valid: true, ... } that means nothing. Downstream code that gates on capsule.verify_all().valid silently admits forged evidence.
SUGGESTED REMEDIATION: Either (a) make 'verified' a non-public, derived field set only by an internal verifier that re-checks receipt_chain_commitment against a trust anchor / chain head; (b) require verify_all to take a verifier closure or a TrustContext and re-derive the verdict from receipt_chain_commitment + proof_type without consulting ev.verified; or (c) rename the existing call to integrity_check() and add a separate cryptographic verify(trust_anchor) that returns the verdict. Add an adversarial test: construct an EvidenceCapsule with verified=true and a random receipt_chain_commitment, assert verify(trust_anchor) returns valid=false.
close_reason: Completed: verify_all fails closed without verifier context; explicit context verifies canonical commitments and accepted proof types without trusting producer verified flag.

title: [REASONING] threshold_sig signing message omits artifact_id and connector_id
description:
LENS: Adversarial / Threat-modeler
FILE: crates/franken-node/src/security/threshold_sig.rs:404-412 (build_signing_message), 423-441 (SigningMessage::new), 568-569 (verify_signature)
CONCERN: The signing preimage is 'SIGNING_MESSAGE_DOMAIN || u64_le(content_hash.len()) || content_hash'. Neither PublicationArtifact.artifact_id nor PublicationArtifact.connector_id is hashed into the message. Two artifacts that happen to share the same content_hash (deduplicated payload, identical canonical bytes, or attacker-chosen collision in a higher-level naming scheme) can have signatures interchanged. A signer who authorized publication for connector A can have their partial signature replayed under connector B's PublicationArtifact, and verify_threshold will accept it because key_lookup is global per-config and content_hash matches.
WHY IT MATTERS: Quorum is meant to authorize a *publication*, not just a payload. If the same payload is published in two contexts (e.g. canary vs prod, tenant A vs tenant B) by the same signer set, signatures cross-replay between contexts. The metamorphic test 'Cross-content rejection' in tests/threshold_sig_quorum_metamorphic.rs only varies content_hash; it does not catch this because the test never varies artifact_id/connector_id with constant content_hash.
SUGGESTED REMEDIATION: Extend build_signing_message to length-prefix and concatenate artifact_id and connector_id (and optionally a config_hash) before content_hash, with a new domain separator 'threshold_sig_v2:'. Add a metamorphic property: 'partial signatures produced for (artifact_id=A, content=H) MUST NOT count for (artifact_id=B, content=H)'. Provide a migration/version field in PublicationArtifact so v1 messages can be rejected once v2 is rolled out.
close_reason: Bound threshold signatures to artifact_id and connector_id with context replay regression coverage

title: [10.10] Enforce product-level adoption of canonical deterministic serialization and signature preimage rules (from `10.13` + `10.14`).
description:
Master Plan Source: PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_NODE.md — Section 10.10 (FCP-Inspired Hardening), cross-ref Section 9E.2

## Why This Exists

Enhancement Map 9E.2 identifies that without deterministic serialization and strict signature preimage contracts, any trust artifact (operator receipts, policy checkpoints, delegation tokens) can be silently re-encoded in ways that break signature verification across kernel boundaries. This bead enforces product-level adoption of the canonical serialization and preimage rules defined in Sections 10.13 (FCP trust primitives) and 10.14 (append-only marker streams), ensuring that every signed object produced by franken_node serializes to exactly one byte sequence for any given logical value. Without this discipline, the three-kernel architecture (franken_engine + asupersync + franken_node) cannot exchange signed artifacts reliably, and operators lose the ability to independently verify receipts — breaking the category-defining evidence-by-default guarantee.

## What This Must Do

1. Define a `CanonicalSerializer` trait (or equivalent module boundary) that enforces deterministic field ordering, no-float, length-prefixed encoding, and domain-separated tag bytes for every product trust object type (policy checkpoints, delegation tokens, revocation assertions, session tickets, zone boundary claims).
2. Implement a `SignaturePreimage` builder that constructs the exact byte sequence to be signed/verified, including version prefix, domain-separation tag, and canonical payload — rejecting any non-canonical input at the API boundary.
3. Integrate with the golden vector corpus from 10.13 (bd-3n2u) so that every serialization path is verified against reference test vectors on every CI run.
4. Add a compile-time or module-init assertion that no product code path can produce a signed artifact without routing through the canonical serializer — no bypass paths allowed.
5. Provide a `round_trip_canonical(obj) -> Result<obj>` function that serializes, deserializes, and re-serializes to prove byte-level stability, used as the standard verification primitive across all downstream beads in 10.10.
6. Emit structured log events (`CANONICAL_SERIALIZE`, `PREIMAGE_CONSTRUCT`, `CANONICAL_REJECT`) with the object type, domain tag, byte length, and truncated content hash for audit trail.

## Context from Enhancement Maps

- 9E.2: "Deterministic serialization and signature preimage contracts for operator receipts"
- 9A.3 (Observability): Stable error codes and structured logging across all trust-critical paths support diagnosis when serialization mismatches occur.
- 9D.1 (Interop): Golden vector conformance ensures cross-implementation compatibility of signed artifacts.

## Dependencies

- Upstream: bd-3n2u ([10.13] Publish formal schema spec files and golden vectors for serialization, signatures, and control-channel frames) — provides the reference vectors and schema definitions this bead enforces at the product level.
- Upstream: bd-1l5 ([10.10] Define canonical product trust object IDs with domain separation) — provides the domain-separation tag registry that the signature preimage builder consumes.
- Downstream: bd-174 ([10.10] Implement policy checkpoint chain for product release channels) — depends on canonical serialization for checkpoint integrity.
- Downstream: bd-1jjq ([10.10] Section-wide verification gate) — aggregates verification evidence from this bead.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. All product trust object types (minimum 6: policy checkpoint, delegation token, revocation assertion, session ticket, zone boundary claim, operator receipt) have registered canonical serialization schemas with golden vector coverage.
2. `round_trip_canonical()` passes for every registered object type with zero byte-level divergence across 1000 randomized property-test inputs.
3. The golden vector test suite from 10.13 (bd-3n2u) passes with 100% vector coverage — no skipped or ignored vectors.
4. Attempting to sign any object without routing through `CanonicalSerializer` produces a compile-time error or panics at module-init with a clear diagnostic message.
5. `SignaturePreimage` output is byte-identical across Rust (franken_node), and any future Python/TypeScript verification tooling, proven by cross-language golden vector checks.
6. Structured log events are emitted for every serialize/preimage/reject operation with stable event codes and trace correlation IDs.
7. No floating-point values appear anywhere in serialized trust artifacts (enforced by type system or runtime assertion).
8. Verification evidence JSON artifact passes the section 10.10 gate schema with all fields populated.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: Property-based round-trip tests for each object type (use `proptest` or equivalent). Edge cases: empty fields, maximum-length fields, unicode boundary values, nested structures. Verify that re-ordering struct fields in source code does not change serialized output.
- Integration tests: Cross-validate serialized output against golden vectors from `vectors/` directory. Verify that `SignaturePreimage` output matches reference preimages byte-for-byte. Test that a signature produced by one kernel can be verified by another kernel's deserializer.

Feed malformed/non-canonical byte sequences and verify clean rejection with correct error codes. Test length-prefix overflow and truncation attacks.

acceptance_criteria:

The canonical form MUST sort map keys lexicographically, use fixed-width integer encoding (big-endian), and omit optional fields that are None (not encode them as null).
2. Define a SignaturePreimage struct wrapping: (a) a 4-byte context tag identifying the signing context (e.g., POLICY_SIGN, TOKEN_SIGN, RELEASE_SIGN), (b) canonical_bytes of the payload, (c) a 32-byte domain-separation salt unique per context tag. The preimage is the concatenation of these three fields.

PERF: api fleet_control_routes lease operations allocate heavily per request
description:
**Hot path**: Fleet control API handlers → lease operations per HTTP request
**File**: `crates/franken-node/src/api/fleet_control_routes.rs:472-549, 282-286`

**Current allocation patterns**:
```rust
// list_leases handler (line 478)
state.active_leases()  // -> clones all lease objects

// active_leases method (lines 282-286)  
.map(|stored| stored.lease.clone())  // clone per lease
.collect()

// acquire_lease handler (lines 524-538)
let lease_id = state.next_lease_id(&trace.trace_id);  // format! per ID
lease_id: lease_id.clone(),           // clone ID
holder: identity.principal.clone(),   // clone principal  
resource: resource.clone(),           // clone resource
acquired_at: now.to_rfc3339(),       // String allocation
expires_at: expires_at.to_rfc3339(), // String allocation
lease: lease.clone(),                 // clone entire lease for storage
```

**Multiple allocation sites per request**:
- GET /v1/fleet/leases: N lease clones per request (line 478 → 285)
- POST /v1/fleet/leases: 8+ allocations per lease acquisition
- Error paths: format!() + trace_id.clone() per error (lines 505, 516-520)
- ID generation: format!() per lease/coordination ID (lines 256, 272)

**Fix**: Use references where possible, pre-allocate ID strings with capacity, avoid defensive cloning in hot paths

**Before**: N clones per list + 8+ allocations per acquire  
**After**: Minimize clones, use Cow<> or references for read paths

**Impact**: Reduces allocation churn in fleet management API hot path - lease acquisition/listing operations.

**Message Claims:**
- "SECURITY: Configure all rate limiters as fail-closed to prevent DoS on failure"
- "Operator/Verifier endpoint groups now use fail_closed: true"
- "Health endpoint now protected against DoS amplification attacks"

- sdk/verifier/src/bundle.rs (derive annotations)

🔲 Audit last 50 commits for similar message/content mismatches

**Severity: P0** - False security claims create compliance and operational risk.

title: [8] Architecture Blueprint — 3-kernel design, 10 invariants, 5 alignment contracts
description:
Master Plan Source: PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_NODE.md — Section 8

## Why This Exists
This captures the full architecture blueprint including repository topology, product planes, control planes, three-kernel architecture, 10 hard runtime invariants, and 5 alignment contracts. All implementation must conform to this architecture.

## Repository and Package Topology (8.1)
- Engine: /dp/franken_engine (crates/franken-engine, crates/franken-extension-host)
- Product: /dp/franken_node (crates/franken-node)
- Adjacent substrates: /dp/frankentui, /dp/frankensqlite, /dp/sqlmodel_rust, /dp/fastapi_rust

## Product Planes (8.2)
1. Compatibility plane: Node/Bun behavior surfaces and divergence governance
2. Migration plane: discovery, risk scoring, automated rewrites, rollout guidance
3. Trust plane: policy controls, trust cards, revocation and quarantine UX
4. Ecosystem plane: registry, reputation graph, certification channels
5. Operations plane: fleet control, audit/replay export, benchmark verifier interfaces

## Control Planes (8.3)
1. Release control plane: staged rollout, rollback, feature-policy gating
2. Incident control plane: replay, counterfactual simulation, response automation
3. Economics control plane: expected-loss and attack-cost aware policy guidance

## Three-Kernel Architecture (8.4)
- Execution kernel: /dp/franken_engine (language/runtime internals)
- Correctness/control kernel: /dp/asupersync (concurrency, cancellation, remote effects, epochs, evidence)
- Product kernel: /dp/franken_node (compatibility, migration, trust UX, ecosystem capture)

## 10 Hard Runtime Invariants (8.5, Non-Negotiable)
1. Cx-first control APIs — all high-impact async ops take &Cx
2. Region-owned lifecycle execution — region close implies quiescence
3. Cancellation protocol semantics — request -> drain -> finalize, not task-drop
4. Two-phase effects for high-impact operations — reserve/commit with obligation guarantees
5. Scheduler lane discipline — Cancel/Timed/Ready lanes with starvation protection
6. Remote effects contract — capability-gated, named, idempotent, saga-safe
7. Epoch and transition barriers — epoch-scoped, barrier-mediated transitions
8. Evidence-by-default decisions — deterministic evidence ledger with trace witnesses
9. Deterministic protocol verification gates — lab, cancellation injection, schedule exploration
10. No ambient authority — any ambient network/spawn/privileged side effect is a defect

## 5 Alignment Contracts (8.8)
1. Scope boundary: franken_node defines policy/orchestration/verification; engine internals stay in franken_engine
2. Terminology: "extension" is primary; "connector/provider" maps to extension integration class
3. Dual-oracle: L1 product oracle (Node/Bun/franken_node) + L2 engine boundary oracle
4. Path convention: src/ paths are crate-root relative; docs/ paths are repo-root relative
5. KPI clarity: primary KPI is migration-friction collapse with safety + verifier-backed trust guarantees

## Implementation Mapping
- 8.4-8.6 (Asupersync): Tracked in 10.15
- 8.7 (Adjacent substrates): Tracked in 10.16
- 8.5 invariants: Enforced across 10.13, 10.14, 10.15
- 8.8 alignment: Enforced across all sections

## Acceptance Criteria
- Three-kernel boundaries are enforced by CI
- All 10 runtime invariants have conformance tests
- All 5 alignment contracts are machine-enforceable
- Architecture deviations require signed waiver artifacts


## Success Criteria
- Three-kernel boundaries are encoded in actionable planning constraints and reflected in dependency structure.
- All 10 hard runtime invariants have explicit ownership and verification hooks in downstream tracks.
- All 5 alignment contracts are operationally testable and auditable in planning and implementation gates.

## Testing & Logging Requirements
- Unit tests for architecture-contract validation helpers and invariant-mapping checks.
- E2E architecture-conformance scripts validating cross-kernel boundary compliance across representative workflows.
- Structured logs for architecture scans, invariant violations, and alignment-contract drift diagnostics.

title: [VALAUTO.2] Implement source-only validation-autopilot planner
description:
## What
Implement the source-only planner that reads tracker actionability, blocked freshness, RCH-normalized evidence, and optional Agent Mail handoff metadata, then emits the validation-autopilot decision document defined by VALAUTO.1.

## Why
The repo already has strong component validators, but agents still need a single deterministic planner that chooses the next safe action when br ready is empty or ambiguous. This should be cheap enough to run during every no-ready turn without touching cargo.

## How
Prefer a Python checker under scripts/ with fixture-backed tests under tests/. Compose existing helpers rather than duplicating logic. Accept JSON files or stdin-friendly paths for br ready/list, bv plan/priority/insights, blocked freshness, RCH evidence, and handoff metadata. Emit stable JSON plus a concise human summary. Fail closed on malformed input, stale first-blocker evidence, unknown action kinds, or missing rch prefixes for heavy commands.

## Risks
Do not parse arbitrary command output with brittle regex when existing JSON validators can be reused. Do not mutate Beads, Agent Mail, or files; this planner should be read-only.

## Success Criteria
Unit tests cover ready claim, no-ready create-followup, stale blocker refresh, RCH timeout retry, cross-repo external blocker handoff, and parent-epic non-claimability. The script has --self-test and --json modes, passes py_compile/unittest/git diff --check, and touched-file UBS is run through rch if the validation bundle includes it.

description:
Master Plan Source: PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_NODE.md
Section: 10.6 — Performance + Packaging (Item 1 of 7)
Cross-references: 9D global rule, Section 14 benchmark families

Why This Exists:
The product-level benchmark suite validates that franken_node meets performance targets under realistic security-hardened conditions. This is the foundation for all public benchmark claims and the benchmark ownership strategy (10.0 Initiative #10).

Task Objective:
Build a comprehensive product-level benchmark suite covering all major workflow categories with secure-extension scenarios (not just vanilla performance).

Detailed Acceptance Criteria:
1. Benchmark scenarios cover: cold-start latency, p99 tail latency, extension-host overhead with sandbox active, migration scanner throughput, lockstep harness throughput, quarantine propagation latency, trust-card materialization latency.
2. Secure-extension scenarios: benchmarks run with sandbox enforcement active (not bypassed), measuring realistic overhead.
3. Deterministic benchmarking: identical inputs produce statistically equivalent results across runs (within confidence intervals).
4. Benchmark results include confidence intervals and reproducibility metadata per 9C.10.
5. Results exported in machine-readable format for CI/release gating and public reporting.
6. Baseline profiling methodology: baseline first, profile top hotspots, one lever per change, validate invariance, re-measure with tail metrics (9D global rule).
7. All 14 metric families from Section 14 represented: compatibility correctness, performance under hardening, containment latency, replay determinism, migration speed, adversarial resilience.

Expected Artifacts:
- benchmarks/ directory with harness, scenarios, fixture data, and scoring formulas.
- CI integration for automated benchmark runs with regression detection.
- docs/specs/section_10_6/bd-k4s_contract.md

Testing and Logging Requirements:

- E2E benchmark execution scripts that run representative secure-extension scenarios and emit reproducible result bundles.
- Benchmark suite self-test: harness produces deterministic results on fixture data.
- Regression detection: automatic flagging when metrics degrade beyond threshold.
- Structured logs: BENCHMARK_STARTED, SCENARIO_EXECUTED, METRIC_COMPUTED, REGRESSION_DETECTED with trace IDs and scenario metadata.

title: [10.8] Implement deterministic safe-mode startup and operation flags.
description:
## [10.8] Implement deterministic safe-mode startup and operation flags

### Why This Exists

When franken_node encounters a compromised trust state, repeated crash loops, or epoch mismatches, it needs a well-defined fallback posture that maximizes safety while preserving basic operability. Without a formal safe-mode specification, failure recovery is ad-hoc: operators manually disable features, restart with undocumented flags, and hope for the best. Section 10.8 (Operational Readiness) requires that safe mode be a first-class operational state with deterministic entry conditions, explicit capability restrictions, and a verified exit path back to normal operation.

### What It Must Do

Safe mode is a reduced-functionality operating state where franken_node runs only essential services with maximum safety guarantees. The implementation must cover:

- **Entry triggers**: Safe mode activates via three paths: (a) explicit flag `--safe-mode` at startup, (b) environment variable `FRANKEN_SAFE_MODE=1`, (c) config field `safe_mode: true`, or (d) automatic activation when the runtime detects trust state corruption, three or more crash loops within a configurable window, or an epoch mismatch between local state and federation peers.
- **Capability restrictions**: In safe mode, all non-essential extensions are suspended (not loaded), network listeners are restricted to health and admin endpoints only, no new trust delegations are issued, and all write operations to the trust ledger require explicit operator confirmation.
- **Trust re-verification**: On safe-mode entry, the trust state is verified from scratch against the evidence ledger. Any inconsistencies are logged as incidents and flagged for operator review. The re-verification result is persisted as a safe-mode entry receipt.
- **Maximum verbosity logging**: All operations in safe mode are logged at TRACE level with full context, including every decision point, every skipped capability, and every trust check result. This ensures post-incident forensics have complete data.
- **Exit protocol**: Leaving safe mode requires explicit operator action (not automatic). The exit protocol verifies that: trust state is consistent, no unresolved incidents exist, and the operator acknowledges the transition. Exit is logged as an auditable event.
- **Status reporting**: A dedicated health endpoint and CLI command (`franken_node status --safe-mode`) reports current safe-mode state, entry reason, time in safe mode, and list of suspended capabilities.

### Acceptance Criteria

1. `--safe-mode` flag, `FRANKEN_SAFE_MODE=1` env var, and `safe_mode: true` config all deterministically activate safe mode at startup, verified by integration tests.
2. Automatic safe-mode activation triggers on trust state corruption, crash loop detection (configurable threshold, default 3 crashes in 60 seconds), and epoch mismatch — each trigger path has a dedicated test.
3. In safe mode, non-essential extensions are not loaded, and attempting to load one returns a structured error with recovery hint.
4. Trust state re-verification runs on safe-mode entry and produces a persisted receipt with pass/fail status and details of any inconsistencies found.
5. All safe-mode operations are logged at TRACE level; log output in safe mode is at least 3x more verbose than normal mode for equivalent operations.
6. Exiting safe mode requires explicit operator action and passes a pre-exit verification checklist; automatic exit is not possible.
7. `franken_node status --safe-mode` returns structured JSON with entry reason, duration, and suspended capability list.
8. A drill test simulates each automatic trigger condition and verifies correct safe-mode entry and behavior.

### Key Dependencies

- Trust state model (state_model.rs, fencing.rs) for corruption detection
- Health gate infrastructure (health_gate.rs) for safe-mode health endpoint
- CLI infrastructure (cli.rs) for `--safe-mode` flag and status command
- Config system (config.rs) for `safe_mode` config field
- Crash loop detection requires process supervisor integration or self-monitoring

### Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests for each entry trigger path and the exit protocol.
- Integration tests that simulate crash loops and epoch mismatches.
- Verification script (`scripts/check_safe_mode.py`) with `--json` output and `self_test()`.
- Safe-mode log entries must include a `safe_mode: true` field for filtering.

### Expected Artifacts

- `docs/specs/section_10_8/bd-k6o_contract.md` — safe-mode specification
- `scripts/check_safe_mode.py` — verification script
- `tests/test_check_safe_mode.py` — unit tests
- `artifacts/section_10_8/bd-k6o/verification_evidence.json`
- `artifacts/section_10_8/bd-k6o/verification_summary.md`
acceptance_criteria:
1. Safe-mode startup: when --safe-mode flag is passed (or FRANKEN_SAFE_MODE=1 env var is set), the node starts with a minimal, hardened configuration that disables all non-essential features.
2. Safe-mode operation is deterministic: given identical inputs, safe-mode produces identical outputs across runs (no randomness, no wall-clock dependencies).
3. Safe-mode disables: extension loading, network-initiated migrations, auto-update checks, and any feature flagged as experimental.
4. Safe-mode enables: enhanced logging (debug level), integrity self-checks on startup, and read-only mode for mutable state stores.
5. A health-check endpoint in safe-mode reports which features are disabled and why.
6. Transition from safe-mode to normal-mode requires explicit operator action — no automatic escalation.
7. Integration test verifies safe-mode startup, exercises core workflows, and confirms disabled features are unreachable.

description:

- Program/section verification gates must be able to consume this bead's outputs without manual interpretation.

Why This Improves User Outcomes:
- "[14] Metric family: performance under hardening" is required to reduce operator error, increase deterministic safety guarantees, and improve time-to-diagnosis for failures in real-world workflows.

acceptance_criteria:
METRIC FAMILY: Performance under hardening.
1. Metrics measured: p50, p95, p99 latency (ms); throughput (requests/sec); cold start time (ms); overhead ratio (hardened/unhardened).
2. Measured under 3 hardening profiles: permissive (minimal hardening), balanced (recommended), strict (maximum hardening).
3. Workloads: (a) HTTP request/response (JSON serialization), (b) file I/O (read/write 1MB), (c) crypto operations (AES-256-GCM encrypt/decrypt), (d) stream processing (pipe 10MB through transform), (e) cold start (time to first response).
4. Overhead gates: balanced profile overhead <= 15% vs unhardened; strict profile overhead documented but not gated.
5. Cold start gate: balanced profile cold start <= 500ms on reference hardware.
6. Benchmark is run on defined reference hardware (documented CPU, RAM, OS) for reproducibility.
7. Publication: all metrics included in benchmark report with statistical confidence intervals (>= 10 runs per workload).
8. Evidence: performance_under_hardening.json with per-profile, per-workload, per-percentile metrics.

title: [10.0] Implement benchmark + standard ownership stack.
description:
Master Plan Source: PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_NODE.md
Section: 10.0 — Top 10 Initiative Tracking (Initiative #10)
Cross-references: 9A.10, 9B.10, 9C.10, 9D.10

Why This Exists:
Benchmark and standard ownership is the #10 strategic initiative. It defines and maintains the benchmark and verification standards for secure extension runtime quality, then makes external adoption part of product strategy. Owning the benchmark category means franken_node defines what "good" looks like for the industry.

Task Objective:
Build the benchmark and standardization ownership stack: define benchmark suites, publish verification standards, create verifier toolkits for independent validation, and establish the category-defining measurement infrastructure.

Detailed Acceptance Criteria:
1. Public benchmark suite covering: compatibility correctness by API/risk band, performance under hardening, containment/revocation latency, replay determinism, migration speed, adversarial resilience (14 metric families).
2. Benchmark specs/harness/datasets/scoring formulas published openly with reproducibility guarantees (14).
3. Verifier toolkit for independent validation of all benchmark claims (14).
4. Conformance vectors + external verifier contracts to force reproducible claim standards (9B.10).
5. Statistical rigor: confidence intervals, reproducibility guarantees, verifier receipts for headline claims (9C.10).
6. Benchmark runner determinism and throughput optimized without weakening rigor (9D.10).
7. Version benchmark standards with migration guidance for standard evolution (14).
8. Security and trust co-metrics included alongside performance metrics (14).

Key Dependencies:
- Depends on all other initiatives for benchmark subject matter.
- Consumed by 10.9 (Moonshot) for public benchmark campaign infrastructure.
- Consumed by 10.12 (Frontier) for demo gates with external reproducibility requirements.
- Consumed by 16 (Scientific Contributions) for reproducible technical reports.

Expected Artifacts:
- Benchmark suite with harness, datasets, scoring formulas in benchmarks/ directory.
- Verifier toolkit SDK and CLI.
- Published benchmark specifications.
- docs/specs/section_10_0/bd-khy_contract.md
- artifacts/section_10_0/bd-khy/verification_evidence.json

Testing and Logging Requirements:
- Unit tests: scoring formula correctness, metric computation, determinism validation.
- Integration tests: full benchmark run on fixture workloads producing reproducible scores.
- E2E tests: franken-node bench run CLI producing benchmark report with all metric families.
- Reproducibility tests: same benchmark inputs produce identical scores across runs.
- Structured logs: BENCHMARK_STARTED, METRIC_COMPUTED, SCORE_FINALIZED, VERIFIER_RECEIPT_GENERATED with trace IDs and metric breakdown.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Benchmark suite covers all 4 category targets from Section 3: >= 95% compatibility, >= 3x migration velocity, >= 10x compromise reduction, 100% replay coverage.
2. Each benchmark has: defined methodology, input corpus, measurement procedure, baseline value, target value, and pass/fail threshold.
3. Benchmark results are reproducible: same input corpus and environment produces results within <= 2% variance across 5 consecutive runs.
4. Verification standards define: what constitutes passing evidence, required artifact format, minimum test coverage, and review process for each category.
5. Standard ownership map (10.N cross-reference): each benchmark and standard has a designated canonical owner track; ownership is machine-readable and queryable.
6. External adoption readiness: benchmark definitions published in standalone format (Markdown + JSON schema) suitable for third-party consumption without internal tooling dependencies.
7. Regression detection: CI runs benchmark suite on each release candidate; regression beyond threshold triggers release-gate block and owner notification.
8. Historical tracking: benchmark results stored in append-only time-series; trend visualization available via JSON API (data points: date, version, score, pass/fail).
9. Cross-initiative validation: benchmark suite validates deliverables from all other 9 initiatives (bd-1qp through bd-2g0); each initiative has >= 1 dedicated benchmark.
10. Verification evidence includes: benchmark suite execution report, reproducibility variance measurement, standard ownership map snapshot, regression detection test with intentional regression injection.

Section: 12

Task Objective:
Implement deterministic replay and degraded-mode contract enforcement for trust-system complexity risk.

Execution Requirements:
- Make this requirement machine-verifiable and release-gated where applicable.
- Keep behavior self-documenting so future contributors do not need to re-open the master plan.

Testing & Logging Requirements:
- Unit tests for rule/contract logic and error conditions.
- Integration/E2E tests for workflow-level enforcement.
- Structured logs with stable codes and trace IDs.
- Reproducible artifacts that prove contract satisfaction.

Acceptance Criteria:
- Success and failure invariants for [12] Risk control: trust-system complexity are explicitly quantified and machine-verifiable.
- Determinism requirements for [12] Risk control: trust-system complexity are validated across repeated runs and adversarial perturbations.


Expected Artifacts:
- Machine-readable verification artifact with explicit canonical path under artifacts/section_12/bd-kiqr/verification_evidence.json, suitable for CI/release gating.
- Human-readable verification summary with explicit canonical path under artifacts/section_12/bd-kiqr/verification_summary.md, linking implementation intent to measured validation outcomes.

Task-Specific Clarification:
- The implementation must deliver the exact capability named in the title, with no scope dilution and no silent feature omission.
- Validation artifacts must include capability-specific thresholds, pass/fail criteria, and reproducible evidence bundles tied to this bead ID.
- Program/section verification gates must be able to consume this bead's outputs without manual interpretation.

Why This Improves User Outcomes:
- "[12] Risk control: trust-system complexity" is required to reduce operator error, increase deterministic safety guarantees, and improve time-to-diagnosis for failures in real-world workflows.
- Explicit success/failure evidence for "[12] Risk control: trust-system complexity" prevents false confidence and improves trust in migration/compatibility/security outcomes.
- Detailed unit + integration/E2E + structured logging requirements ensure reproducible quality and faster incident remediation for users.
acceptance_criteria:
RISK: Trust-system complexity — the trust subsystem becomes so complex that reasoning about its behavior is impossible, leading to subtle security gaps.
IMPACT: Undetectable trust violations, inability to audit trust decisions, security incidents from logic errors in trust evaluation.
COUNTERMEASURES:
  (a) Deterministic replay: every trust decision is replayable from a recorded input state, producing identical output.
  (b) Degraded-mode contracts: explicit specification of trust-system behavior when components fail (e.g., default-deny, cached decisions with TTL).
  (c) Trust decision logging: every trust evaluation logs input, decision, reasoning chain, and timestamp.
VERIFICATION:
  1. Deterministic replay test: record N trust decisions, replay them, verify bit-identical outputs for >= 99.9% of cases.
  2. Degraded-mode test: simulate trust-component failure; verify system falls back to specified degraded behavior (not undefined).
  3. Trust decision audit log is complete — no trust evaluation occurs without a log entry.
  4. Trust logic has < 500 lines of core decision code (complexity budget).
TEST SCENARIOS:
  - Scenario A: Replay 1000 recorded trust decisions; verify 100% deterministic reproduction.
  - Scenario B: Kill the trust-evaluation service; verify degraded-mode contract activates (default-deny within 1s).
  - Scenario C: Inject a novel trust input not in training data; verify it is logged and handled by fallback policy.
close_reason: done

comments.text: 2026-07-24 CrimsonCrane, verified by reading. control_plane/control_epoch.rs:160-191. EpochTransition::compute_mac hashes b'control_epoch_mac_v1:' plus the fields with plain SHA-256 and NO key — the doc comment says so outright ('In production, this would use HMAC-SHA256 with a signing key'). verify() ct_eq's against a value anyone can recompute, so any party can mint EpochTransition{old_epoch:5, new_epoch:1_000_000, ...} with a valid event_mac. INV-EPOCH-SIGNED-EVENT is vacuous, and tests/e2e_control_epoch_lifecycle.rs:126,136,164,201 assert it holds, so green tests actively mask the gap. In-tree verify() callers are currently tests/harnesses only, so this is a latent authenticity hole rather than a live bypass — but the primitive is pub and is the 'signed event' the epoch invariants rest on. Deliberately NOT patched blind: it changes a public signature plus e2e expectations and must land with runnable tests.

Keep the key type infallible at the EpochStore constructors so call sites stay clean: EpochSigningKey::new(material) -> Result<_, EpochError>, then EpochStore::new(key) / EpochStore::recover(epoch, key) infallible. comments.text: 2026-07-28 CrimsonCrane — SUPERSEDES my earlier 'not fixed this session' note: the prerequisite cleared and this IS now implemented. Removing the stale root [patch.crates-io] (bd-3mj98) made the canonical inline lane compilable again ('rch exec -- env RUSTFLAGS="--cfg franken_node_inline_tests" cargo test -p frankenengine-node --lib --features extended-surfaces,test-support'), which was the stated blocker, so the ~40 inline call sites are no longer unverifiable. title: Implement swarm resource governor telemetry and backoff budgets
description:
## Scope
Expose resource-governor telemetry that tells agents and operators when to run, defer, or dedupe expensive validation. The initial target is cargo/RCH process contention, but the model should generalize to CPU, memory, queue depth, target-dir pressure, and active proof classes.

title: Reality-check concurrency: top-5 highest-confidence TOCTOU vulnerabilities in production paths
description:
**TOP 5 PRODUCTION TOCTOU VULNERABILITIES**

**1. storage/cleanup_receipts.rs:260** - Receipt deletion TOCTOU  
`if metadata.file_path.exists() { fs::remove_file(&metadata.file_path) }`  
**Exploit:** Concurrent deletion between exists() check and remove_file() causes spurious errors  
**Fix:** Use `fs::remove_file().or_else(|e| if e.kind() == NotFound { Ok(()) } else { Err(e) })` pattern

**2. storage/cleanup_receipts.rs:120** - Storage directory creation TOCTOU  
`if !storage_dir.exists() { fs::create_dir_all(&storage_dir) }`  
**Exploit:** Concurrent creation between check and create_dir_all causes AlreadyExists errors  
**Fix:** Use `fs::create_dir_all().or_else(|e| if e.kind() == AlreadyExists { Ok(()) } else { Err(e) })` pattern

**3. storage/cleanup_receipts.rs:354** - Index loading TOCTOU  
`if index_path.exists() { fs::read_to_string(&index_path) }`  
**Exploit:** Concurrent deletion between exists() check and read causes NotFound errors  
**Fix:** Direct read with error handling: `fs::read_to_string().or_else(|e| if e.kind() == NotFound { Ok(String::new()) } else { Err(e) })`

**4. migration/mod.rs:2350** - Backup directory creation TOCTOU  
`if !backup_root.exists() { std::fs::create_dir(&backup_root) }`  
**Exploit:** Concurrent creation causes AlreadyExists errors in backup preparation  
**Fix:** Use `create_dir().or_else()` pattern with AlreadyExists tolerance

**5. migration/mod.rs:2382** - Incremental path creation TOCTOU  
`if !current_path.exists() { std::fs::create_dir(&current_path) }`  
**Exploit:** Concurrent creation during incremental backup path setup  
**Fix:** Use `create_dir().or_else()` pattern with AlreadyExists tolerance

**Pattern:** All use exists() + file_operation instead of atomic error-handled operations. Replace with direct operations + appropriate error handling for NotFound/AlreadyExists.

title: Migrate replay_bundle integrity + signature to crate::crypto::Ed25519Scheme (bd-18dd1 follow-on)
description:
**Parent design**: `docs/specs/crypto_trait_abstraction.md` (bd-18dd1, closed 2026-04-27).

**Current state.** `crates/franken-node/src/tools/replay_bundle.rs` builds `.fnbundle` artifacts (the wire format the verifier SDK consumes). The SDK side at `sdk/verifier/src/bundle.rs` already has its own `sign_bundle`, `verify_signed_bundle`, `verify_ed25519_signature` paths using direct `ed25519_dalek` calls; the tool side mirrors them. Both sides implement the spec's security patterns inline: domain-separated integrity hash, length-prefixed canonical bytes, constant-time signature comparison.

**Target.** Route bundle signing + integrity verification through `crate::crypto::Ed25519Scheme::{sign_raw, verify_raw}` (inheriting bd-dwx4l's compat-preserving API). The verifier SDK side may stay direct because it's an externally consumable crate with a more constrained dep surface — that's a design call for the implementer.

**Critical signature-compat consideration.** `.fnbundle` artifacts are designed to be replayable years later. Changing the signature input bytes via the wrapper domain would break every existing bundle. **The migration MUST preserve byte-identical canonical preimages.**

**Two-sided design call.** The SDK crate (`frankenengine-verifier-sdk`) is intentionally minimal and stable. Pulling in `crate::crypto::Ed25519Scheme` would either (a) duplicate the trait in the SDK or (b) add a dep from the SDK to the product crate, which the engine-split contract prohibits. The likely correct outcome: migrate the *tool* side (`tools/replay_bundle.rs`) and leave the SDK side direct, with both sides asserted by `tests/replay_bundle_*_conformance.rs` to produce identical signatures.

**Files to touch.**
- `crates/franken-node/src/tools/replay_bundle.rs` — sign/verify call sites.
- `crates/franken-node/tests/replay_bundle_*.rs` — assert byte-identical canonical preimages between tool side and SDK side.
- Possibly: a new doctest or integration test wiring the SDK and tool sides through a shared key to prove round-trip compat.

**Depends on.** bd-dwx4l (provides the `_raw` API).

**Done when.**
- `cargo build`, `cargo test -p frankenengine-node replay_bundle`, and `cargo test -p frankenengine-verifier-sdk` all pass.
- `tests/replay_bundle_golden_artifacts.rs` and `tests/replay_bundle_integrity_conformance.rs` pass with existing goldens.
- The tool side imports `crate::crypto` for signing; the SDK side may stay independent.

**Pre-commit guard.** Run `rch exec -- cargo test -p frankenengine-node replay_bundle && rch exec -- cargo test -p frankenengine-verifier-sdk`.
close_reason: Shipped via 55799ffc: tools/replay_bundle.rs now routes sign_replay_bundle and verify_replay_bundle_signature through crate::crypto::Ed25519Scheme::{sign_raw,verify_raw} (crates/franken-node/src/tools/replay_bundle.rs:1010-1030 and :1075-1110); picked sign_raw to preserve byte-identity with the pre-migration direct ed25519_dalek path because replay_bundle_signature_payload already prepends REPLAY_BUNDLE_SIGNATURE_PAYLOAD_DOMAIN+length-prefix framing. New regression harness crates/franken-node/tests/replay_bundle_crypto_trait_adoption.rs with three tests (replay_bundle_trait_raw_path_preserves_legacy_signature_bytes, verify_replay_bundle_signature_accepts_trait_routed_sign_output, verify_replay_bundle_signature_rejects_wrapper_domain_signatures) all pass; replay_bundle_metamorphic suite (6/6) confirms byte-stable serde roundtrip. Verifier SDK side (sdk/verifier/src/bundle.rs) intentionally left direct per engine-split contract.

title: Add RCH adapter with worker capability and timeout classification
description:
## Scope
Add a broker adapter for `rch exec -- ...` commands that classifies remote execution outcomes without falling back locally, records worker identity, recognizes SSH timeout/no-local-fallback errors, and probes worker capability drift separately from product failures.

## Implementation Notes
The adapter should wrap only explicitly allowed cargo-heavy validation commands. It must preserve the repo rule that cargo builds/tests go through RCH. It should classify at least: passed, command_failed, compile_failed, test_failed, worker_timeout, worker_missing_toolchain, worker_filesystem_error, local_fallback_refused, contention_deferred, and broker_internal_error.

## Tests and Evidence
Unit tests use deterministic command-output fixtures for `[RCH] remote`, `[RCH-E104] SSH command timed out`, missing toolchain, target-dir rewrite, and local fallback refusal. E2E tests should use a mock-free dry-run/probe mode where possible and store stdout/stderr snippets as digested artifacts.

## Acceptance
A blocked proof bead can cite a broker receipt that says whether the problem is product code, test failure, worker timeout, capability drift, or contention deferral. The adapter never reports a timeout as a product failure and never reports skipped proof as green.

title: [10.11] Integrate canonical scheduler lane and global bulkhead policies (from `10.14` + `10.15`) for product operations.
description:
Master Plan Source: PLAN_TO_CREATE_FRANKEN_NODE.md — Section 10.11 (FrankenSQLite-Inspired Runtime Systems), cross-ref Section 9G.8, 9J.11, 9J.20

## Why This Exists

Product operations in franken_node span a wide range of latency and criticality profiles: real-time cancellation signals, timed migration checkpoints, background anti-entropy sweeps, and bulk trust-state replication. Without explicit scheduler lane discipline and global bulkhead enforcement, a burst of low-priority background work can starve time-critical cancel signals, or a retry storm against a failing remote endpoint can exhaust all available concurrency and cause cascading p99 blowups. Enhancement Map 9G.8 mandates formal scheduler lanes with priority preemption and bulkheads for p99 stability. 9J.11 specifically requires a global remote bulkhead to prevent retry-storm self-DoS, and 9J.20 elevates lane-aware scheduling to a formal product SLA mechanism.

This bead integrates the canonical lane definitions and bulkhead primitives from 10.14 (bd-qlc6 lane mapping, bd-v4l0 global remote bulkhead) and the lane mapping policy from 10.15 (bd-cuut) into the franken_node product service layer, ensuring every async entrypoint is assigned to a named lane and every remote call passes through the global bulkhead.

## What This Must Do

1. Define the product-layer lane taxonomy: `Cancel` (highest priority, preemptive), `Timed` (deadline-aware, e.g., migration checkpoints), `Realtime` (interactive control-plane RPCs), `Background` (anti-entropy, replication, telemetry flush) — adapting the canonical definitions from bd-cuut/bd-qlc6.
2. Implement a `LaneRouter` that assigns every incoming product operation to a lane based on its `CapabilityContext` metadata (Cx-first, per invariant #1 from 8.5), rejecting operations that lack a lane annotation.
3. Integrate the global remote bulkhead (from bd-v4l0) with a configurable `remote_max_in_flight` limit, shared across all lanes, that rejects new remote calls with a structured backpressure signal when capacity is exhausted.
4. Implement per-lane concurrency limits and queue depth bounds, with overflow behavior configurable per lane (reject, enqueue-with-timeout, or shed-oldest for Background lane only).
5. Emit lane utilization metrics: per-lane active count, queue depth, rejection count, and p99 latency — exposed via the telemetry namespace and logged as structured events.
6. Ensure all lane and bulkhead decisions respect cancellation protocol (bd-7om): a cancelled operation immediately releases its lane slot and bulkhead permit.

## Context from Enhancement Maps

- 9G.8: "Scheduler lanes + bulkheads for p99 stability"
- 9J.11: "Global remote bulkhead to prevent retry-storm self-DoS"
- 9J.20: "Lane-aware scheduling as a formal product SLA mechanism"
- Architecture invariant #1 (8.5): Cx-first control — lane assignment must be derived from the capability context, not ambient state.
- Architecture invariant #5 (8.5): Scheduler lane discipline — every async entrypoint must declare its lane.
- Architecture invariant #3 (8.5): Cancellation protocol semantics — cancelled work must release lane/bulkhead resources immediately.

## Dependencies

- Upstream: bd-qlc6 (10.14 lane-aware scheduler classes), bd-v4l0 (10.14 global remote bulkhead), bd-cuut (10.15 lane mapping policy), bd-7om (cancel-drain-finalize protocol)
- Downstream: bd-390 (anti-entropy reconciliation uses Background lane), bd-3hw (remote saga workflows use Realtime lane + bulkhead), bd-1jpo (10.11 section-wide verification gate)

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Every product async entrypoint is annotated with a lane; compile-time or startup-time check rejects unannotated entrypoints.
2. Cancel-lane operations preempt Background-lane operations under contention (demonstrated by test with saturated Background queue).
3. Global remote bulkhead at capacity returns a structured `BulkheadExhausted` error with retry-after hint, not a hang or timeout.
4. Per-lane concurrency limits are enforced: exceeding the limit for Timed lane results in enqueue-with-timeout behavior; exceeding Background limit results in shed-oldest.
5. Lane utilization metrics are emitted at 1-second granularity with fields: `lane_name`, `active_count`, `queue_depth`, `rejected_count`, `p99_latency_ms`.
6. Cancellation of an in-flight operation releases its lane slot within one event-loop tick (verified by test measuring slot release latency).
7. Under a simulated retry storm (1000 concurrent remote calls), the bulkhead caps in-flight to `remote_max_in_flight` and the Cancel lane remains responsive (p99 < 10ms).
8. Verification evidence JSON includes per-lane throughput, rejection rates, bulkhead saturation events, and p99 latency measurements.

## Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests: (a) Lane assignment from CapabilityContext metadata; (b) Rejection of unannotated operations; (c) Per-lane concurrency limit enforcement; (d) Bulkhead permit acquire/release lifecycle; (e) Shed-oldest behavior for Background lane overflow.
- Integration tests: (a) End-to-end request flow through LaneRouter to execution with correct lane accounting; (b) Mixed-lane workload with Cancel-lane preemption verified; (c) Bulkhead integration with actual remote calls (mocked endpoint).
- Adversarial tests: (a) Retry storm: 10x normal remote call rate, verify bulkhead holds and Cancel lane stays responsive; (b) All lanes saturated simultaneously, verify graceful degradation; (c) Rapid cancel/re-submit cycles to test slot release correctness; (d) Bulkhead limit set to 1, verify serialization of remote calls.
- Structured logs: Events use stable codes (FN-LN-001 through FN-LN-010), include `lane_name`, `trace_id`, `operation_type`, `bulkhead_permits_available`. JSON-formatted for machine parsing.

## Expected Artifacts

- docs/specs/section_10_11/bd-lus_contract.md
- crates/franken-node/src/runtime/lane_router.rs (or equivalent module path)
- crates/franken-node/src/runtime/bulkhead.rs (product-layer bulkhead integration)
- scripts/check_scheduler_lanes.py (with --json flag and self_test())
- tests/test_check_scheduler_lanes.py
- artifacts/section_10_11/bd-lus/verification_evidence.json
- artifacts/section_10_11/bd-lus/verification_summary.md

1. Integrate the canonical scheduler lane model from 10.14 + 10.15: all product operations are assigned to one of the defined lanes (e.g., Cancel, Timed, Ready, Background) based on a LanePolicy mapping; operations without an explicit lane assignment default to Background.
2. Each lane has configurable concurrency limits (max_concurrent), priority weight, and preemption rules; the scheduler respects lane isolation such that a saturated Background lane cannot starve Cancel or Timed lanes.
3. A global bulkhead enforces a system-wide max_in_flight limit across all lanes; when the global limit is reached, new operations are rejected with BULKHEAD_OVERLOAD error and backpressure signal rather than silently queuing.
4. Lane configuration is loaded from the same config system (config.rs) and can be updated at runtime via config reload; lane limit changes take effect for newly submitted operations (in-flight operations retain their lane assignment).
5. Priority ordering within a lane follows: Cancel > Timed > Ready > Background. Operations in the Cancel lane are always scheduled first, ensuring cancellation signals are never starved by application work.

title: Epic: Content-addressed validation proof cache and reuse planner
description:
## Background
The validation broker and resource governor now make validation explicit, but large agent swarms still waste time and worker capacity by rerunning equivalent cargo/RCH proofs after the same command, inputs, feature set, and toolchain have already produced a trustworthy receipt. The next accretive step is a content-addressed proof cache that lets agents reuse fresh receipts safely instead of treating every closeout as a new expensive build.

## Idea-Wizard Phase 2/3 Rationale
Best idea after the validation broker: turn command digests, input digests, target-dir policy, feature flags, toolchain, and dirty-state policy into a reusable proof identity. This improves responsiveness for 64+ CPU / 256GB+ RAM swarm deployments because it reduces duplicate remote builds, lets low-priority agents wait on existing proof work, and gives operators deterministic evidence explaining why a cached receipt was trusted or rejected.

Next-best supporting ideas folded into this graph: freshness index, cache hit/miss diagnostics, stale-proof garbage collection, quota-aware disk pressure controls, planner integration, doctor/readiness visibility, and mock-free concurrent stress coverage.

## Goals
Make proof reuse a first-class, fail-closed product capability. Future agents should be able to ask whether a proof already exists, why it is trustworthy, what changed if it is not reusable, and what artifact path proves the decision.

## Non-Goals
Do not replace RCH, CI, or the existing validation broker. Do not trust cached output without validating command/input digests and freshness. Do not silently skip required validation; every reuse decision must emit a receipt or structured rejection.

## Acceptance
The sub-beads must define cache schemas, implement an atomic proof-cache store, integrate it with planner/broker/readiness/closeout surfaces, enforce quota and stale-proof invalidation, and add mock-free concurrent E2E/stress coverage with structured logs. The graph must remain self-contained and acyclic.

title: [10.9] Build verifier economy portal and external attestation publishing flow.
description:
## [10.9] Build verifier economy portal and external attestation publishing flow

### Why This Exists

Section 9H.3 (Verifier Economy Program) envisions a marketplace where external parties can verify franken_node's claims and publish their attestations, creating a trust network that extends beyond the core team. The verifier SDK (10.17) provides the technical tools, but without a portal and publishing flow, external verification remains an isolated activity with no network effect. This bead builds the market-facing surface: a web portal where verifiers register, access toolkits, submit results, and where the public can view a trust scoreboard backed by cryptographic evidence.

### What It Must Do

Build a verifier economy portal and attestation publishing flow:

- **Verifier registration**: External verifiers register via the portal with: identity (organization or individual), verification capabilities (which benchmark dimensions they can verify), and public key for attestation signing. Registration is lightweight (no approval gate for basic verification; advanced verification tiers may require vetting).
- **Verification toolkit access**: Registered verifiers can download: the verification SDK (tooling for running verification suites), replay capsules (deterministic execution recordings that can be independently verified), benchmark datasets, and reference results for comparison.
- **Result submission**: Verifiers submit verification results through a structured API. Submissions include: verifier identity, verification suite executed, raw measurements, computed scores, execution environment description, and a cryptographic signature over the entire result payload.
- **Attestation publishing flow**: Verified claims (results that pass integrity checks and consistency validation) are published as attestations. Each attestation includes: the claim (what was verified), the evidence (measurements and execution trace), the verifier identity, the cryptographic signature, and a timestamp. Attestations are immutable once published.
- **Public trust scoreboard**: A public-facing view showing: aggregate trust scores across all verifiers, individual attestation details, historical score trends, and verifier reputation (based on consistency and coverage of their attestations). The scoreboard is filterable by verification dimension, time range, and verifier.
- **Replay capsule access**: The portal provides access to replay capsules — deterministic execution recordings that allow anyone to independently verify a specific claim. Capsules include: input state, execution trace, output state, and expected result. Capsule integrity is cryptographically verifiable.
- **Anti-gaming measures**: The system must resist: sybil attacks (fake verifiers inflating scores), selective reporting (verifiers only submitting favorable results), and result fabrication (submitting results without actually running verification). Measures include: result consistency cross-checks, execution environment attestation, and statistical anomaly detection.

### Acceptance Criteria

1. Verifier registration flow works end-to-end: register, receive credentials, download toolkit, submit results, see attestation published.
2. Verification toolkit download includes SDK, replay capsules, benchmark datasets, and reference results with integrity hashes.
3. Result submission API validates payload structure, cryptographic signature, and basic consistency before accepting submissions.
4. Published attestations are immutable, cryptographically signed, and include full provenance metadata.
5. Public trust scoreboard displays aggregate scores, individual attestations, and historical trends; data is queryable via API.
6. Replay capsules can be independently executed and produce results matching the published attestation.
7. At least two anti-gaming measures are implemented and tested (sybil resistance and selective reporting detection).
8. Portal API has structured JSON responses throughout; a verification script validates all API endpoints.

### Key Dependencies

- Verifier SDK (10.17) for verification tooling
- Benchmark infrastructure (bd-f5d) for benchmark datasets and scoring
- Replay determinism infrastructure for capsule generation
- Cryptographic signing infrastructure for attestation integrity

### Testing & Logging Requirements

- Unit tests for registration, submission validation, attestation publishing, and anti-gaming checks.

title: [bug] Align packaging profile selection contract with runtime profile parsing
description:
## Problem
`packaging/profiles.toml`, `docs/specs/section_10_6/bd-3kn_contract.md`, `docs/policy/packaging_profiles.md`, and AGENTS all state that `--profile <name>` / `FRANKEN_NODE_PROFILE` select packaging profiles `local`, `dev`, or `enterprise`.

title: Epic: Swarm-scale validation proof coalescer and admission controller
description:
## Background
The content-addressed validation proof cache now lets agents reuse completed validation receipts, but a busy swarm can still waste worker capacity before a receipt exists: many agents can discover the same proof is missing and launch duplicate RCH/cargo validations in parallel. On 64+ CPU / 256GB+ RAM deployments this is still expensive because worker slots, target directories, logs, and human attention are consumed by equivalent in-flight work.

## Idea-Wizard Phase 2/3 Rationale
Best idea after proof-cache completion: add an in-flight proof coalescer and admission controller. Phase 2 generated broader candidates including distributed proof scheduling, adaptive RCH admission, swarm-aware fairness, validation observability, resource caps, stale lease recovery, and operator-facing diagnostics. Winnowing chose this graph because it directly compounds the proof cache: it prevents duplicate work before cached proof exists, then hands completed receipts back into the existing cache/readiness/closeout path.

Next 10 ideas considered and folded in: capacity-aware scheduling, priority inheritance, stale lease fencing, lease replay artifacts, doctor/readiness visibility, Agent Mail handoff text, structured NDJSON event logs, simulation fixtures, fail-closed admission, and deterministic E2E stress coverage.

## Goals
Make validation proof work coalesce across concurrent agents. Equivalent requests should share one authoritative in-flight proof, divergent requests should be admitted or queued based on resource policy, and every decision should explain whether the agent should join, wait, run, retry, or fail closed.

## Non-Goals
Do not replace RCH, the proof cache, Beads, or Agent Mail. Do not trust in-flight leases without freshness/fencing checks. Do not silently skip validation; coalescing only changes who runs the proof and how waiters receive evidence.

## Acceptance
The sub-beads must define the contract, implement an atomic in-flight lease store, add RCH/resource admission policy fixtures, integrate planner/broker decisions, expose readiness/doctor/closeout/log visibility, and add mock-free concurrent E2E stress coverage. All heavy cargo validation must use rch. The bead graph must remain self-contained and acyclic.

title: Fail closed when VEF proof scheduler job registry is full of live jobs
description: Fresh audit found that crates/franken-node/src/vef/proof_scheduler.rs evicts self.jobs.keys().next() whenever MAX_JOBS is reached during enqueue_windows().
